Christa Pike’s failed execution followed other death penalty miscues in Tennessee, which performs just a fraction of the nation’s executions but is now halting them for a second time since 2022, reigniting questions over the state’s handling of capital punishment.

Pike, 50, remained on a ventilator and unconscious at a Nashville-area hospital on Friday, according to her attorneys, who say she was poked with needles at least seven times in the state's death chamber and then hospitalized with burned and blistered arms after being given two doses of lethal drugs.

The unsuccessful attempt was the second failed execution in four months in Tennessee. Since 2022, the state has carried out just four of the more than 140 executions that have taken place nationwide, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Republican Gov. Bill Lee paused executions in the state following the unsuccessful attempt to put Pike to death and ordered an independent investigation into what went wrong, as both critics and supporters of the death penalty called for changes.

“Number one, I think we need to get better people that are doing these executions because I don’t know that they’re trained well enough to be doing this on difficult patients,” said Republican state Sen. Joey Hensley, a family physician, adding that he suspects the IV line was not properly inserted.

Pike's attorneys say executioners failed to properly set IV lines

Days after the attempt to execute Pike, who received two lethal doses of pentobarbital, she had blisters on her arms from the bleach-like, caustic substance that was injected into her body, her attorneys wrote in an emergency court filing on Friday.

Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote.

They wrote that instead of “remedying this failure” prison officials prepared and administered a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.

Tennessee has come under fire before

Pike's case is not the first time Tennessee's execution practices have drawn criticism.

Earlier this year, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after medical workers placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line, proceeding to attempt to place one into his other arm, his left hand and his left foot, then finally failing to establish a central line.

Lee ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute Carruthers again.

Four years before that, the governor ordered an independent review into capital punishment after abruptly stopping the April 2022 execution of Oscar Smith in the 11th hour when officials became aware of a mishandling of the drugs. Lee paused all executions over a week later after acknowledging the state had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were properly tested.

The report he ordered, released in late December 2022, found that the state hadn’t complied with its own lethal injection process since it was revised in 2018.

In that time period, Tennessee put seven inmates to death — two by injection and five in the electric chair. The report said that in none of those, nor in the execution Lee halted, did the pharmacy conduct the required test for endotoxins, and in one of the lethal injections, the drug midazolam was not tested for potency.

At the time, the state's lethal injections were performed through a three-drug series of midazolam, vecuronium bromide and potassium chloride. The state later switched to using just pentobarbital.

The report, conducted by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton, also found that the state’s unidentified executioner had no formal healthcare training and learned the role mainly through on-the-job experience.

After the release of the report, the Tennessee Department of Correction fired its longtime top attorney and another employee.

One of Pike’s attorneys, Steve Ferrell, was skeptical of the progress made since those revelations, saying the investigation resulted in “a less detailed protocol and more secrecy."

Executioners often have little medical training, expert says

It's not uncommon for executioners to have minimal medical training, according to Corinna Lain, a law professor at the University of Richmond and author of a book on lethal injections.

Lain said lethal injection has become more popular because it is considered less gruesome and hides the violence of state killing. But she said that, even when states follow protocol, the method still poses risks. A number of attorneys have echoed those concerns in lawsuits, arguing that the method is unconstitutional.

Lain said she has only found about 10 medically licensed doctors in the entire country who work with states on executions. Doctors she interviewed told her that they believed executions to be contrary to their oath to take care of people.

In many ways, executions are shrouded in secrecy. The identity of execution team members, the details about where and how lethal drugs are procured, and in some states even what happens in the death chamber is hidden from public view.

“Tennessee has botched executions so badly that two people this year have survived their own executions,” Lain said. “That’s quite something."

Still, experts like Jordan Steiker, the co-director of the Capital Punishment Center at the University of Texas, say that the method is likely to continue to be an option for states with the death penalty.

That is in large part, Steiker said, because of a deferential judicial approach to the execution process, which has consistently empowered states to carry out executions.

“I think it gives states confidence that even if they take shortcuts, it’s unlikely that the courts will intervene in their ability to carry out executions,” Steiker said.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has revealed that he is considering retirement, potentially handing President Donald Trump another nomination.

“It’s something that I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term,” the 76-year-old justice told CBS News in a clip from an interview set to air Monday.

“But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place.”

There are already three Trump-nominated justices on the bench — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

open image in gallery Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has revealed that he is considering retirement, potentially handing President Donald Trump another nomination ( AP )

The Supreme Court’s 6-3 conservative lean wouldn’t change if Alito retired and Trump nominated a new justice. But Alito’s retirement would allow Trump to appoint a fourth justice to the court. Alito was nominated by then-President George W. Bush in the fall of 2005 and took his seat on the bench in January 2006.

Trump has lashed out at the Supreme Court for several rulings against him on controversial issues like his sweeping tariff policy and his challenge to birthright citizenship. Alito sided with Trump on those two issues.

The timing of a Supreme Court justice’s retirement is crucial because the party in power can change the court’s political leaning for decades.

Republicans blocked then-President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016 after conservative Justice Antonin Scalia died more than 11 months before Trump would be sworn into office. Trump then replaced Scalia with Gorsuch, who took his seat in April 2017.

While Trump has another two years in office, if Democrats take control of the Senate in November’s midterms, they could make it harder for a potential Alito replacement to be confirmed.

open image in gallery 'It’s something that I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term,' the 76-year-old justice said about retirement in a new interview ( Getty Images )

“You decided not to retire this year despite, I think, some pretty intense pressure from Republicans who thought, ‘Well, Republicans are in control of the Senate, so it would be easier to confirm your replacement,’” CBS News Chief Legal Correspondent Jan Crawford said in her interview with Alito.

When then-Fox Business host Maria Bartiromo asked Trump in April about rumors of Alito stepping down, the president said, “it’d be nice to say now I have somebody for 40 years,” but then praised the justice’s work.

“Justice Alito is an unbelievable justice and a brilliant justice — and he gets the country. He does what’s right for the country,” Trump said.

Alito said in his interview with CBS News that “it’s too hard to predict how, for anybody and particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be a year from now, two years from now and so forth. And it’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.”

North Korea fired at least one ballistic missile toward the sea on Saturday, South Korea’s military said, extending a recent run of weapons tests during heightened tensions between the rivals over border land mine blasts that injured three South Korean soldiers.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the missile being launched from the North’s eastern coastal Wonsan area, but didn’t immediately say how far the weapon flew. Japanese broadcaster NHK reported that the missile likely landed outside the country’s exclusive economic zone.

The South’s joint chiefs said the military stepped up surveillance and vigilance for possible further launches from the North and was closely sharing information with the United States and Japan.

The launch came a day after the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologize over the land mine blasts that South Korea and the U.S.-led United Nations Command said were caused by North Korean mines planted south of the military demarcation line.

South Korea has also called on the North to halt its recent border fortification efforts, including the installation of mines and anti-tank barriers, which have accelerated after Kim Jong Un in 2024 abandoned his government’s long-standing goal of reconciliation with the South and declared Seoul a permanent adversary.

Kim Yo Jong, the leader’s sister and possibly the second-most powerful figure in Pyongyang, dismissed Seoul’s demands over the mine blasts as “utterly pathetic” on Friday, saying the North intends to cut ties with the South forever. In a previous statement, she denied North Korean responsibility for the blasts and threatened to retaliate if South Korea fires on North Korean troops fortifying the border.

Saturday’s launch was the latest in a series of North Korean military displays in recent weeks, including missile tests, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship, as Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his growing nuclear program despite U.S. calls to revive diplomacy. Wonsan was also the site where the North on Sept. 20 tested what state media described as a hypersonic missile system, part of a broad range of weapons North Korea has developed in recent years that are designed to overwhelm missile defenses in the South. Kim has largely abandoned diplomacy with Washington and Seoul since his nuclear negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019, and he has made Moscow the new focus of his foreign policy, sending thousands of troops and large quantities of weapons to support President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine.

Following years of intensified testing, Kim now has an extensive arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles, including long-range weapons potentially capable of reaching the U.S. mainland and shorter-range systems that threaten South Korea and Japan.

Trump in August scaled back a major military exercise with South Korea in an apparent effort to restart diplomacy with Kim, who has condemned such drills as rehearsals for invasion.

North Korea has so far rebuffed Trump’s outreach. It says Washington must first abandon its “hostile policy” — a term Pyongyang has traditionally used to describe U.S.-led sanctions and joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises — and drop denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

Recent heatwaves are allowing disease-carrying ticks to survive for longer periods in the UK, a specialist has warned.

In the past, temperatures were too cool to enable hyalomma ticks to reach full maturity.

Dr Jolyon Medlock, head of medical entomology at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), noted that although cases remain rare, public health authorities are "starting to pick up a bit more".

The hyalomma tick serves as the primary vector for Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, a condition that can prove severe and life-threatening.

These parasites occasionally enter the UK by attaching themselves to birds migrating from Africa and the Mediterranean during their nymph stage.

At this intermediate point in their development, the ticks are approximately the size of a poppy seed.

They transition to adulthood through moulting, a phase where they cast off their hard outer layer.

open image in gallery The virus can incubate anywhere from one to nine days following a tick bite ( Getty/iStock )

Dr Medlock said: “They would normally come in on migratory birds as a nymph, and then fall off, and they wouldn’t be able to moult. It’s not warm enough.

“What we’re seeing now in heatwave years is that they can moult through to the adult stage, and we then could be able to pick up records of adults through our tick surveillance.

“These have happened less than probably five times in the last 10 years or so, but it’s something that we and colleagues across northern Europe are starting to pick up a bit more.

“It doesn’t mean the tick will survive, and it doesn’t necessarily mean it’s an infection risk.”

The UKHSA’s Tick Surveillance Scheme was set up in 2005 to map and monitor ticks across the UK.

Dr Medlock said there have been records of hyalomma nymphs on migratory birds from observatories over the last 50 years.

He added: “In their native area, they’re vectors of Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus, which is a relatively common virus that occurs in the Balkans that started to emerge in Spain recently.

“So these are the sort of climate-sensitive tick-borne disease pathogens that we might see.”

According to the World Health Organisation, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever is endemic in Africa, the Balkans, the Middle East and Asia, with a fatality rate of up to 40 per cent.

The virus can incubate anywhere from one to nine days following a tick bite.

open image in gallery According to the World Health Organisation, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever is endemic in Africa, the Balkans, the Middle East and Asia ( AFP/Getty )

It can also be transmitted through contact with infected animal blood or tissues.

The onset of symptoms is sudden and can include fever, dizziness, neck pain, a headache and sore eyes, as well as nausea, vomiting, mood swings and confusion.

Elsewhere, milder winters and hotter summers may also lead to a “shift in the seasonality” of ticks more broadly in the UK, according to Dr Medlock.

He said: “The simple way of collecting ticks is to go and drag a blanket through the undergrowth, and if it’s a hot, humid day, they’re running around quite quickly.

“If you’ve got mild winters, then they will remain active throughout the winter.

“Usually they say 7C is the critical temperature for activity, I’ve seen them active at 3C.

“So as we have milder winters, and hotter, drier summers, we’ll see a shift in the seasonality of ticks.”

Analysing breast milk could pave the way for earlier diagnoses of breast cancer, according to researchers.

A team at the University of Manchester is assessing whether circulating tumour DNA present in breast milk might identify the disease sooner than standard blood tests or imaging scans.

While breastfeeding is known to reduce long-term breast cancer risk, women face a heightened risk of developing the condition during pregnancy and after giving birth.

Additionally, specific genetic faults leave some women at a higher risk of developing the disease when they are young.

In the UK, breast cancer represents the most common cause of cancer-related death in women aged 35 to 64.

Cases linked to pregnancy are believed to affect roughly one in 3,000 pregnancies, though the risk can reach one in 50 for those at higher risk, such as women carrying a faulty BRCA gen

Dr Niki Flaum, who is leading the study and is a consultant oncologist at the Christie NHS Foundation Trust In Manchester, said: “There is an urgent need to find better, more reliable ways to detect breast cancer in women during and after pregnancy.

“We believe breast milk may provide a unique and non-invasive window into what is happening inside the breast.

“We know surprisingly little about the genetic changes to breast milk, as this bio-fluid has been remarkably under-researched until now.

open image in gallery Scientists are examining whether circulating tumour DNA from cancer, which can show up in breast milk, could identify the disease earlier than a blood test or scan ( Alamy/PA )

“Pregnancy-related breast cancer is more likely to be diagnosed at a later stage, when the cancer has already spread, and survival outcomes are significantly worse compared with women of the same age who have not recently given birth.

“Diagnosis is particularly challenging because breast imaging during pregnancy and lactation is often unreliable.

“If reliable methods for detecting cancer-related DNA in breast milk can be found, we hope future research will test whether this approach could be developed into a screening tool for women with breast cancer or those at high risk.”

The new research, funded by The Christie Charity, is initially recruiting 40 women producing breast milk – 25 with general population risk and 15 from a high-risk category where there is a family history of breast cancer.

The aim is to create a Manchester Breast Biofluid Biobank with more than 200 samples available for future research.

The University of Manchester team will analyse the samples of fluid at the National Biomarker Centre at the Christie.

One of the first mothers to donate breast milk for the study was Hannah Brennan, 31, from Glossop in Derbyshire, who has a 12-month-old girl, Ada, as well as a five-year old daughter and two-year-old son.

A registered midwife, who is studying for a PhD at the University of Manchester, she said: “As soon as I saw the research team were looking to recruit women who were breastfeeding, I wanted to do it.

open image in gallery Breast cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death in women aged 35 to 64 in the UK ( Valerii Apetroaiei - stock.adobe )

“As I’m doing my doctorate, I’m passionate about people being involved in research.

“My paternal grandmother died aged 51 from breast cancer and sadly I never met her. However, I was named after her and I’m told I look like her so I’m doing this for her as well as my two daughters.

“Participating in the study was really straightforward.

“I just gave a blood sample and donated some breast milk and answered a few questions.

“As a midwife I feel it’s really important to help other women, so if my small contribution can benefit other mothers in the future, I’m just glad to be able to make a difference and would encourage other breastfeeding mums to take part.”

Dr Florent Mouliere, who leads the research team analysing samples, said: “Scientists in our laboratories have identified tiny fragments of genetic material shed by cells in some samples of breast milk that have been donated for this study.

“The DNA structure is unique in breast milk, and we now understand what this DNA looks like, which is a major step forward.”

Louise Hadley, chief executive of The Christie Charity, said “We are very pleased to be able to fund this important research which could improve early detection of breast cancer in high-risk women, including BRCA carrier, enable screening specifically for pregnancy-related breast cancer and help predict risk of postpartum breast cancer.

“It would also provide reassurance for high-risk women wishing to breastfeed, who are currently often advised to stop early so MRI screening can resume.

“This support is part of The Christie Charity’s commitment to providing £30 million of much-needed funding by 2030 to enable our brightest researchers to make game-changing discoveries right here in Manchester.

“We are very grateful for the continued support of all our donors in helping us reach this goal.”

The University of Oregon has received five sexual assault reports in the first week of classes — while an Ivy League school on the other side of the country deals with the fallout of an alleged gang rape that was not prosecuted for years.

A lawsuit filed last month by a former Cornell University student who goes by Jane Doe, alleging that she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at the New York school in October 2024, has sparked a national conversation on campus safety and the culture of silence surrounding sexual assault. The case has been reopened, and New York State Attorney General Letitia James has taken it over.

Now, the University of Oregon has alerted students to five new sexual assault cases that occurred on or near campus. The alert went out on Wednesday, two days after classes began.

Four of the reported sexual assaults involved students, and the fifth happened near a park next to university property. All of the cases occurred in the past week, the university said.

open image in gallery The University of Oregon has received five sexual assault reports in the first week of classes — while an Ivy League school on the other side of the country deals with the fallout of an alleged gang rape that was not prosecuted for years ( Getty Images )

Authorities arrested someone in the fifth case, but it’s unclear whether anyone has been arrested in the other four.

While the five sexual assaults are not believed to be related, “several alleged perpetrators may have taken advantage of the fact that the victims were intoxicated at social events,” the University of Oregon said.

When reached for comment, the university said it could not confirm any other details at this time, citing multiple ongoing investigations.

The university told The Independent that it issued the alert, “because we are very concerned to see a pattern of assaults with similar characteristics and wanted to let our campus community know that these have occurred, that investigations are occurring at both the university and law enforcement levels, and most importantly, that our first concern is for survivors and that the university does not tolerate nonconsensual sexual activity in any form.”

open image in gallery The new reports of sexual assault in Oregon follow a lawsuit by a former Cornell University student, alleging that she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at the New York school in October 2024 ( Getty Images )

Newly unsealed documents in Cornell University’s investigation into Jane Doe’s case have revealed how drugs played a role in the alleged gang rape.

One of Jane Doe’s roommates said she overheard the woman tell one of the men, “You had penetrative sex with me. I had so much ketamine, my eyes were crossed, and you still had sex with me,” according to documents obtained by CBS News New York.

In a summary of Jane Doe’s statement to university police that Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten released before he was removed from the case, the woman said she came to the frat house as a “5 out of 10” on a scale of drunkenness and that she became an “8 out of 10” throughout the hours-long ordeal.

She also said she took Ketamine multiple times.

“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me,” Jane Doe said during a May 2025 disciplinary hearing. “It just was a totally debilitating place to be in.”

open image in gallery While the five sexual assaults are not believed to be related, ‘several alleged perpetrators may have taken advantage of the fact that the victims were intoxicated at social events,’ the University of Oregon said ( AFP via Getty Images )

Cornell University has defended its handling of Jane Doe’s case, which ended in expulsions and suspensions.

“Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” Cornell said in a Monday statement.

The school also welcomed the reopening of the case, which could result in criminal prosecution.

For those affected by rape and sexual abuse, if you are in the United States, you can call Rainn on 800-656-HOPE (4673).

Rape Crisis also offers support. You can call them on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, and 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland, or visit their website at www.rapecrisis.org.uk.

The United Arab Emirates has warned the Government it could cancel billions of pounds of investment in the UK over the Premier League’s Manchester City ruling, according to reports.

Emirati officials said “the Premier League’s actions” would “have an influence on the bilateral state relationship”, Bloomberg reported.

The Telegraph said the UAE is threatening to scrap billions of pounds of private investment for a hi-tech Silicon Valley-style hub between Oxford and Cambridge.

The newspaper also reported that Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak met Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, in Downing Street two weeks before the Premier League announced its decision.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham speaks to Manchester City Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak prior to the Vincent Kompany Testimonial at the Etihad Stadium in 2019 ( PA )

On Thursday, Downing Street insisted the guilty verdict against City is “serious”, after Andy Burnham was accused of making a “frankly extraordinary” intervention in support of the football club’s owners.

A No 10 spokesperson issued the statement after the Prime Minister said he would be “really concerned” to see the current owners sell up.

Conservative shadow sport minister Louie French had accused Mr Burnham of “publicly backing the owners” amid a probe into the club’s funding over recent years, describing his comments as “frankly extraordinary”.

The Liberal Democrats called on Burnham to publish all details of his meetings with Manchester City’s owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), and declare all hospitality he has accepted at the Etihad Stadium.

Asked by the BBC earlier this week if he was worried about the current owners selling the club, Mr Burnham said: “I would be really concerned to lose them.

“They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester.

“Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.”

open image in gallery The then Manchester mayor joins Prince Harry at Manchester City's training ground ( PA )

Asked also if his dealings with the club would stand up to scrutiny, he said: “I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad and the campus around it but also into the city – but yes, of course.”

Downing Street was forced to issue two clarifications of his position on Thursday, with a spokesperson for the PM insisting the guilty verdict against Manchester City is “serious”.

Former City and FA chairman David Bernstein said he was “concerned” about Mr Burnham’s comments and the issue was “something that politicians should be seen to be staying well away from”.

City were found guilty of charges related to breaches of financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.

The commission found that the remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

News.title: Bath complete revenge mission on Exeter despite imperious Feyi-Waboso
News.content:
Bath held off a furious Exeter comeback led by the irrepressible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso to avenge their Gallagher Prem semi-final defeat here in June.

It felt as if lightning might strike Bath twice. Once again Exeter overturned a 26-10 half-time deficit, to manufacture a second-half lead thanks to a pair of blistering finishes by Feyi-Waboso. Four months ago, Bath failed to take a drop goal in the closing stages, but this time with the reassuring presence of Finn Russell at fly-half, they kept their cool.

The Scotland playmaker twice sent penalties deep into the Exeter 22 from where Stephen Varney conceded a yellow card and penalty try before Bath replacement Ted Hill powered through a thicket of Exeter tacklers.

“Finn is one of the world’s best 10s in the world and I thought he had a very good game,” Bath head of rugby Johann van Graan said. “His decision making is above most players in the world and I thought that came through tonight.”

Despite the appearance of yet another high-scoring shootout, both teams defended with real bite, although Bath struggled to lay a finger on Feyi-Waboso who ended up in a scrap with a fan in the stands here when he was a spectator in May. He exacted a measure of revenge beating eight defenders and carried for 132 metres.

“Manny still needs game time,” Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter said. “When he’s on the ball, you see something incredible, but it is ability to get on the ball again is just getting his game minutes and match fitness up.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco, which is placed between the cheek and lower gum, is particularly popular in south Asia. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Eight tips for improving your laptop’s performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

News.content:
Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

I knew exactly where I wanted to go, where I needed to go but I needed some guidance. I think the same way as him [Jude]. We don’t think there’s any limit on what we can achieve, wanting to win, wanting to win in a good way by going for the throat. Fearlessness.

I want to stay as far away from that [regret] as possible.

[Did you ever think you would sign for Barcelona?] Yes. No one ever achieves anything in life by playing it safe. My personality is based on being bold, taking risks and going for whatever you want.

At this level we’re all as talented as each other but only the most mentally competitive and driven people can maintain success for a long time.

I always thought in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never respected my quality and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick. In Barcelona if you’re not technical, if you’re not smart, you’d stand out like a sore thumb.

Sports.title: ‘Piece of c***’ – Man Utd flop Fred launches savage attack on former Red Devils boss who ‘fought with Cristiano Ronaldo’
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED flop Fred lambasted former manager Erik ten Hag by dubbing him a “piece of c***.”

The 33-year-old joined United in 2018 from Shakhtar Donetsk and spent five years at Old Trafford playing under the likes of Jose Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Ralf Rangnick and Ten Hag.



The midfielder, who now plays for Atletico Mineiro in his native Brazil, worked with the Dutch tactician for a year until his departure for Fenerbahce in 2023.

Fred was full of praise regarding the ex-Ajax boss’ tactical nous but didn’t hold back when it came to squad management.



He claimed Ten Hag “argued with everyone” and named the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Casemiro and Marcus Rashford among the players the manager fell out with.

The Brazilian also suggested the ex-Bayer Leverkusen boss was “clique-ridden” because he favoured Dutch players.



Fred told the Charla Podcast: “Ten Hag was tactically very good, but with the group he was a piece of c***.

“He argued with everyone. He argued with me, with Cristiano, with Casemiro, with Rashford… he wouldn’t put me in to play, sometimes it got stressful.

“[With Ten Hag] Only his Dutch players played. A clique-ridden coach. But, tactically, one of the best I’ve ever worked with.

“He wanted the team to run, but Cristiano [was already] older. He took Cristiano out [of the starting lineup], and then there was a falling out.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Fred also reminisced on his time with Solskjaer, with whom he worked for three years until the United legend’s dismissal in 2021.

He presented the Norwegian tactician as the exact opposite to Ten Hag.

The central midfielder claimed Solskjaer had great people skills but needed help from his then assistants Kieran McKenna and current Man Utd manager Michael Carrick in the tactical side.

Fred added: “Solskjaer was good with the group, but he was helped [in training] by the assistants. He united the group.”

Sports.title: ‘We tamed a beast’ – Arsenal fans baffled as Viktor Gyokeres breaks Nations League record by scoring again
Sports.content:

ARSENAL fans ruthlessly hit out at boss Mikel Arteta – after Viktor Gyokeres shattered a goalscoring record on international duty.

The striker, 28, has fallen down the Gunners’ pecking order in the early stages of their title defence.



But Gyokeres, who saw the funny side when Manchester City were found guilty of financial breaches, made history after finding the net in Sweden’s 1-1 draw with Bosnia and Herzegovina.

And that meant the Arsenal No14 became the first star to score in SIX consecutive Nations League showdowns.



His clinical finish came after also being on target against Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Estonia, while he hit four when he faced hapless Azerbaijan.

Gyokeres was put through on goal when Alexander Bernhardsson regained possession and he sent a vicious strike beyond Bosnian keeper Salko Hamzic.

SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta refuses to follow Tottenham’s lead as Arsenal unveil Emirates redevelopment plan – but WON’T boost capacity
Sports.content:
Next

ARSENAL have revealed their redevelopment plans for their Emirates Stadium that won’t see the team moving away, like rivals Tottenham did.

The Gunners have spent over two years exploring ways to upgrade their ground, which opened in 2006 and has a capacity of 60,704.



For many years the Premier League giants had the largest club stadium in London until 2019 when bitter foes Spurs built Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which boasts 62,850 seats.

According to The Times, however, the North Londoners have ruled out a significant expansion of the Emirates that would have potentially increased its capacity to a staggering 80,000.



Any significant works would have required a temporary move to an alternative home ground.

Just like Tottenham did when they played at Wembley between 2017 and 2019 while their new state-of-the-art ground was being constructed on the site of the old White Hart Lane.

However, manager Mikel Arteta did not want to disrupt his winning team, which finally won the Premier League again after 22 years, by conceding home advantage.

Therefore, the Gunners have instead opted on the Emirates’ “continued evolution” rather than a grander revamp, citing cost and logistical reasons.

Arsenal issued the following statement: “We shared a commitment to the continued evolution of Emirates Stadium, rather than a huge-scale masterplan, building on improvement we have made to date in partnership with our catering partner, Legends, the introduction of safe standing (this season in the Clock End, and next season in the North Bank), improving hospitality and retail experiences, and upgrading visitor experiences.”

Liverpool have had a similar strategy in expanding Anfield, with capacity rising from 45,000 to over 61,000 in the past decade, without the Reds ever leaving temporarily.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Arsenal added 780 seats in 2018 and digging down to add more would have posed logistical issues around pipework.

And the Premier League champions have found different ways to generate matchday income, which has doubled in the last five seasons to about £154million.

That is partly thanks to their transformation into title contenders as well as their return to the Champions League.

Arsenal are back in action at the Emirates on October 10 against in-form Leeds.

Sports.title: Ballon d’Or winner’s son joins non-league Sholing FC in English seventh tier after spells with Chelsea and Tottenham
Sports.content:
Next

ANDRIY SHEVCHENKO’S son Kristian has completed a shock move to non-league club Sholing after brief spells with Chelsea and Tottenham.

Andriy, 50, will go down in football history having won the Ballon d’Or in 2004 as well as a raft of silverware during a glittering 19-year career playing for AC Milan, Chelsea and Dynamo Kyiv.



The iconic striker led Milan to the Serie A, Coppa Italia and Champions League title during a successful eight-year stint across two spells with the Italian giants.

And although the Ukraine great never managed to live up to expectations at Chelsea between 2006 and 2009, he still picked up an FA Cup and League Cup honour.



Kristian, 19, is hoping to follow into his famous dad’s footsteps – but will have to start at the bottom as he gets his professional career underway with Sholing in England’s seventh division.

The winger looks set to link up with the Southern League outfit ahead of Saturday’s FA Cup third-round qualifier at Ebbsfleet.



Sholing made the following announcement: “Join us in welcoming our new signing, Kristian Shevchenko!

“The 19-year-old joins the Boatmen having developed through the youth setups at Chelsea, Tottenham Hotspur and Watford, signing his first professional contract with the Hornets in 2025.

“Kristian also represented Ukraine at the 2025 U20 World Cup, bringing international youth experience to SO19. Welcome to the Boatmen.”

Kristian started out at Chelsea, where Andriy registered a total of 22 goals and 13 assists in 77 appearances – a far cry from his 175 goals and 46 assists in 322 games with Milan.

The Ukraine Under-20 international moved to Tottenham in 2022 where he spent about a year before moving to Watford.

The forward played across the Hornets’ Under-18s and Under-21s until he signed his first ever professional contract in 2025.

However, Kristian never managed to play for the first team and was released by the Championship club in May.

Sports.title: Booting Man City out of Premier League will backfire like Juventus scandal – here’s how I’d make them pay for cheating
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER CITY should absolutely have the book thrown at them for their part in the biggest scandal in football history.

But the Premier League must be careful not to set itself back 15 years by booting City out and letting another league steal the top spot – the same way Juventus ruined Serie A.



There’s no denying that what the Etihad club have been accused of is a monumental level of cheating, which leaves me questioning every City side I played against.

The teams I faced are some of the best I have ever seen.



But now you have to ask whether they were simply built on years of financial doping.

For that reason, Premier League chiefs need to lay down a marker and scare any team from being able to do anything like this again.



Especially before we start sending a message to young fans that they can do what they want as long as they have the money to fund it.

However, it is a fine balancing act between laying down the law and throwing away years of growth that have made the Premier League the best division in the world.

When I was growing up I used to watch Serie A in awe of the quality of football, the competitive nature and – above all else – the star-studded squads.

Juventus’ match-fixing scandal of 2006 changed that and the Italian league is now far inferior to the English top flight.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Juve were kicked out of Serie A and made to play in the second tier, while the reputation of Italian football was in the gutter and the league was set back 20 years.

If the Premier League is not careful, the same thing will happen over here.

Relegating City would mean a mass exodus of their players, likely leaving to go abroad since the club will surely be unwilling to sell them to their domestic rivals.

That can only strengthen the rest of Europe, paving the way for LaLiga or the Bundesliga to pip the Premier League to the throne as the best league.

Imagine losing Erling Haaland to Barcelona or Real Madrid.



The Norwegian has brought a whole new audience to the Premier League after his World Cup exploits and they would surely follow him to Spain.

Serie A used to have stars like Ronaldo, Zinedine Zidane and Diego Maradona, but that level has dropped significantly.

Now Juventus are giving minutes to players like Lloyd Kelly, who – with all due respect – should never be able to represent a club of that stature after his time at Bournemouth and Newcastle.

Too hefty a punishment could also see the Premier League lose its competitive edge – the very thing that makes it so attractive to players and viewers.



Arsenal look miles ahead of the rest of the league with Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester United and Tottenham all in periods of transition.

Mikel Arteta’s side could very well win five titles on the bounce and completely kill the competitive nature of the division.

I am sure that would be music to the ears of Arsenal fans but the truth is it would make the Premier League look more like Ligue 1.

It is Paris Saint-Germain’s persistent dominance in the French top-flight that sees the division labelled as a “farmers’ league”, we can’t have that reputation over here too.

Expelling City from the Premier League or handing them such a hefty points deduction that relegation is inevitable seems like the wrong decision.



Instead I think they should be consigned to mid-table mediocrity by hitting them with a 30-point deduction for five consecutive seasons, as well as a three-year transfer ban and a mammoth fine.

That would kill their development and stop them from being able to compete for the league.

What are Man City charged with? THE Premier League claim Man City hid £900m in 'sham' deals across a nine-year period. They were found guilty on 114 of the initial 115 charges – with the number now up to 130 charges – which fit into six categories… Failing to give accurate financial information over sponsorship revenue, related parties and operating costs between 2009-10 and 2017/18. Total charges: 50

Failing to provide full details of managerial remuneration between 2009/10 and 2012/13. Total charges 8

Failing to provide full details of player remuneration between 2010/11 and 2015/16. Total charges 12

Failing to comply with Uefa Licencing and Financial Fair Play regulations between 2013/14 and 2017/18. Total charges 5

Breaching Premier League Profitability and Sustainability rules between 2015/16 and 2017/18. Total charges 25

Failing to co-operate with the Premier League investigation between 2018/19 and 2022/23. Total charges 30

Total charges: 130

Even Champions League qualification would be out of reach barring a repeat of Pep Guardiola’s centurion season.

We don’t need to mess about with retrospective punishments either, nobody should be asking for City’s titles to be handed to second place.



I was on the receiving end of a 6-0 spanking with Watford at the hands of City in the 2019 FA Cup final.

Those players earned that trophy and, even if there was some dodgy dealing going on above their paygrade, they beat us on the day fair and square.

We could have played that City team another 70 times and we might have won once if we were lucky. That was the best City team I have ever seen.

What the players have done on the pitch can’t be taken away from them – that is what sport is all about.

RECOMMENDED STORIES



We can go round in circles about what the best punishment should be and what is fair but the whole thing is a s***show from top to bottom with endless ramifications.

The most important thing is making sure that City are punished but at the same time ensuring we don’t let this all ruin the product we have in the English game.

Sports.title: Man City’s appeal against Premier League’s guilty verdict already hit with major blow – from their own sponsor Etihad
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER CITY’S appeal against their guilty verdict may have already been undermined — by their own major sponsor.

The crisis club yesterday confirmed they have lodged their appeal over the financial wrongdoing and took another swipe at the Premier League.



But on a day when the FA warned they could also take action, City’s vow to overturn the damning decision looked increasingly in doubt.

They are pinning their hopes on the claim that £830 million in top-up payments to sponsorship deals were made by the Abu Dhabi government — rather than City’s owners — over a nine-year period.



But it emerged Etihad themselves appeared to contradict that stance in a 2015 testimony to the United States authorities — when the Department of Commerce, Transportation and State investigated state-owned airlines.

The US Department of Commerce, Transportation and State were investigating state-owned airlines.

Etihad directly addressed the question of their sponsorship of City’s shirts and stadium.

The firm’s submission said: “The assertion that the Abu Dhabi government paid for Etihad’s sponsorship of English Premier League football club Manchester City is false.”

Etihad later added: “We are government-owned and have been since our founding.

“We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Etihad would be in huge trouble if they misled a US government enquiry and were found to have since altered their version of events.

The independent commission described City’s commercial agreements as “shams” with owners the Abu Dhabi United Group providing £830m of the £950m supposedly from sponsors.

Any hope of winning an appeal look to be on shaky ground in light of the revelations — but City are in no mood to throw in the towel.

City chief executive Ferran Soriano claimed the club have “irrefutable evidence” proving their innocence.

City feel the statement in 2015 strengthens rather than undermines the case.



They will insist the funding was part of the airline’s “liquidity” — so the government did not pay City directly on behalf of Etihad.

The club took another swipe at the Prem as they confirmed the appeal, branding the guilty verdict of the independent commission an “opinion”.

TThe club said in their latest statement the ruling ‘contained clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe’.

City said: “At 7pm on Thursday, the club lodged its comprehensive appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Committee in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter.

“The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.”



There was a fresh concern for City as the FA did not rule out taking action themselves – saying they will continue to monitor developments.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The FA said yesterday: “The Independent Commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game.

“We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.”

Sports.content:

RANGERS co-owner Jed York has broken his silence following his prostitution bust – as the NFL slapped him with a huge fine and ban.

We previously told you how the dad-of-two, 46, was nicked at the Wheat Hill Mobile Home Community in East Palestine, Ohio.



Cops said the San Francisco 49ers supremo had arranged to meet with a woman before being stopped by human trafficking task force agents.

Officers in the village were assisting the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force when they arrested the Rangers co-owner.



He was then locked up at the Columbiana County Jail before appearing in court.

It was revealed in late August that the NFL would be opening an investigation into the San Franciso 49ers owner



And now they have dished out a SIX game ban for regular season games and also hit the 46-year-old with a $500,000 for violating the personal-conduct policy.

In a statement released by the NFL, York said: “Today, the NFL concluded its review, and I accept its decision in full.

“To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of the San Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry.

“This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility.



“What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family.

OUR BEST FREE BETS & SIGN-UP OFFERS

“While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one’s failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better.

“Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don’t take lightly.

“Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead.”

York was a key figure in the 49ers’ takeover at Rangers.



49ers Enterprises, the investment wing of the NFL giants, bought 51 per cent of the Ibrox side in a multi-million pound takeover after months of crucial talks.

York is a lead man in the investment side of the business – that also owns English Premier League outfit Leeds United – and was even named on Rangers’ website after the megabucks deal confirming Andrew Cavenagh as chairman and 49ers Enterprises chief Paraag Marathe as vice chair.

Sports.title: Wade and Aspinall make statement ahead of World Grand Prix semi-finals
Sports.content:
James Wade and Nathan Aspinall put in statement performances that will have made their semi-final opponents take note ahead of a mouthwatering Saturday night line-up at the World Grand Prix.

Aspinall threatened to set a new tournament record average when storming to a 3-0 win over Ryan Joyce, his 105.15 mark ultimately landing as the fourth-highest in history and the best-ever in a quarter-final.

Wade, meanwhile, dropped only one leg as he, in his words, "bashed up" world No 2 Gian van Veen in a match that lasted little more than 20 minutes.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player James Wade felt Gian van Veen was ‘pretty poor’ in their World Grand Prix Darts quarter-final, so he ‘bashed him up’!

"That really was a performance to remember from Wade," Sky Sports' Wayne Mardle said. "From start to finish, he was absolutely devastating. World Class."

Three-time world champion John Part concurred with that assesment, saying: "James is not just looking like a great dart thrower to me, he's looking like a winner.

"I really have a lot of faith in James managing the other players, and that's what winners do. They see what they have to work with, and work against.

"At the start of the match, James saw his opponent struggling and put his foot down to get the job done.

"I think he's a legitimate title contender here."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player It’s not often you see both a fly and a spider grace the darts board on the same night, which is exactly what happened during the quarter-finals of the World Grand Prix Darts.

Humphries 'disappointed' despite clinching semi-final spot

Wade will face former world No 1 Luke Humphries in the final four, who was, by contrast, far from convincing despite the 3-0 scoreline from his quarter-final victory over debutant Neils Zonneveld.

Humphries averaged 85.91, the same as the Dutchmand, but his clutch doubling ultimately proved the difference as the 2023 champion reached the final four for a fourth-straight year.

Image: Luke Humphries won 3-0 in his quarter-final against Neils Zonneveld despite being 'dissapointed' with how he played

Despite that, Humphries told Sky Sports afterwards: "I'm really disappointed. I felt really good in practice, but I came out here tonight and it didn't feel great to be honest.

"It kind of felt like I was the second-best player for the first two sets, but I got away with it.

"It's one of those performances where you're not thrilled, but I won 3-0.

"Hopefully tomorrow night is a lot better, because if it isn't I won't be here on Sunday."

Humphries added on his semi-final opponent: "James [Wade] is a tough task in itself. He's a tough player to play against.

"If I score the way I know I can, then it will be a tough night for James. If I don't, it's going to be a tough night for myself."

Aspinall thrilled by 'one of carrer-best performances'

Aspinall will face Price in Saturday's other semi-final after The Iceman came back from two sets down to beat Jonny Clayton in an all-Welsh affair, surving three match darts before edging the contest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gerwyn Price snatched victory from the jaws of defeat as compatriot Jonny Clayton missed three match darts in their quarter-final of the World Grand Prix Darts

But it's Aspinall who is feeling particularly bullish going into a repeat of the 2022 semi-final, which The Asp won as he finished runner-up to Michael van Gerwen that year.

Aspinall's last major title came at the World Matchplay in 2023, but he's ready to change that.

"I feel like I can win this tournament, and I feel like I'm ready to win another major again. There's no reason why I can't," Aspinall told Sky Sports after his stunning quarter-final win over Joyce.

"I'm absolutely buzzing. All day I've felt so relaxed. I turned up tonight and felt so focussed.

"I'm really happy with that performance. My starting, my finishing, my 180s - it's probably one of my best performances ever on stage for my whole career."

Sports.title: Brown scores twice as Northen Ireland cruise to win over Ukraine
Sports.content:
Ciaron Brown's first international goals came as a pair to help a young Northern Ireland side stun Ukraine 3-0 and go clear at the top of Nations League Group B2.

Brown, the only player in Michael O'Neill's starting line-up over the age of 24, scrambled in early on before Isaac Price doubled the lead in the 22nd minute at the Stadion Antona Malatinskeho in Trnava, Slovakia.

Brown's second then came in bizarre fashion just after the hour - the 28-year-old Oxford defender went up to flick on Pierce Charles' free-kick from inside the Northern Ireland half and Ukraine goalkeeper Dmytro Riznyk let the bouncing ball through his legs.

On paper this was the hardest game in the group, away to a side ranked 37 places above Northern Ireland, but they brushed Ukraine aside to move on to seven points from their opening three games since returning to their second tier, still yet to concede going into Monday's game with Georgia in Belfast.

This was the first competitive meeting with Ukraine since Northern Ireland's famous 2-0 win at Euro 2016, and they delivered a performance which will have fans believing a major tournament beckons for this new generation.

O'Neill made three changes from Monday's goalless draw against Hungary - one enforced with Ethan Galbraith one of two players, Callum Marshall the other, absent for personal reasons.

Justin Devenny and Patrick Kelly also dropped out as Brodie Spencer, Terry Devlin and teenager Kieran Morrison came in, with the 19-year-old Morrison, on loan at Sheffield Wednesday from Liverpool, helping to bring the average age down to a flat 22, Northern Ireland's youngest post-war starting XI.

A positive start from Northern Ireland was quickly rewarded as Morrison floated a corner to the back post where Ruairi McConville headed it back for Brown, earning his 33rd cap, to prod home despite the desperate efforts of Illia Zabarnyi on the line.

Ukraine bossed the ball but struggled to break down Northern Ireland. Georgiy Sudakov was the first to get a sight of goal but his 19th-minute effort was straight at Charles.

Moments later Northern Ireland doubled their lead. As they countered, Morrison's first-time ball into the box was met powerfully by Price at the back post - giving Morrison an assist in his first competitive international.

Charles clawed away a powerful strike from Eduard Sarapii, but although Northern Ireland were needing to do a lot of defending, a Ukraine side sporting 10 changes for a second straight match created few clear chances.

Mykola Matviyenko threatened less than two minutes after the restart but that was a false dawn for the hosts, who found themselves three down thanks to Riznyk's horror moment in the 61st minute, with Brown's header trickling over the line.

Ukraine substitute Matvii Ponomarenko hit the outside of the post but a shellshocked Ukraine side rarely looked like getting back into it.

Late on Ceadach O'Neill came off the bench to make his fourth Northern Ireland appearance, ending any discussion of a possible switch to the Republic of Ireland for the Arsenal teenager.

Sports.title: NFL London: 651-day wait over... Sauce's Colts go globe-trotting again
Sports.content:
Sauce Gardner just ended a 651-day wait for an NFL win in the United States. Now the Indianapolis Colts cornerback is back on international soil.

The Colts clinched their first victory of the campaign in Week Three as they beat the Houston Texans 19-17, before which Gardner's last win in the U.S. came on December 15, 2024 during his time with the New York Jets.

Gardner was traded to the Colts in November 2025, his only win after that coming against the Atlanta Falcons in Berlin before Indianapolis lost their final seven games of the season.

He returns to Europe once again this week as the Colts face the Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, live on Sky Sports NFL.

"The crazy thing I was saying to [team-mate] Josh Downs is imagine we had lost that game in the States, and then ended up playing international, win international but lose in the States. That was giving me a lot of pain," Gardner told Sky Sports.

Colts offensive tackle Bernhard Raimann was in attendance as a teenage fan for his first live NFL game at Wembley Stadium back in 2013. The Austrian now returns to London as a player in awe of his own career journey.

"Back then, I just started playing football," Raimann told reporters on Friday. "We took this trip with the club team that I was playing for and back then I was just a kid, just getting into football.

"And you know, I thought those guys on the field were like freaking superheroes. I mean that was an unbelievable experience. So yeah, so now being back here and getting to play and knowing what it means to the people here, it's just, it's extremely special for me

"I really hope that some kids can see me and listen to my story or see what's possible and hopefully they can embrace their dreams and keep working every day and shoot, see what happens."

Sunday's game represents the first of three successive London matchups in October, while featuring as part of a record nine international games this season following the NFL's debut in both Melbourne and Rio de Janeiro.

It arrives as the latest indication of the NFL's commitment to global growth, the Commissioner Roger Goodell having repeatedly alluded to the ambition of 16 international games per season.

"I love traveling , so if I could play overseas games every single week, I would," said Colts safety Cam Bynum.

"But I think the only downfall is not having your typical routine as far as your bodywork people, whether you do acupuncture, massage therapist, that's probably the hardest thing, being able to get out of your routine. Because normally my Thursday, I'm having acupuncture and my person will fly to Indy to go to work on me.

"Then Friday I have a specific different massage therapists that will work on me that day. So I think the hardest thing is your routine with your bodywork, but everything else we'll figure out with the sleep, lack of sleep. Our night of sleep was the plane ride, and that was only six hours, so it wasn't that much sleep. But at the end of the day we both had to do it, both teams had to go through a flight and so it's an even playing field at the end of the day."

Still, for all its challenges, football overseas appears to be embraced by many granted the chance to ply their trade beyond the borders of the US.

Colts running back Jonathan Taylor arrives as one of the chief attractions and legitimate stars of the league, having led the league with 18 rushing touchdowns from his 1,585 yards on the ground.

"So we'd play on Thanksgiving Day every year and in my senior year, it was a thousand people there, and that was the largest...that's the largest crowd I'd ever been in and played in front of.

"So to go from that to the University of Wisconsin, to now in Indianapolis, and then like you mentioned, international, it's just the most amazing feeling in the world. I don't take it for granted at all."

The Commanders come into Sunday fresh from their upset win over the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks, with Marcus Mariota primed to start at quarterback again in place of the injured Jayden Daniels.

Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs had looked set to be at his disposal, though the former was ruled questionable on Friday due to a hamstring issue.

"Terry McLaurin, he's a fast kid," said Gardner. "He's got a lot of speed, explosiveness and things like that.

"Stefon is also a playmaker. Diggs don't have McLaurin's speed, but he's very smart. He's got great hands, he's able to create separation."

Shane Steichen's side swerved the prospect of starting the season 0-3 with last weekend's win after dropping their opening two games against the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs.

"A win can change the whole energy, everything," said Gardner. "It might not sound like it, but it's a huge difference between 1-2 and 0-3.

"We didn't win the Chiefs game, but it was very close. It's not something that we're going to be like, it's going to be very close, but it's something that was like, if we're this close, we've got to win the next one.

"We should have won that game. We don't have no choice, but we've got to win this one."
