Sports.title: Watching Lee Carsley's England's U21s is a breath of fresh air and they will embrace the target on their backs in pursuit of a historic Euros three-peat next summer
Sports.content:
England men's U21s qualified for next summer's European Championships with a game to spare after their goalless draw against Slovakia.

The reigning champions are seeking their third consecutive European crown under manager Lee Carsley and sealed qualification undefeated, winning seven and drawing two of their nine fixtures.

They now head to Ireland next week, with Carsley saying emphatically at full time that he 'definitely' does not plan to mix things up in a bid to secure a perfect record.

Daily Mail Sport football reporter Tara Anson-Walsh was at Stoke City's Bet365 Stadium to bring you the things we learned…

1. Most importantly, get the job done

Carsley can sleep easy tonight knowing the first obstacle has been cleared on the road to a historic Euros three-peat with England's U21s.

Qualification? Check. Goals? Plenty of them. Fun? Well, based on England's journey through this qualifying campaign, it certainly looks like it.

Lee Carsley can sleep easy tonight after England U21s secured qualification for next year's Euros

England found the back of the net 22 times in their previous eight qualifying matches, and the beauty of this side is that goals can come from virtually anywhere.

Against Kazakhstan last week, centre backs Josh Acheampong and Max Alleyne got on the scoresheet before Middlesbrough striker Will Lankshear sealed the victory.

With four goals scored in three of their previous four matches, confidence was sky high. 'Every time I step on the pitch I believe I'm going to score,' Lankshear said after that game.

There was something slightly ironic, then, that England's first match without a goal was the one that simultaneously secured their place at next summer's tournament.

In front of 8,313 fans at Stoke City's Bet365 Stadium, England knocked on the door all evening but simply could not find a breakthrough.

Lankshear came closest. Fresh from scoring on his debut, the Middlesbrough striker twice escaped his marker at the back post but could not keep his headers on target.

There was frustration at full time after 16 shots at goal failed to find the back of the net, but Carsley was quick to remind his squad that qualification was the priority.

'They were very frustrated at the end of the game, but I made the point to them that to play in a major competition it's the story of a season, not just one game,' he said.

'They've put themselves in a great position now to do something no other country has done before in terms of potentially winning the tournament for a third time, so it's exciting times.'

2. Carsley leads the charge

It is worth a quick reminder that England went 39 years without winning this tournament before retaining it at the first time of asking last year.

The quality and depth of young talent available to Carsley is jaw-dropping, but the England boss has also played a significant role in creating the environment that allows those players to flourish.

Carsley's importance to this team's success cannot be overstated, though he would probably be the last person to say so.

Asked last week how he maintained continuity despite the constant turnover that comes with Under21 football, he instead praised the mentality of his players, particularly their ability to stay ready even when they might 'think it's not going to be their day'.

Will Lankshear had been freescoring before drawing a blank against Slovakia in Stoke on Friday

Manchester City's Rico Lewis and his team-mates knocked on the door all night but could not find the back of the net

Watching Carsley's England is a breath of fresh air. The shackles are off, and this is a team that wants to dominate possession, move the ball quickly and attack.

England had 69 per cent possession against Slovakia and registered 16 shots to their opponents' four. Against Kazakhstan, they enjoyed 81 per cent of the ball. Before that, they recorded 74 per cent possession against Moldova.

They have dominated this qualifying group from start to finish, with a 1-1 draw against Andorra and this one against Slovakia the only mild blemishes on an otherwise outstanding campaign.

No wonder they are embracing the target on their backs heading into next summer.

3. England tie up loose ends with Alleyne the man of the hour

Slovakia, sitting second in the group, should have posed a sterner test than bottom-placed Kazakhstan.

But unlike against Kazakhstan, where England conceded twice through lapses in concentration and Carsley admitted they would need to 'play better if we're going to be a serious team', they were far more assured against a stronger Slovakian side.

At the heart of that defensive display was Max Alleyne.

The Burnley centre-back, on loan from Manchester City, delivered another assured performance and the numbers backed it up.

Four tackles made and four tackles won. Four interceptions. Six of eight duels won. Eleven recoveries.

'He was outstanding,' Carsley said. 'There was once or twice in the first half where they counterattacked, one-v-one and Max cleaned it up. We shouldn't be in that position, but it was only because of Max's outstanding attributes that we got away with that.

'I thought Max, Ash (Phillips), Josh (Acheampong) and Rico (Lewis) were outstanding tonight. The concentration is something that we have to be better at in terms of Under 21s.

'Generally, when they perform with their senior teams, they've got older, more experienced players around them that are constantly talking them through the game. But they really stood up for themselves tonight. As forward-thinking as we were, I thought we were solid at the back.'

Sports.title: Revealed: Man City's claim that 'sham' sponsorship deals were funded by Abu Dhabi government was DENIED by Etihad to a US investigation in 2015
Sports.content:
Revealed: Man City's claim that 'sham' sponsorship deals were funded by Abu Dhabi government was DENIED by Etihad to a US investigation in 2015

One of Manchester City's key defences in their case against breaching the Premier League's financial rules could be in tatters after previous statements made by their main sponsor came to light.

City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 charges, many of which allege City cooked the books to the tune of nearly £900million through money artificially pumped into the club by their Abu Dhabi owners over a nine-year period.

An appeal was confirmed by the club on Friday, with much of their defence suggesting commercial contracts were paid for by the Abu Dhabi government rather than their owner.

Now, though, it has emerged that sponsors Etihad, the state-owned national airline of the United Arab Emirates, told the United States' department of commerce, transportation and state in 2015 that suggestions the government have paid for sponsorships are 'false'.

The statement was made as part of an investigation into state-owned airlines. It read: 'We are government-owned and have been since our founding. We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government, and that we are financed through a combination of equity, shareholder and commercial loans.

'Our shareholder's equity and loans are not subsidies under any applicable definition; they are the means by which the Abu Dhabi government has sensibly invested in a successful business model.'

A key defence around Manchester City's appeal against the Premier League could be in tatters after a previous statement emerged

New Premier League rules state that a hearing must be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing, which can only last five days, concluding. Any punishment could, therefore, be imposed this season.

City claim they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that they have worked within rules in the form of bank statements and witness accounts.

They said in a statement on Friday: 'The club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

'The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.'

The club's 'disguised funding' process – where the ownership group was topping up commercial partnerships to the tune of £830.69million – it found, allowed them to illegally sign the players that ushered in an era of success at the Etihad Stadium.

However, those with knowledge of the situation claim that City's argument is that the monies were actually paid by the government, which owns the sponsors, rather than the club's owners Abu Dhabi United Group – a private company owned by Sheikh Mansour – and as such, no rules were broken.

Sponsorship deals with government-funded companies are commonplace throughout the Premier League, particularly in the case of airlines, and are not banned.

Thomas Tuchel has admitted England's Man City players are anxious following the revelation

Thomas Tuchel, meanwhile, has revealed that England's Manchester City stars Marc Guehi, Elliot Anderson and Nico O'Reilly are worried for their immediate futures after this week's bombshell guilty verdict for breaching financial rules.

The trio have been inundated with calls and messages over the past week, with O'Reilly now having flown back to Manchester for treatment on an injury.

'Are they worried or are they concerned? I think that would be a very human reaction if you don't know what's going on for the club that you signed,' Tuchel said.

'They're still young. They're ambitious. They're told they are totally innocent and don't know what's going on.

'We speak about it at dinner and at a table of eight or 12 people. Of course, we speak about it at breakfast.'

Tuchel – whose side face Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday afternoon - claimed that the news around City being found guilty of the vast majority of charges had represented a 'distraction' before then clarifying that the City trio had been focused in meetings and training sessions.

'It's a big topic in camp,' he added. 'We had some time off between the matches and it is a big subject. How can it not be a topic? We talk with them but only briefly.'

The Football Association are also 'carefully considering' the implications of the findings into City's breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

A statement from the FA read: 'The independent commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game. We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

'As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely.'

Sports.title: A parallel universe where Man City didn't cheat: Brendan Rodgers has a statue outside Anfield - but is it Jurgen Klopp's heavy metal football or a Pep Guardiola dynasty at Man United?
Sports.content:
On a wet and windy Sunday afternoon a week from now, supporters of Liverpool and Manchester City will make their way across Stanley Park towards Anfield. Home fans will pose for selfies under the Shankly Gates before heading towards the turnstiles, wrapped up tight against the elements, pints and chips in hand, and cast an adoring eye at the bronze statues of legends that forever live in their hearts.

John Houlding, just outside the Main Stand. Bill Shankly, by the Kop. The one of Bob Paisley in Paisley Square and then, of course, that beautiful little one of Brendan Rodgers clutching the Premier League trophy just outside the club shop. The man who finally, after 24 long years, ended Liverpool's wait for the title.

In this world, in this life, Manchester City never cooked the books. They never inflated their revenue with sham sponsorship agreements over the course of nearly a decade to the tune of £900million. They never paid a manager with a secret second contract. They just, quite simply, played by the rules.

Had they done so, English football would look a whole lot different. Ever since the damning guilty verdict landed this week – one they are appealing – we have all gone through those silverware seasons, scratched out the trophies and titles, and worked out who might have triumphed instead. Congratulations, Tony Pulis on your FA Cup, thoroughly deserved.

But what we will never, really, know is how the entire landscape of would have shifted. What futures did all that money prevent? What legends did it stop from being forged?

In the aftermath of the verdict, a lot of the focus has been on heralding the even greater genius of Jurgen Klopp. How far he pushed that City side, finishing second twice on 90+ points, and how, in a clean world, the German is the one heralded as the most influential manager in recent Premier League history. Is it his style of play, not Pep Guardiola's, that shapes a generation of our game?

Brendan Rodgers would have won the Premier League title with Liverpool has Manchester City not cheated - though they deny doing so

Klopp joked recently that if Liverpool ended up with their open-top bus parade after all, then he'd be there.

Only, that's the thing. Would he have been there at all? If City aren't the artificially inflated force they were, if Steven Gerrard's slip doesn't cost Liverpool the title, if Rodgers sees them over the line in 2013-14 then does Klopp ever end up at Liverpool?

Rodgers is the hero now. He's the man who builds his Liverpool dynasty instead of being sacked within 18 months. He shapes the club in his image. He gets the murals. He gets the statue.

Klopp once said he had no interest in having one until after he was dead. Rodgers, you imagine, may have taken a different approach.

But this is the issue with City's cheating. As soon as you start to follow one new branch of reality, trying to undo tainted history, it entangles all the infinite others that could just as easily have arisen.

What of Arsenal? The Gunners welcome Leeds to the Emirates Stadium next Saturday. Mikel Arteta is in the dugout, of course, four games into his ninth full season in charge. He replaced Arsene Wenger, after all, following the Frenchman's retirement in 2018. Before that, the former Arsenal skipper led the club's academy side for two years following his own retirement after Wenger offered him the role as part of the club's succession plan.

Arteta never learns his coaching craft from Guardiola. If City could only spend what they were allowed, they don't build the foundations (or the fortune) to entice him. They had two Premier League titles by the time he arrived in our world, in this one they don't have any. Neither, probably, do Arsenal, since 2004.

Meanwhile, Vincent Kompany stands in the away dugout at Anfield. A City hero, signed before the takeover as a 22-year-old who developed into a superstar, won them a couple of League Cups, before making his mega money move to a European giant when he felt he'd taken the club as far as he could. But his heart was blue and he always promised he'd come back one day.

Tony Pulis would have won the FA Cup with Stoke City after they lost to City in the 2011 final

It's certainly not Enzo Maresca, who never got to work with Guardiola at City either.

What is unclear, though, is which Manchester United hosts Tottenham next weekend. It might be the one that Klopp inherited in 2016 instead of Jose Mourinho. Alex Ferguson always considered him as potential successor but, back then, Klopp stayed loyal to Borussia Dortmund. They got their man eventually and, even if they did have to endure Louis Van Gaal, Klopp brought his heavy metal football to Old Trafford and the music hasn't stopped since.

Only, it's not that United actually. Because City weren't cheating, Martin Tyler never got his Sergio Aguerrrooo moment and Sir Alex Ferguson bagged his 20th title a year early. Without the fire fuelled inside him to win it back from the Noisy Neighbours, he calls it a day. David Moyes gets a better crack at the job he was chosen for.

Oh, sorry, Moyes didn't get the job at all, did he? Guardiola got it. Silly me.

Ferguson and Guardiola met for dinner in New York in 2012 where the former United boss says he urged Guardiola, on sabbatical after leaving Barcelona, to call him before taking another job. By the time Fergie left United, Guardiola had already agreed to join Bayern Munich.

Not now. With Ferguson now retired a year earlier, Guardiola builds his dynasty at Old Trafford. The Guardiolafication of English football happens even earlier. United remain the dominant force and while we can no longer congratulate Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer for their titles in 2018 and 2021, it doesn't matter. They won it all under Guardiola anyway.

You see, it doesn't matter at which thread of history you start to unpick, it all soon begins to unravel.

Take Leicester, for example. For two successive seasons between 2019 and 2021 they finished fifth and missed out on the Champions League on the final day. Now, they're in League One. So much of their subsequent decline, and complete mismanagement, stems from that as they began to act – and spend – like a Champions League club despite not being one, nor having the funds to do so, and breaking rules themselves in the process.

So, in this new life, surely, they make it. They bank the millions and, perhaps, establish themselves among the elite. They host Everton next weekend but Eddie Howe will have to mix up his selection with Champions League duty a few days later.

Jurgen Klopp (right) may never have gone to Liverpool at all, and may have ended up at Man United - or maybe it would have been Pep Guardiola (centre)

Only, they don't make it. Because Rodgers never goes there and Leicester don't make the leap. He's no longer a manager trying to get his foot back on to the Premier League ladder. He's a man with a statue that's probably either England manager by now or coaching Barcelona and doing all his team talks in Spanish.

All of these new alternate realities are before you even consider how the star names behind City's now asterisked triumphs become scattered in a different life.

Chelsea finally got John Stones as their long-term John Terry successor after multiple failed bids. David Silva joined them, too, years earlier at a club the midfielder once described as 'where I could fulfil my ambition'. He sure does.

Kevin De Bruyne flourishes under Guardiola at United. Raheem Sterling is already a title winner at Liverpool and enjoys a very different career under Rodgers at Liverpool.

Tottenham met Aguero's release clause at Atletico Madrid six months before he moved to City only for the bid to be rejected but, in this life, they get him in the end. Oh, wait, what does that do to Harry Kane's career?

And so another domino falls. Another rabbit hole to go down. In many ways, it is these endless ripples and repercussions that lie at the heart of why City's systemic cheating leaves such a stain on the game. Not only did they strip others of glory and opportunity but, in doing so, altered the course of history beyond anything, however hard we try, any of us will truly ever be able to conceive.

Sports.title: Awkward moment Graham Potter tries to make a joke about Man City's guilty verdict - but Arsenal star Viktor Gyokeres can't hide his smirk
Sports.content:
Sweden manager Graham Potter poked fun at Manchester City in a press conference, with Arsenal forward Viktor Gyokeres looking on with a smirk on his face.

The official verdict was released on Tuesday afternoon, which showed City had cooked the books to the tune of nearly £900million through money artificially pumped into the club by their Abu Dhabi owners over a nine-year period.

City have denied any wrongdoing, and have confirmed they have appealed.

But that hasn't stopped fans having a pop at the Manchester club, and Potter, who was manager of Chelsea between 2022 and 2023, has done the same.

'We've been hit by an infection or a bug, whatever,' he said ahead of Sweden's Nations League game against Bosnia and Herzegovina. 'Not ideal, but it happens.

'We've called in some players who have been fantastic. In terms of how many withdrawals, I think we have had a similar number to Man City's charges.'

He later clarified: 'It was a joke.'

‘In terms of how many withdrawals, I think we’ve had a similar number to Man City’s charges.’



Graham Potter when speaking about the amount of players his Sweden side have had lost due to an infection…



How did no one laugh at that 😂😂😂 pic.twitter.com/q2ROi3FtLb — Now Football (@Nowfootball) October 2, 2026

Arsenal's Victor Gyokeres (right) was unable to hide his amusement after Sweden manager Graham Potter joked about Manchester City's charges

Gyokeres, meanwhile, was sat next to Potter as the player chosen to take part in the press conference, and could hardly hold back his smile as his manager made the jibe.

Gyokeres is contracted to City's rivals, Arsenal, who could benefit from any punishment handed to City.

The Manchester club came second to the Gunners in the Premier League race last year, and any points deduction or transfer ban imposed will play majorly in Arsenal's favour.

City said in a statement on Friday: 'The club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

'The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.'

New Premier League rules state that a hearing must be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing, which can only last five days, concluding.

Daily Mail Sport reported on Thursday that City will attempt to prove their innocence by arguing that the government of Abu Dhabi – rather than the club's owners – part-funded 'sham' sponsorship.

The club's 'disguised funding' process – where the ownership group topping up commercial partnerships to the tune of £830.69m - it found, allowed them to illegally sign the players that ushered in an era of success at the Etihad Stadium.

City have appealed their guilty verdict of breaching 'all charges related to serious breaches' of the Premier League's financial regulations

However, those with knowledge of the situation claim that City's argument is that the monies were actually paid by the government, which owns the sponsors, rather than the club's owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) – a private company owned by Sheikh Mansour – and as such, no rules were broken.

Sponsorship deals with government-funded companies are commonplace throughout the Premier League, particularly in the case of airlines, and are not banned.

That argument, aided by what the club claim is 'irrefutable evidence' in the form of bank statements and witness accounts, is likely to be made in front of a new panel after City appealed the seismic findings.

Sports.title: Man United handed boost as £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba plays in behind-closed-doors friendly - with Michael Carrick sweating over injury setbacks during international break
Sports.content:
Manchester United have been handed a significant injury boost with summer signing Carlos Baleba playing in a behind-closed-doors friendly on Friday.

Baleba, who joined the club for £70million from Brighton in the summer, is yet to play for his new side after carrying an ankle injury into the season.

Fans have been anticipating his debut, and it appears that could come sooner rather than later after the 22-year-old featured against Swiss side Lausanne-Sport in a game held at Carrington.

He had been on the bench against Fulham in United's last game before the international break – a 1-1 draw – but did not come on.

United manager Michael Carrick had previously said Baleba was 'pushing to get back as quickly as possible'.

The news comes as a huge boost for United, who have injury concerns amid the three-week international break.

Carlos Baleba featured for Manchester United in a behind-closed-doors friendly on Friday

Bruno Fernandes missed Portugal's game against Norway through injury but recovered to start the 4-2 win over Norway.

Portugal manager Jorge Jesus described Fernandes's issue as a 'complicated' shin problem.

Noussair Mazraoui, meanwhile, hobbled off in Morocco's Africa Cup of Nations game against Lesotho earlier this week.

As the Moroccan dived in for a tackle in the 68th minute of the game, he landed awkwardly and immediately signalled towards the bench, appearing in a lot of discomfort.

Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo pulled out of England duty before the break, while Amad Diallo, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu are also fitness concerns for United.

The Red Devils' first game back after the break is on October 10, when they will take on Tottenham at Old Trafford.

Sports.title: Erling Haaland to Arsenal? Would Marc Guehi finally end up at rivals Liverpool? And what would happen to £125m man Enzo Fernandez? Where stars might land in a Man City fire sale
Sports.content:
Amid the gleeful aftermath of Manchester City’s guilty verdict among rival supporters, a piece of AI slop did the rounds on social media that showed Erling Haaland, or at least something supposed to look like Erling Haaland, trudging across a boggy pitch. ‘Boss, what the hell is this place?’ the AI Haaland asks before tripping through a muddy puddle, cartwheeling in the air and landing flat on his face. The prospect of City’s star names being forced to run out at Bromley or Barnet should the eight-time Premier League champions be sent hurtling down the divisions as punishment for their flouting of financial rules is almost too much for their rivals to bear. City will lodge an appeal but if the verdict stands, all manner of punishments remain on the table, including points deductions that would certainly see City relegated from the top flight, or even expulsion, raising the possibility of the club tumbling into Leagues One or Two. Should that be the case, it remains hard to see how they will be able to keep hold of their star players on huge wages, even though it is believed no relegation clauses are in their contracts that would make their exits easier. If there is to be a fire sale, then, Daily Mail Sport wonders which Premier League clubs might be the perfect bargain hunters for their wares... If Man City are sent to the bottom of the football pyramid they could lose their top stars Erling Haaland to Arsenal What better way for Arsenal to solve their striker problem once and for all than snaffling one of the best in the world? No more wondering about whether Viktor Gyokeres’s ability to run in behind defences is more important for this game rather than the excellent craft and guile of Kai Havertz dropping in, linking up play, making things happen, even if he might miss the odd sitter. Don’t worry about all that. Just buy Haaland, stick him up top and let him do the rest. Haaland can keep winning trophies, keep playing in the Champions League and keep working under another Pep Guardiola protege in Mikel Arteta (albeit one that’s become more like Jose Mourinho over the years). Haaland may have to settle, however, for heading in most of his goals in from corners rather than gliding into the box to finish off beautiful, flowing passing moves. Real Madrid and Barcelona are said to be circling but maybe he’d just be better off jumping across town to United, who are creating tons of chances from open play, but have long needed a reliable striker to poke them in. Haaland, you would like to think, would be a little more ruthless than Benjamin Sesko, Joshua Zirkzee, Rasmus Hojlund and Wout Weghorst. He wouldn’t even need to move house. Erling Haaland up front for the already dominant Arsenal team would be a scary prospect Marc Guehi to Liverpool This move nearly happened just over a year ago anyway. Crystal Palace agreed to sell him for £35million on deadline day, with Guehi booked in for the first part of his medical and the deal sheet submitted, only to pull the plug at the last minute when they couldn’t find a replacement. Four months later, he was a Man City player. If City get what’s coming to them and the fire sale ensues, this feels like a simple solution. Liverpool are in search of their Virgil van Dijk successor, as their captain continues his stroll into the twilight of his career. Only this week, he was forced to hit back at ‘nonsense’ claims he told former Netherlands head coach Ronald Koeman to switch to a back five at the World Cup to help protect him. Regardless, Liverpool need to think of life after Van Dijk. Who better than another left-sided centre-back, with an abundance of leadership qualities? Liverpool missed out last time, might they get one more chance? Jeremy Doku to Tottenham Spurs have just bought two players with questionable goal records from City for massive money in Omar Marmoush and Savio so why not make it an unimpressive hat-trick. Five goals in 30 Premier League games for Doku last season, and three in 29 the campaign before, so he should fit right in at Spurs. The only potential downside, of course, is that Tottenham may not be in the Premier League come next season either, though that would be down to their own incompetence rather than impropriety on an industrial scale. Arsenal could do with some strengthening down their left flank, too, with Gabriel Martinelli and Leandro Trossard both leaving this summer. Christos Tzolis is doing a fine job but he can’t do it all on his own.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Nico O’Reilly to Brighton You suspect any City players jumping clear of the sinking ship would prefer their agents to wrangle moves to another club in the rough and tumble of a title race. Brighton, perhaps? The Seagulls are soaring under Fabian Hurzeler, a manager who loves his full-backs to think like midfielders, one tucking inside to overload the central areas of the pitch while the other bombs forward, or both pushing high and wide as part of Brighton’s breathless press. Who better to understand those roles and responsibilities than Nico O’Reilly, who can do them all? He can play as a left-back, a holding midfielder, a box-to-box engine runner or even a No10. He was named the Premier League young player of the season. Liverpool could do with a decent left-back too with Kostas Tsimikas and Milos Kerkez not pulling up any trees but, hey, if Brighton can get him on the cheap, they can probably flog him for three times the price in a few years like they usually do. Elliot Anderson to Manchester United He’s the one they wanted. He’s the one United planned to build their midfield around before Anderson chose the blue side of Manchester, so what better way to stick it to those soon-to-be ‘Quiet Neighbours’ than by pinching him off City in a cut-price deal. For all their midfield summer signings of Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, it still feels like something is missing. Anderson showed them exactly what in the Manchester derby as he bossed the midfield despite City being down to ten men. If they get the chance to get their man once more, surely they take it. England star Elliot Anderson (right) was who Man United wanted but he opted for their rivals Rayan Cherki to Fulham Fulham had an offer of an initial £12million accepted by Lyon for Cherki two years ago, only for the then 21-year-old to reportedly decide he didn’t fancy the move to west London. Maybe the prospect of a Tuesday night trip to Bromley’s Hayes Lane might make him reconsider. Probably not. Cherki is too good. Zinedine Zidane called him a ‘real baller’, which probably means he’ll just go to Real Madrid. Ruben Dias to Chelsea Ever since the departure of Thiago Silva, Chelsea have been in desperate, desperate need of some maturity, experience and leadership in their back line. Wesley Fofana is a fine defender when he’s fit but none of Xabi Alonso’s options, even after spending £52million on Maxence Lacroix, can touch the organisation and winning mentality of Dias. They reportedly considered a move for John Stones after his summer exit, too, so you suspect they know the value of tapping into that City defence. Antoine Semenyo to Liverpool Liverpool still need to replace Mo Salah. Bradley Barcola is yet to prove he’s the man to do so, despite joining for £123million. Who better, then, to help fill that void than the winger turned into a player good enough for Pep Guardiola by the man now standing in the Liverpool dugout. A reunion between Semenyo and Andoni Iraola from their days on the south coast at Bournemouth feels like the perfect match and one, you’d imagine, that won’t cost anything like £123million. Enzo Fernandez to Aston Villa For a team that’s spent its last few years having to flog its players to keep in line with Premier League financial rules, it’s unlikely they would be able to land a player who has now been sold twice for more than £100million. Good job, in this playful experiment, he’s going on the cheap. He’d be the ideal fit for Unai Emery, who has just lost Youri Tielemans to Manchester United. Tielemans could sit deep and dictate tempo like a quarterback or push high behind the striker and create from the No10 role. That’s just what Fernandez can do. But if we’re being realistic, Real Madrid wanted him in the summer so that’ll be the more likely destination. How boring. Enzo Fernandez has only just joined Man City in a massive £125million deal Abdukodir Khusanov to Sunderland Young, quick and with bags of raw talent still to be developed. That fits the Black Cats’ recruitment brief of signing young players with high resale value. Khusanov’s one of the quickest defenders in the league but it’s his physical dominance – he’s won every single aerial duel this season – that would make the Sunderland fans love him. It’s just a shame someone like Chelsea might snap him up first. Iliman Ndiaye to Everton I mean the ink probably isn’t even dry on the contract yet, is it? He’s likely only just figured out where the canteen is. Wouldn’t it be lovely for David Moyes to re-sign his best player for less than Everton sold him for and bank not only Ndiaye’s goals but a bit of cash too. Phil Foden to…Manchester City? Is Foden the one who stays? The local lad, who came through the academy, is he the one who sticks with a club that’s stuck by him and repays that faith by trying to get them back to where they want to be? His form in recent seasons suggests he’s unlikely to get the Real Madrids and Barcelonas and Paris Saint-Germains queueing up. Arsenal were interested in the summer, and a player like Foden who looks a world beater one moment but frustrates the next screams Tottenham, but maybe, depending on the wage cut, he’s the one they rebuild around.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel reveals England's Man City stars are WORRIED about their futures after bombshell guilty verdict - and admits it is a 'big subject' in the Three Lions camp
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel revealed that England's Manchester City stars are worried for their immediate futures after this week's bombshell guilty verdict for breaching financial rules.

City were found to have artificially swelled their coffers to the tune of £900million over a nine-year period by what an Independent Commission described as disguised funding scheme and 'sham' sponsorship contracts.

While City stress their innocence and have appealed the decision, Tuchel admitted that Marc Guehi, Elliot Anderson and Nico O'Reilly are naturally anxious.

The trio have been inundated with calls and messages over the past week, with O'Reilly now having flown back to Manchester for treatment on an injury.

'Are they worried or are they concerned? I think that would be a very human reaction if you don't know what's going on for the club that you signed,' Tuchel said.

'They're still young. They're ambitious. They're told they are totally innocent and don't know what's going on.

Thomas Tuchel speaking in Croatia ahead of Saturday's gam

'We speak about it at dinner and at a table of eight or 12 people. Of course, we speak about it at breakfast.'

Tuchel – whose side face Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday afternoon - claimed that the news around City being found guilty of the vast majority of charges had represented a 'distraction' before then clarifying that the City trio had been focused in meetings and training sessions.

'It's a big topic in camp,' he added. 'We had some time off between the matches and it is a big subject. How can it not be a topic? We talk with them but only briefly.'

The German did also suggest that he would continue considering picking players in the event that they are relegated from the Premier League as a punishment, should an appeal fail.

'I would always try to pick the best team for the camp, occasion, tournament,' he said. 'I will never rule that out because they don't play in the top flight in their country. We need to look at it case by case.'

Meanwhile, Tuchel expressed sadness at Raheem Sterling's 'downward spiral', with the ex-England winger a free agent and having pled guilty to dangerous driving after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini.

Sterling admitted possession of nitrous oxide and a refusal to provide a specimen when stopped by police in late May and is awaiting sentencing or a referral to Crown Court in November.

Tuchel pushed hard for Chelsea to land Sterling for £47.5m from City back in 2021 but has not been in touch with his former player in recent weeks.

'I have a lot of sympathy for him and I feel that he has struggled ever since he left Man City, when he was at the peak of his career,' Tuchel said.

'It's sad to see that someone struggles because he was a devoted father for his children and he was a family guy, a nice guy to be around.

'It just seems that he's gone through a difficult period. I'm not sure how much is his fault, sometimes you just enter a strange spiral in your life, a downward spiral. My thoughts of with him of course, the belief is always that he can turn it around and I wish him the best.'

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
