General Assembly, Ghana's president John Dramani Mahama said the country rejected the American proposal after seeing the stipulations requiring Ghana to hand over medical records of patients and pathogen data, and accept the FDA as the ultimate drug authority.

Sponsor Message

"It was humiliating," Mahama said. "Ghana is a sovereign nation and we have our processes. We're a democratic country." He referred to the funding proposition from the U.S. as "a pittance, 100 and something million."

The consequences for not signing can be quite serious. Also on September 25, U.S. Ambassador to Zimbabwe Pamela Tremont said the U.S. was stopping all global health funding to the country because it declined the agreement for the same reasons as Ghana. Instead, she said the U.S. would shift the focus of its relations with Zimbabwe from health to economic investments and trade.

Bollyky says the question is whether other countries who refuse will also be totally cut off.

With the rollout expected this fall, Bollyky says it's only a matter of time before "we see whether the administration is really willing to follow through with that."

What the experts are saying

Global health specialists interviewed for this story say that American First represents a pragmatic approach to healthcare aid.

"When it comes to public health, it does make sense to actually coordinate closely with governments, and countries should eventually run and pay for their own health systems," says Jocilyn Estes of the Center for Global Development.

Yet, she says, "the scope and scale of this pivot is really unprecedented, and the pace that the administration wants to move seems pretty incompatible with the kind of careful planning required when the stakes are this high."

On the ground implementation of the agreements was originally supposed to have begun in April 2026. When the administration couldn't meet that goal, it extended the start by six months to October 1. But it's not clear yet if the money from the State Department will flow on time.

Estes says this rapid-fire rollout is a high-risk moment for the future of U.S. global health assistance.

Sponsor Message

"They're sort of building the plane while flying it, and so if this administration's bet on this new approach doesn't work, there are real patients and real people who will suffer the consequences."

And there's another concern: The amount of U.S. aid will be far less than in past years, says Stephen Morrison , who oversees global health policy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

"At the end of the day, the baseline funding that the United States has brought to the table has been significantly reduced. So if you're a country with a large at-risk population for HIV, you're going to be upset with what has happened with the United States," he says.

Yet many countries may feel they have no choice but to sign on: "You're still going to be engaging with them because it's still the biggest game in town," Morrison says.

One of the biggest questions is whether countries will be able to meet the goals they agree to for their own contributions and also up their spending on healthcare to compensate for the drop in U.S. funds.

Take Rwanda, for example. It's set to receive $157 million from the U.S. over the next five years. In 2024 alone, Rwanda received over $200 million from the U.S. for health programs. But Rwanda, like many countries, is facing economic strains from high inflation and ripple effects from the Iran war.

"We've looked at the domestic budgets announced by those countries and whether or not we see a sign that they are picking up the slack that's expected to come from the shortfall in U.S. development assistance," says Bollyky. "And it seems that [they are] not."

The speed with which the administration rolled this out didn't give countries much time to adjust, he says — and that makes it more difficult to create "a more stable environment for countries to assume the burden of addressing their health needs, which everybody wants, including those governments themselves."

Sponsor Message

NPR reached out to the State Department for comment on criticisms of its America First strategy. The State Department sent this statement:

"Rather than investing in 'forever aid,' the United States is working directly with recipient nations to advance shared global health goals, save lives and support nations in building more locally-led, self-reliant health systems through the Trump Administration's America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS) Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs). This is what long-term partnership looks like."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Cloaked in anonymity, Israeli soldiers describe mass civilian killings in 'NAZA'
World.content:
Cloaked in anonymity, Israeli soldiers describe mass civilian killings in 'NAZA'

toggle caption i The Guardian

For most of the shattering and damning new documentary NAZA, we are on a series of rooftops in Tel Aviv, watching the Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham conduct one-on-one interviews with Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel.

The rooftop footage was filmed at night, mostly by Abraham's co-director, Rachel Szor, and their interview subjects — 24 of them in total — are all cloaked in darkness. We're told that their appearances and voices have been digitally altered to protect their anonymity. In precise detail, they speak about their role in launching the airstrikes that have killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, when around 1,200 people were killed and 250 hostages were taken.

Sponsor Message

Unsurprisingly, NAZA has already stirred considerable outrage — much of it, it should be noted, from people who haven't seen and maybe never will see it. Abraham and Szor, both Israeli filmmakers, have been denounced as traitors in Israel, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu himself has threatened to revoke their citizenship. The anonymization of sources has been one of the more contested issues; Israel supporters have said it discredits the soldiers' testimony, while Palestine supporters have criticized the film for shielding self-confessed war criminals.

Without the promise of anonymity, of course, NAZA as a film wouldn't exist. But the reporting that it presents would exist. Much of it has already been published in outlets including +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication; Local Call, a Hebrew-language outlet; and The Guardian, which co-produced the film. Abraham wrote many of those investigative pieces himself; he's also credited the many Palestinian journalists who brought these revelations to light.

The testimony is riveting. Some of the interview subjects speak about how they were motivated to help the Israeli military annihilate Hamas after Oct. 7. Some express guilt and regret for their involvement. Others see themselves as cogs in a necessary war machine. But for the most part, the filmmakers are less interested in the questions of why than in the mechanics of how. They want us to understand how these systems of remote surveillance and mass killing work, and to grasp the horrific scale of the civilian deaths.

Sponsor Message

NAZA is an acronym for nezek agavi, Hebrew for "collateral damage." It refers to the estimated number of civilian casualties considered acceptable by the Israeli military. "Twenty NAZA" would mean that up to 20 civilian deaths were approved in the elimination of a single target. For one high-value target, a figure of 500 NAZA was approved — the population of a small Israeli town, Abraham notes.

The logistics of trackings and killings are calmly and methodically laid out. Because the military can hack into any Palestinian's phone in Gaza, their power of surveillance is near-total. We learn about the military's practice of bombing the homes of suspected Hamas operatives at night, while their wives and children were with them. We also hear about the widespread use of AI systems to gather intelligence, much of it faulty, about potential targets.

One of the most chilling passages describes a tracking technology referred to as "Where's Daddy?," which uses children's words to confirm whether their targeted fathers are at home. One soldier talks about having used this method on a 12-year-old girl, saying, "You hack her phone and then you kill her." At one point, Abraham asks a subject if Israel is committing a genocide. Without hesitating, he responds, "Yes. Completely." As the film notes, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since Oct. 7 — and the death toll continues to rise.

I've watched NAZA twice now, both times in a state of quiet horror and fury — and with enormous admiration for Abraham and Szor's courage in holding their government to account. My admiration extends to the unerring precision of their filmmaking. NAZA runs just 77 minutes. It doesn't linger on the atrocities it describes, mainly because there are so many of them to address. There's some archival material, including footage from the early days of Israeli intelligence and the building of Tel Aviv in the 1920s.

Sponsor Message

But most of the imagery we see is of modern-day Tel Aviv at night. Szor's camera captures the glittering lights of the city and often peers into apartment windows, showing us Israeli citizens working out, eating meals and watching the news. There's tremendous power — and, I think, a stealthy indictment — in these everyday images. It's as if the filmmakers are holding up a mirror image to Gaza, turning our thoughts toward the thousands of slain Palestinians who were, once upon a time, also just going about their evenings. The most radical thing about NAZA isn't that it exposes the machinery of death; it's the film's insistence on the value of Palestinian life.

World.title: The U.S. added only 29,000 jobs in September as job market lacks spark
World.content:
The U.S. added only 29,000 jobs in September as job market lacks spark

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

The U.S. job market showed signs of weakness in September as hiring slowed and the unemployment rate inched higher.

A report from the Labor Department on Friday shows employers added just 29,000 jobs last month — far fewer than forecasters had expected. Job gains for July and August were also revised down by a total of 60,000, pushing July's job totals into the red.

The September report doesn't show widespread job cuts, although financial services and government shed workers. Most industries continued to add workers, but at a slow pace. Even healthcare, which has been a steady source of employment gains, added just 17,000 jobs last month.

Sponsor Message

"The good news is you're not seeing a lot of layoffs," says Sarah House, senior economist at Wells Fargo. "But it's really hard if you are one of those workers who loses your job or you're new to the labor force or you're coming back, there's not a lot of turnover. So it makes it harder to get your foot in the door right now."

Wages are still not keeping up with inflation

Average wages in September were up just 3% from a year ago. That's a smaller annual increase than the previous month, and probably not enough to keep pace with inflation. Prices have been rising faster than paychecks in recent months, so workers' real buying power is being eroded.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point two weeks ago in an effort to curb inflation. The lackluster jobs report makes it less likely the central bank will raise rates again when policymakers meet later this month. That caused a modest rally in the stock and bond markets. Investors still expect at least one additional rate hike, however, before the end of the year.

Meanwhile, the unemployment rate in September rose to 4.2%, from 4.1% the month before. That was largely due to an influx of 485,000 additional workers. The share of adults who are working or looking for work inched up by two-tenths of a percent.

World.title: Cornell rape case gets special prosecutor. And, Renee Good's family sues the government
World.content:
Cornell rape case gets special prosecutor. And, Renee Good's family sues the government

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A Cornell University sexual assault case that produced no criminal charges is now under state scrutiny. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James' office as special prosecutor after new information raised questions about what campus police shared with the local district attorney. NPR confirmed the woman who reported the assault gave police a detailed account, including that she had been raped.

toggle caption i Spencer Platt/Getty Images

🎧 NPR's Brian Mann tells Up First the case has shattered students' trust in Cornell. Hundreds gathered Thursday night, some sobbing as they spoke. One student told Mann the woman at the center of the case "could have been any one of my friends or a classmate."

Tennessee tried to execute Christa Pike on Wednesday. She survived. Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, remains in critical condition after receiving two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital. Gov. Bill Lee has now paused executions for the remainder of his term and ordered an independent review of what went wrong.



Sponsor Message

🎧 It's the second failed execution in Tennessee this year. WPLN's Marianna Bacallao says that one failed execution might be a fluke, but two suggest a pattern. Lee previously paused executions from 2022 to 2025 after a review found problems with the state's execution drugs. The current protocol grew out of that review, but the state is again investigating what went wrong.

The monthly jobs report will be released this morning. For many Americans, the math is getting harder: prices are up, wages aren't keeping pace and borrowing costs more.



🎧 Forecasters expect today's report to show that employers added 80,000 to 90,000 jobs in September, NPR's Scott Horsley says. That would be slower than August but stronger than earlier in the summer. Horsley says wage growth is another key measure, and pay increases aren't keeping pace with prices.

Renee Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government yesterday over her death last January. The 37-year-old was fatally shot by a federal agent during an immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota. The first lawsuit alleges ICE officer Jonathan Ross used excessive force. The second alleges that federal officials conspired to interfere with the civil rights of individuals in Minnesota.

Today's listen

toggle caption i Stefano Rellandini/AFP via Getty Images

NAZA features 24 anonymous Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers describing the surveillance and targeting systems they used in Israel's war in Gaza – including AI — and the civilian deaths they say those systems allowed. Palestinian and international journalists have long documented that toll; the film brings testimony from inside the Israeli military system. Its title loosely translates to "collateral damage." The film turns that abstraction back into human lives. NAZA opens in U.S. theaters this week after winning praise abroad, while in Israel it has drawn protests, accusations of treason and threats to revoke the filmmakers' citizenship.

Sponsor Message

🎧 Morning Edition's Leila Fadel speaks with filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor about what they learned and the backlash that followed. Listen to the full interview here.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Jason Kempin/Getty Images for ACM



Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Forgotten Island follows childhood friends Jo and Raissa, who are unexpectedly transported to a magical island just before they are about to part ways.

📺 TV: The Spanish-language miniseries My Sad Dead follows an Argentinian doctor who can communicate with ghosts. Fresh Air critic John Powers describes it as a unique blend of creepiness, sarcastic humor and political anger, unlike anything else on TV.

📚 Books: Min Jin Lee's American Hagwon is the third installment in a planned four-novel series about the Korean diaspora. It explores the complexities of immigration, the fragile promise of America and the purpose of education.

🎵 Music: Now in her 60s, singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow says she has aged out of pop music. She describes her latest album, Pick You Up, as exploring questions many of us ask about our identity at this moment in humanity.

❓ Quiz: Bears, Beyoncé, and colleges. This week's news features a mix of serious headlines and lighter moments. Test your memory with this week's quiz.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

SpaceX launched four astronauts on NASA's Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station for a six-month stay before returning to Earth. Google launched a refrigerator-sized satellite equipped with AI chips as part of Project Suncatcher, its effort to put AI data centers in space. The Pearly Kings were once a fixture of East London, raising money in their mother-of-pearl suits. Now, NPR looks back at George Major, who died in August, and the tradition he helped carry on.

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: Why is diesel more expensive than regular gas?
World.content:
Why is diesel more expensive than regular gas?

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

toggle caption i Screenshot via @matt.j.Robb, permission given/Threads

This week, a guy had random buyers show up to his house thanks to Meta's new AI agent Muse! A cautionary tale for you... Matt Robb, a YouTube creator, posted online that he let Muse manage his Facebook Marketplace account. When he let Jarvis (the name of this AI agent) sell a wireless keyboard, things did NOT go as planned. The bot accepted a low-ball offer and consequently handed out Matt's ADDRESS to a potential buyer.

The Indicator team has been talking about Muse a lot this week after the app popped off with around 5 million downloads since its Sept. 8 launch. Is it trustworthy? How useful can it really be? Host Wailin Wong says her mom is already finding a use for it!

"My mother named her Muse agent after Mr. Darcy from Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice. She had Darcy design a greeting card for a relative and a t-shirt as an 80th birthday gift for someone in her senior living community," Wailin says. "Then she got them printed at the public library maker-space. I never imagined my mom would use an AI agent!"

Coming up:



Sponsor Message

Why people are spending so much on their hobbies

Why diesel seems to always be more expensive

What strategies colleges can use to boost applications

Trivia Question: What is one mechanism hedge funds use to help people sidestep paying the government? Email us indicator@npr.org.

New's We're Watching

Is it getting more expensive to have fun?

What to know: Bloomberg wrote this week that American consumers are spending less on bowling, arcades or amusement parks. With inflation tightening people's purse strings, spots like Dave & Buster's and Lucky Strike are seeing less traffic and it's hurting their bottom line. Six Flags is seeing lower attendance, too.

On the OTHER hand, CNBC wrote how consumers are spending more on hobbies at home compared to last year. People are making more transactions AND hobbies are costing more. We're talking arts & crafts, video games, books, the list goes on.

So IS fun over?: Of course not, but people may be substituting treks out of the house for more in-home activities. It's pricey as heck to travel right now, whether you're driving or flying!

So is it getting more expensive to have fun? Whether it's out of the house, or in the house, it's costing more. But people are willing to spend on more localized activities.

Sponsor Message

One interesting note from Bank of America's analysis on the price of fun: people with the least free time are spending the most on hobbies, aka older millennials. Part of the reason: they're buying for their kids too.

Why is diesel more expensive than regular gas?

What to know: When you go to the gas station, diesel is often the pricier option compared to unleaded or premium gas. Can you remember a time when it was less expensive?? Right now, the price of diesel is a BIT of an aberration. The national average this week is $6.38... last year, the average was $3.60. It's gotten so bad, Republican members of Congress have been lobbying President Trump to ban diesel exports in hopes of lowering prices. Apparently, the administration is seriously weighing the move, though the American Petroleum Institute is adamantly against it.

REGARDLESS! Diesel prices are consistently higher than unleaded or premium gas prices. Why is that?

toggle caption i David Zalubowski/AP Photo/David Zalubowski/AP

When diesel got expensive: This week, diesel fuel costs just under $2 more than regular gasoline per gallon. But once upon a time, diesel actually cost LESS than regular-grade gas. The switch happened back in Sept. 2004. The Energy Information Administration points to three primary reasons.

Demand: Back in the early 2000s, China and India were motorizing and industrializing at new levels, according to Clay Seigl, who leads the energy practice at Beacon Global Strategies. He adds they were ramping up agriculture alongside big construction and infrastructure projects too. That's all powered by diesel.

At the same time, in Europe, diesel grew from just 13.8% of new car registrations in 1990 to 53% in 2007.

It's worth noting though, that nowadays, the price hike on diesel is less about demand, and more about supply. There's a lot less diesel due to the Iran and Ukraine wars limiting refining capacity and crude production, and yet the need for diesel fuel is still essential from trucks and trains to generator farms and heating.

Sponsor Message

Air quality standards: In June 2006, federal regulation kicked in that reduced the maximum amount of sulfur that could be included in diesel fuel. The hope? Reduce air pollution. But it costs more to produce ultra-low sulfur diesel due to higher refining and distribution costs. This came after 2004, but may have contributed to higher prices later on.

Taxes: In 1993, the federal excise tax increased to 24.4 cents per gallon for on-highway diesel. That's 6 cents more than the equivalent for gasoline.

Today's Indicator

Why colleges spend so much money on athletics

If you HAVEN'T listened: Back in 1984, Doug Flutie threw a Hail Mary pass in the final seconds of a college Bowl game against Miami. He made the pass and Boston College was victorious. The win boosted the entire college's admissions, starting something called the "Flutie effect." The idea: when your sports programs do well, your whole admissions does well.

Nowadays, the stakes are high for colleges to increase enrollment. In the coming years, fewer high school students are expected to go to college in the U.S. So … universities are investing in their sports programs and advertising them hard. Is it working?

LISTEN TO THE EPISODE

If you HAVE listened: Doug Chung, our Flutie Effect researcher, found if a school elevates their sports team from "mediocre" to "great," it boosts their applications by nearly 18%. BUT … there are other proven ways to get to that same figure.

Schools can:



Decrease tuition by 4%

Paying faculty 5% more than market rate

Our reporter Ricky Mulvey's take-away: "Football is the flashiest part of a school, but boring economic decisions get more people coming through."

Rest of the Week



Listener Mailbag

Listener Laura sent in a question from Belton, TX

Question: I just listened to your episode on AQR tax-loss harvesting, which appears to only be available to the rich. Could you discuss in an episode the difference between that and direct indexing which also involves tax loss harvesting? Direct indexing has been available on sites like Public.com for as little as $1,000 recently.

Sponsor Message

Answer: Oh, the ways we Americans can avoid paying the government. So numerous! Laura, you are right, direct indexing is another way to do tax-loss harvesting, distinct from the tax-aware long-short strategy we talk about in the episode. So let's break it down.

I spoke with Alex Matturri, who used to run the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Indices, to help me understand. He explains that direct indexing, at a basic level, is just customizing an index. For example, you might start with S&P 500 and then only choose companies for ESG purposes. But when it comes to saving money on your tax bill, you can build a portfolio GEARED towards tax efficiency. And you don't need a ton of money to do that.

That's different from what AQR is doing, which is much more sophisticated. But at the basic level, the tax-aware long-short strategy is both buying stocks and shorting some of them to create losses that can then offset your tax bill. Thank you for the question, Laura!

If you have an economics question, email us at indicator@npr.org

In Our Spare Time

Producer Julia Ritchey is watching silent films at her local arthouse theater

toggle caption i Julia Ritchey

Opened in 1921, the Lucas Theater in Savannah, Ga., regularly screens old movies that have been digitally restored. Notably, the theater also houses its original Wurlitzer pipe organ from 1925 that would regularly accompany movies during the silent film era. Of the 2,100 or so Wurlitzer pipe organs produced by the Wurlitzer Company up until 1943, fewer than 15 remain in the building where they were originally installed, let alone restored and played regularly! Unlike other pipe organs, these engineering marvels have percussive sound effects for thunderclaps, horse hooves and train whistles, perfect for old movie palaces.

For the 100th anniversary screening of Buster Keaton's The General, considered one of the greatest comedic films ever made, the Lucas' organist scored the entire 75-minute film without one break, including several of Keaton's legendary locomotive stunts. It was a delightful cinematic treat for any film buff.

Sponsor Message

Enjoying This Newsletter?

Forward to a friend! They can sign up here.

This newsletter was fact-checked by Sierra Juarez edited by Kate Concannon.

World.title: Hidden cameras show some stores unlocking speed limits on e-bikes, selling e-scooters that go up to 120 km/h
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Whether it's children cruising down a suburban street, drivers delivering food downtown or a daredevil taking their need for speed to the highway, electric bikes and electric scooters are becoming more common across Canada.

A new hidden camera investigation by Marketplace shows how some stores are selling e-scooters and e-bikes with top speeds much higher than provincial speed limits and with recommended rider ages younger than provincial regulations allow.

Most provincial traffic laws limit e-bikes and e-scooters to 32 kilometres per hour or less. Age restrictions, meanwhile, vary across the country, ranging from 12 to 18. The territories and some provinces have no minimum age to ride.

That means it is mostly up to local police services to enforce these rules at a time when the number of injuries caused by these vehicles is climbing yearly, and public calls are growing for stronger, consistent rules nationwide and better enforcement .

Marketplace visited some of Canada's most well-known big box and specialty shops in the Greater Toronto Area — Amego, Emmo, EZbike, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Costco — that sell popular brands. The undercover journalists tested how easy it is to find an e-bike or e-scooter that either had a maximum speed or age recommendation contravening Ontario limits.

In Ontario, e-scooter and e-bike riders must be at least 16. E-scooters cannot travel faster than 24 km/h on a flat surface, and e-bikes cannot travel faster than 32 km/h, according to provincial laws.

10 of 12 stores exceeded Ontario limits

Of the 12 stores journalists visited undercover, salespeople at six stores told us or showed us how to bypass built-in speed limits.

While most stores reminded us of Ontario rules, 10 stores sold e-bikes or e-scooters with maximum speeds beyond Ontario limits.

Stores are allowed to sell the e-bikes no matter how fast they go, but Michael Pasquali, founder of the Canadian Electric Bicycle Association (CEBA), says it's "heartbreaking."

"Shops that are selling products that are way beyond the legal limit, they're putting a lot of people in danger."

Seven stores also had e-scooters for sale with manufacturer-recommended rider ages under 16, though some medical experts say e-bikes and e-scooters are too unsafe for anyone under 16.

Watch the full Marketplace investigation on Friday, Oct. 2, on CBC-TV and YouTube.

"It's not just a toy; it's a motorized vehicle," said April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton.

"We're seeing kids who are presenting with brain bleeds, with abdominal injuries, solid organ injuries."

Recently released data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows 150 people ages 15 and under were hospitalized for falls involving an e-scooter in the 2025-2026 fiscal year across Canada, compared to 54 the year prior. That's an increase of roughly 178 per cent — and reflects a steady year-over-year increase for the last three years.

The number of head injuries related to e-scooters has also increased, from 50 in the 2022-2023 fiscal year to 157 in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Fractures, dislocations and or muscle and tendon injuries have more than doubled in that same period, with 544 last fiscal year.

The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program released its own survey in August and found 10 children have died from using devices like e-scooters and e-bikes in 2025.

Meanwhile, sales for the electric rides have more than quadrupled in Canada since 2019, with roughly 372,000 e-bikes and 76,000 e-scooters sold so far this year, according to Statista.

Marketing to kids 'deceiving' parents, doctor says

The youngest age recommendation the Marketplace journalists found was at Canadian Tire — a Razor e-scooter that hits a maximum speed of 16 km/h and is recommended for children who are eight or older.

"That just boggles my mind. Kids at this age don't necessarily have the developmental ability to maneuver these motorized vehicles," said Kam, who is also president of the Canadian Paediatric Society's emergency medicine section.

"It's very concerning that there's this huge market for selling children these motorized vehicles, essentially, and deceiving the parents and family, marketing them as toys."

WATCH | Doctor says kids 16 and under shouldn't ride e-bikes, e-scooters : Doctor says kids 16 and under shouldn't ride e-bikes, e-scooters | Duration closed caption 1:51 April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton, says e-bikes and e-scooters are vehicles, not toys.

Razor, the manufacturer of that particular e-scooter at Canadian Tire, said in a statement its device meets U.S. safety guidelines that say eight-year-olds can operate slow-moving motorized vehicles.

The company said its e-scooter is safe when properly used, isn't meant to be on public roads and that riders should follow local laws.

In statements to Marketplace, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Emmo said customers should follow local laws. Best Buy said rules for e-bikes and e-scooters are evolving and that it tries to keep product information updated.

Costco didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.

E-bike stores can modify speed controls

At an EZbike location in Richmond Hill, a salesperson told undercover journalists it sells e-scooters that can reach 120 km/h — a speed that could get you a ticket on most highways.

At other stores, some e-bikes have their speed limited to 32 kilometres, adhering to Ontario's rules. But when asked if they modify vehicles, a salesperson at an Emmo location in Toronto said yes, they could modify a bike to go up to 150 km/h for off-road use.

"That's horrible," said Pasquali, of CEBA, who owns his own e-bike store in Hamilton.

Emmo and the company that operates the Emmo stores Marketplace visited said in a statement that a product's technical capabilities should not be confused with what's allowed on the roads.

But as an employee at an Emmo in Vaughan, Ont., described it: bypassing the speed limiter is "just like a toggle switch."

WATCH | E-bike stores can modify speed control: E-bike stores can modify speed control | Duration closed caption 2:53 Undercover CBC journalists visited 12 stores selling e-bikes and e-scooters across the Greater Toronto Area. Salespeople at six stores told them or showed them how to bypass built-in speed limits on the vehicles.

Passing on that kind of advice is "extremely unethical," Pasquali said.

"If you're showing consumers how to push a button and make it faster or offering to modify it to go faster with the caveat that you keep it off road, well, that's technically right. But most consumers aren't doing that, right?"

A salesperson at an Amego store in North York, Ont., went a step further, unlocking the 32 km/h speed limit in front of undercover journalists and revving the motor, showing the e-bike exceeding the speed limit and saying it could hit a top speed of roughly 50 km/h.

Amego said in a statement it does not offer or perform modifications, and its salesperson likely exaggerated the top speed.

EZbike didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.

Mom wants change after son's devastating injury

Amy Richards, of St. John's, became one of those parents pleading for change after watching her son spend 102 days in the hospital after losing control of his e-scooter.

Jayden King, 14, was riding his e-scooter on a quiet street in May when he hit a speed bump and lost control.

King's mom says he was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident but suffered a traumatic brain injury. He spent 21 days in a coma and had to have part of his skull surgically removed due to brain swelling. Once he's healthier, King will have to undergo another surgery to get the rest of his skull put back in place, Richards said.

WATCH | Mom wants change after son's devastating e-scooter injury: Mom wants change after son's devastating e-scooter injury | Duration closed caption 2:30 Amy Richards of St. John's wants stronger e-bike and e-scooter legislation after her 14-year-old son crashed an e-scooter in May.

He learned to walk, talk and eat again but still lives with a long list of issues, including memory loss.

"I can't remember nothing in my whole life," King said. He says there's not a chance he'll ride an e-scooter again.

Newfoundland and Labrador has no rules governing e-bikes or e-scooters, but a spokesperson for Government Services said in a statement that it has consulted the public and is looking at changes to the Highway Traffic Act to include micro-mobility devices.

Richards said it should have happened a long time ago, and no one under 16 should be able to ride one.

"We need to protect our children. That should come first and foremost," she said.

Pasquali says the federal government needs to step in and stop the sale and importation of e-bikes and e-scooters that can be modified with the flick of a switch.

Safety is top priority, federal minister says

Canada's Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told Marketplace in an interview in late September that he has heard stories of people being injured riding e-bikes and e-scooters, and he wants to talk to his provincial counterparts about how to respond.

Most of the legislation governing e-bikes and e-scooters is provincial, he said, and there is "impetus" for provinces and municipalities to act.

But, MacKinon also said the federal government needs "to absolutely consider what we will do in terms of regulating the safety of those devices."

"We'll always work with safety in mind. Safety is our principal priority."

World.title: 'I am Jane Doe': Online rally to protect Cornell rape accuser's identity becomes a reckoning
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article references sexual assault and may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

They're saying it in videos posted on TikTok in solidarity, in Instagram posts where they hope to protect her identity, and in comments on Threads where they share their own harrowing experiences:

"I am Jane Doe."

The repeated refrain, part of a wave of online support this week for the complainant in the Cornell University gang-rape allegations, is being compared to the cultural and structural reckoning of the 2017 #MeToo movement that changed the culture of silence around sexual assault.

The Cornell case recently came under the spotlight after the complainant, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16 alleging the Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7."

The #iamjanedoe movement seems to have been born out of an attempt to protect Jane Doe's identity after an independent journalist put out a public call Monday to name her "so we can all evaluate her veracity … since her lawsuit didn't hesitate to name and shame seven of her peers as gang-rapists."

He later claimed to have identified her, posting and then deleting her information, adding "the principle has been served."

The global response across the internet was swift.

People gather outside Willard Straight Hall after a hearing on sexual assault at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Thursday. (Matt Rourke/The Associated Press)

"He is trying to expose her identity. We won't let him. I am Jane Doe," a content creator posted in a video on TikTok viewed more than 5.2 million times by Friday.

"You are Jane Doe, I am Jane Doe, we are ALL Jane Doe until no one is Jane Doe," someone else commented.

"We all are Jane Doe, good luck finding her, men," another person commented on one user's Instagram video.

Jane Doe alleges the men named in her lawsuit plied her with ketamine and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024. None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged. On Monday, after intense backlash, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.

By Thursday evening, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she'd lost faith in the DA's ability to handle the case and was appointing New York attorney general Letitia James to oversee the investigation.

On Friday, Hochul says she intends to "close the loophole" in her state's law that currently makes it difficult for sexual assault survivors to claim they were mentally incapacitated during an assault if they were voluntarily intoxicated.

WATCH | New York Gov. Kathy Hochul says she 'wants the truth': New York governor says 'I want the truth' in Cornell case | Duration 1:41 New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and the state attorney general provided an update about the criminal investigation into a woman's allegations that she was gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house.

'It's happening all the time'

Takara Small, a technology journalist in Toronto, told CBC News Network Friday that the global movement is meant to confuse the algorithm and search engines, but that it's impossible to fully scrub a digital footprint.

"I understand this action, but I think it's important people don't share any information that could be linked to her," Small said.

There are currently thousands of online "I am Jane Doe" posts across multiple platforms, reaching millions of people. And while one of the goals is to bury any identifying information of the actual Jane Doe, it is also a moment of reckoning.

Many of the posters have been describing their own sexual assault experiences, the difficulties in coming forward and, in some cases, naming the people they say harmed them.

"Four men at once. I was 22," someone posted on TikTok.

"I was 18," someone posted on Instagram.

"People need to realize this is happening to so many women, not just one brave woman at Cornell University. It’s happening all the time. Everywhere to SOOO MANY women," she added.

A screen grab of an 'I am Jane Doe' Instagram post by @naabamii from Sept. 30, 2026. (@naabamii/Instagram)

In Canada, about 44 per cent of the population over age 15 say they have been sexually assaulted in their lifetime, with women three times as likely to say so as men, according to a 2025 survey by Statistics Canada. Fewer than one in 10 reported it to the police.

According to the U.S. Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network (RAINN), about one in four undergraduate women experience rape or sexual assault after enrolling in college.

'We are so damn tired'

U.S. journalist Katie Couric gathered some of the responses she'd seen online and posted them on Threads on Wednesday.

"The Cornell case has unleashed a torrent of first-person accounts from women revisiting traumatic experiences they had long kept buried," Couric wrote.

A Threads post by U.S. journalist Katie Couric from Sept. 30, 2026. (@katiecouric/Threads)

They included posts by one user who said they'd been assaulted by their professor, who was allowed to retire early and is now a dean at another school. Another said they'd been raped while asleep, still another said they had been drugged and raped for hours on a college campus while people watched and nobody was prosecuted.

"It feels like shouting into a void," someone commented. "It's infuriating."

The feeling was echoed on Substack, where an author asked what's really changed since #MeToo.

"The viral #MeToo movement in 2017 felt so significant because it was the largest collective reckoning of rape culture maybe ever, and happened mostly in an online space. It was the first time I said things out loud that I had kept to myself for most of my life," she wrote in a post Tuesday.

"The same is happening now with the Cornell 7, but we are almost 10 years on from #MeToo and we are so damn tired."

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database . ​​

World.title: Stephen Harper warns Alberta separatism will bring 'no benefit'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper cautioned against the prospect of Alberta separation in a column Friday, writing that even voting just to "send a message" would represent a fraught approach.

" No one will be surprised to learn that I am against separation. That would involve much risk and be extremely difficult to bring about," Harper wrote in the Calgary Herald.

"Besides, there is nothing resembling the credible leadership necessary to establish a new country. "

On Oct. 19, voters will be asked whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or whether the government of Alberta should hold a second, binding referendum to separate from Canada.

Earlier this year, as his official prime ministerial portrait was unveiled on Parliament Hill, Harper called for Liberals and Conservatives to come together amid reinvigorated separatist movements in Alberta and Quebec.

In September, Harper backed the federal government's decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States at the Canada Investment Summit, arguing that Canada needed to pursue "diminished reliance" on the United States in order to maintain its sovereignty.

Current Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has also said he supports a united Canada.

Speaking in Edmonton earlier this week, he blamed the Liberal government for what he said was its role in seeding discontent, but said separating from Canada wouldn't help resolve provincial grievances.

Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic, left to right, former prime minister Stephen Harper, Prime Minister Mark Carney, former prime minister Jean Chretien, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and Saskatchewan's Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison pose for a photo at Canada's National Investment Summit in Toronto on Sept. 14, 2026. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

Harper dismisses voting to send message

While many Albertans may feel alienated from Ottawa, Harper wrote in his Friday column that pursuing independence would pose "significant risk."

" Whatever the results of the Alberta vote, it is incumbent upon Canada to move with immediacy and urgency to address the barriers, many self-imposed, to our long-term stability and prosperity," Harper wrote.

"It is on this objective that I believe the passion and legitimate frustration of Albertans should also remain focused."

Polling has consistently indicated that a majority of Albertans are in favour of remaining in Canada.

Separatist leaders have been trying to close the gap.

They've argued that voting to hold a future, binding referendum would provide Alberta leverage against Ottawa when it comes to resolving its grievances.

Keith Wilson, a leader of a pro-independence group, often argues on social media that voting for the separation option is an opportunity to send a message that the "status quo with Ottawa is unacceptable."

"For me, Oct. 19 is not simply a debate about staying or leaving; it is also about strategy. What position gives Alberta the strongest voice in determining its future?" Wilson wrote on Thursday.

"My case is that Option 2 creates leverage and strengthens Alberta’s hand at the negotiating table."

UCP MLA Jason Stephan argued the same this week after he confirmed to CBC News that he has voted via a mail-in ballot for Option 2: "I've always supported having a referendum on independence because I want Ottawa to be compelled to fix the things that are broken."

In his column, Harper disagreed with that argument, writing that "over two generations of Quebec politics were spent debating the goal of the separatists."

"Most voting for it will do so just to 'send a message,' in other words, to keep the threat alive in the hope of retaining the benevolent attention that the province has recently been receiving from Ottawa," Harper wrote. "I believe that approach is mistaken."

WATCH | Carney designates new pipeline project of national interest: Carney designates Alberta's pipeline a project of 'national interest' | Duration closed caption 1:43:24 Alberta's proposed pipeline to the West Coast becomes the first project to be designated in the national interest by the federal government, but it still lacks a private proponent. As of now, a majority of the pipeline will be publicly owned — with more potential private investment to come. Power & Politics hears from Energy Minister Tim Hodgson and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. The Power Panel weighs in.

Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, said the former prime minister's comments were unsurprising, given his reputation as a federalist.

But he added that recent developments, such as those tied to the West Coast oil pipeline, could be seen as the referendum already sending a message and getting results.

"It is getting attention from Ottawa for the first time in decades," he said.

Harper also contended that the federal government under his leadership helped stamp out separatist sentiment, including when it came to its approach to energy policy.

Poilievre also recently claimed that separatist sentiments were wiped out in Alberta and Quebec under Harper’s government — comments that received pushback from the Bloc Québécois.

A spokesperson for Harper declined to provide additional comment.

World.title: Hudson Williams wore this cardigan. Then the Indigenous designer's business went viral
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Canadian actor Hudson Williams stepped out wearing a piece by Canadian Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis on Wednesday, Louis didn't expect to go viral.

In fact, he nearly forgot it was happening.

The Samson Cree Nation-born designer was spending National Day for Truth and Reconciliation away from work. He was with his family, unplugged and out paddling on the lake.

And then he checked his phone.

"There was, like, a whole bunch of sales and the social media was lighting up and I was just like, 'What is going on? Did something happen?'" he said in an interview with CBC News.

"I realized that, like, every cardigan had sold out. At that time, there was like $12,000 in sales in a matter of an hour. And I was like, 'What the hell?'"

From left: Jacob Tierney, Brendan Brady, Jayme Alter Wilson, Williams, Connor Storrie, Rachel Reid, Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova and Christina Chang appear at the summit on Wednesday. (Jason Lowrie/BFA)

The Heated Rivalry star wore Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women's Mental Health, along with an orange ribbon on his chest marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

For Louis, seeing his work worn that day by a prominent Canadian actor made the moment "pretty special."

"There was intention and genuine interest in supporting us behind it, so that made it more meaningful for me," Louis said.

The cardigan, which costs $350, was designed by Louis, founder and creative director of Section 35 and the Justin Jacob Louis label. And it made its way to Williams as part of a last minute request.

How they connected

Louis said someone from Williams's team initially contacted him by email and over Instagram about the actor's interest in buying the piece — just last weekend.

Shipping it from his warehouse wasn't feasible within the timeframe, but he happened to have the right size at his studio in the Fraser Valley in Chilliwack, B.C.

Someone from Williams's team drove from Vancouver to Louis's studio that Sunday to pick it up.

Months of sales in two days

That choice had an immediate impact on Louis's small business.

The brand gained hundreds of new followers throughout the day. The cardigan sold out and other pieces began selling, too.

Louis estimates the shop did two to three months worth of sales in just two days.

While the brand hadn't planned on restocking the cardigan, the huge surge in demand persuaded Louis to open up pre-orders.

"For an independent small business, it helps out so much," he said. "It's just been kind of a whirlwind."

Design based on a dream

Louis says the design came to him in a dream he had while feeling disconnected and homesick and living about 12 hours from the community where he grew up.

Loius says the design for the cardigan came to him in a dream. (Alex Waber)

In the dream, he was back at his father's place, walking across the pasture in winter under the night sky, wondering where his ancestors were.

"The stars in the sky lit up and then they turned into eyeballs and looked right at me," Louis said.

"It was just kind of like this reminder that they're always with you wherever you are, no matter how far from home you are."

Louis says Williams messaged him directly to thank him for the cardigan. They've stayed in touch, and the designer says he'd love to work with Williams again.

But for now, he's focused on continuing to design and build his labels.

Here's his advice to other designers and small businesses: stay intentional and true to your values and culture.

"That makes us who we are," he said. "Showcasing the beauty that exists within our communities. I think there's so much talent and the storytelling that comes from our people and our stories. It's what sets us apart. And I think staying true to that is so important."

World.title: LNG Canada to use Chinese steel on $33B expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LNG Canada will once again use Chinese steel for the "specialized fabrication capability" it says it requires for its $33-billion Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.

When the proposed expansion led the list of early projects referred to the new federal Major Projects Office in September 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters these ambitious building projects would be "at the heart of our new, comprehensive Buy Canadian policy."

In fact, LNG Canada will buy more components from the state-owned China Offshore Oil Engineering Co., Ltd. (COOEC), which also manufactured its first two liquified natural gas processing units, known as trains, now in operation.

The private consortium of five international energy companies announced the expansion on Tuesday. LNG Canada is adding two more trains for a total of four on the site, increasing its production from 14 to 28 megatonnes per year once Phase 2 construction is complete, likely in the early 2030s.

At the event marking the final investment decision, CBC News asked the prime minister if the expansion would be built with Canadian or Chinese steel.

"It's a great question for the proponents of Phase 2," Carney said. "I'll leave it to them."

"There will be full opportunities to buy Canadian steel, and we'll continue to invest in the Canadian steel industry to make sure that's the case. But it will be for them to decide," the prime minister said.

WATCH | Carney says use of Chinese steel is LNG Canada's decision: LNG Canada 'to decide' whether to use Canadian or Chinese steel in B.C. project, says Carney | Duration closed caption 0:35 Asked by the CBC on Sept. 29 whether the multibillion-dollar Phase 2 expansion of LNG Canada's project in Kitimat, B.C. will use Chinese steel, Prime Minister Mark Carney said it will be up to the proponent but noted there will be 'full opportunities to buy Canadian steel.'

Accordingly, CBC News asked LNG Canada where it intends to source steel for its expansion.

"For the plant construction in Kitimat, the challenge is not a preference for offshore steel, but the specialized fabrication capability required for modules of this scale and complexity," LNG Canada spokesperson Paul Hagel wrote in an email.

"There are no fabrication yards in Canada that can manufacture and deliver the additional modules required for Phase 2. Only five fabrication yards globally have the combination of space, capacity, quality systems and marine access required for this scope of work, including COOEC in China, which successfully fabricated modules for LNG Canada's Phase 1."

A spokesperson for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said this expansion will patronize Canadian suppliers in other ways.

"Put together, these modules represent a singular part of a bigger project whose combined components stand to benefit Canadian manufacturers and made-in-Canada products writ large," the spokesperson, John Fragos, wrote to CBC News.

"This project, once operational, will change Canada’s energy status, drastically increase capacity, grow the economy and support Canadian producers and jobs alike."

Chinese state-owned producer holds 15% stake

Shell Canada Energy is the majority operator and project leader in Kitimat, holding a 40 per cent stake in LNG Canada.

State-owned PetroChina, the largest oil and gas producer, supplier and global investor in China, is a 15 per cent shareholder. The other three partners in the joint venture are Malaysia's Petronas (25 per cent), Japan's Mitsubishi Corporation (15 per cent) and the Korea Gas Corporation, or KOGAS (five per cent).

LNG exported from Kitimat is distributed by these five energy giants to Asian markets, based on their relative stake in the project.

Prior to a final investment decision for Phase 1 of the Kitimat facility in 2018, the joint venture sought and received an exemption from steep anti-dumping and countervailing duties that had been levied on fabricated industrial steel from China to protect Canada's steel industry.

Canada is among many countries that implement safeguards based on threats identified by its domestic steel producers. State-subsidized Chinese steelmakers produce more than China's domestic economy requires. The surplus ships overseas, undermining the cost-competitiveness of steel manufactured in countries like Canada that have higher-paid, unionized workers and higher environmental standards.

The value of the concession the federal government made to LNG Canada for Phase 1 was estimated at $1 billion.

The 2019 remission order published in the Canada Gazette said that LNG Canada, as well as the Singapore investors behind the Woodfibre LNG project in Squamish, B.C., (slated to come online in 2027), had told the finance department there was no Canadian capacity to produce what they needed.

They also framed the cost impact of these duties as having a "negative impact on investment decisions."

In other words: without it, the deal may not have gone ahead.

However, the duties in effect when the use of Chinese steel first drew negative attention in 2018 expired after five years and have not been renewed.

LNG Canada told CBC News there are no tariffs now on importing steel components from its Chinese supplier.

Champagne's office told told CBC News that the Canada Border Services Agency determines whether additional levies are required on Chinese steel to avoid predatory dumping. In this case, the measures were dropped and Canadian producers have not objected, because these particular components don't directly compete with what they make.

In 2024, other surtaxes and tariff rate quotas (volume restrictions) were placed on a list of specific Chinese steel products that could threaten the viability of Canada's domestic industry. That list, however, does not include what LNG Canada is importing.

Compressor stations target 70% Canadian steel

Other aspects of the Kitimat expansion may, however, use Canadian steel. For example, in order to expand storage and production at the export terminal, Coastal GasLink needs to expand the volume of gas moving in its pipeline network to Kitimat.

The new compression stations required along the pipeline will be "targeting almost 15,000 tonnes of steel from Canadian suppliers or mills, representing approximately 70 per cent of the steel required for that work," the LNG Canada spokesperson wrote.

Champagne's spokesperson added that this should be seen as a "floor, not a ceiling," and it speaks to how much Canadian steel has been used building and maintaining the pipeline network.

That apparent prioritization of Canadian supply chains would be more consistent with the assurances the prime minister gave in September 2025, when LNG Canada's Phase 2 expansion led the first list of priority referrals to the new federal Major Projects Office.

WATCH | Carney announces LNG Canada Phase 2: Carney, LNG Canada announce $33B Kitimat expansion to reach Asian markets | Duration closed caption 2:56 With new U.S. tariffs taking effect on Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney and LNG Canada announced a $33-billion investment to roughly double production capacity at the Kitimat, B.C., liquefied natural gas facility to serve Asian and European markets.

"These major projects will be at the heart of our new, comprehensive Buy Canadian policy," Carney said in his remarks a year ago. "To strengthen Canada's independence, resilience and security, we will build with Canadian steel, lumber, aluminum, and by Canadian engineers and tradespeople. We will be our own best customer."

Unlike public purchasing contracts now subject to the federal government's Buy Canadian procurement guidelines, the supply chains used by private sector energy companies are, as Carney noted Tuesday, up to them to decide.

Could Canadians do the work?

Members of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction (CISC) dispute the suggestion that Canadian steel fabricators aren't capable of building modules for Kitimat. LNG Canada hasn't reached out to them, but they now want to know more about the specifications, scope of work and project schedule before an assessment is made about what's really possible.

"The next phase of the LNG project represents a significant opportunity for Canada's steel sector. Through collaboration across the industry, we are confident that Canadian fabricators can deliver a substantial portion of the work, including the modules required for Phase 2," said spokesperson Rita Rahmati in an emailed statement.

"We look forward to engaging with LNG in the coming weeks to better understand the project requirements and explore how Canada's steel fabrication sector can contribute to this important project."

The Cedar LNG project in Kitimat is one of several now under construction in B.C. (Jesse Winter/Reuters)

Blair Dickerson, the president and and CEO of the Canadian Steel Producers Association, acknowledged to CBC News that ultimately procurement decisions are made by the builders and proponents of a project like this.

"Our message is clear: when we're building major projects in Canada, we should be looking to Canadian suppliers and Canadian steel wherever possible," he said. "Buying Canadian to build Canada will maximize the economic benefits of public investments to Canadian workers, manufacturers and communities, while reinforcing the long-term competitiveness and resilience of Canada's steel industry."

Eight years ago when the use of Chinese steel first sparked alarm, LNG Canada's Phase 1 was somewhat of a bespoke project. Phase 2, however, may come onstream alongside at least three other export terminals in B.C. alone over the next five years or so: Woodfibre LNG in Squamish, Cedar LNG in Kitimat, and Ksi Lisims in Gingolx.

Additional projects are also at the development stage, suggesting strong future demand for the steel products LNG terminal construction requires.

"After saying his major projects would ensure that Canada was 'our own best customer,' the prime minister is now telling suffering steelworkers that it's up to proponents 'to decide' whether Buy Canadian applies," said Hamilton Conservative MP Ned Kuruc in a statement on Friday.

"The fact that the steel fabrication cannot be done in Canada is another failure of Mr. Carney's government to create the environment for steelmaking here at home."

Shipping issues also in play

LNG Canada told CBC News that difficult transportation logistics were part of its market rationale for continuing to buy steel modules offshore.

"Marine access is essential," the spokesperson wrote. "Modules of this scale cannot be transported to Kitimat by road; they must be fabricated at a facility with direct access to tidewater and shipped by sea. Once in Kitimat, they can be received through LNG Canada's existing module offloading facility, moved into position and integrated into the plant."

The federal finance minister's office also echoed this reasoning, in its explanation to CBC News of why this decision by LNG Canada shouldn't be seen as contradicting or undermining the federal government's Buy Canadian efforts.

But the CISC says it's not true that a Canadian steel fabricator wouldn't be able to deliver modules to Kitimat's marine facility.

While road access for large components may be unfeasible, Canada does have rail networks to West Coast port facilities, where steel could be loaded onto ships for transport to Kitimat's offloading facility.

But a frequent complaint shared by Canadian manufacturers and exporters, labour unions and provincial governments, has been that Canada's rail and port infrastructure struggles with frequent backlogs and needs upgrades and expansion to meet the evolving needs of domestic supply chains.

World.title: Actor and advocate Michael J. Fox promoted to companion level in Order of Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Celebrated actor and Parkinson's disease activist Michael J. Fox said he felt both "pride" and "humility" while receiving a promotion within the Order of Canada on Friday.

Spectators stood and applauded Fox at Rideau Hall as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially named him to the companion level of the Order of Canada.

Rideau Hall says Fox was elevated to the companion level to honour his "powerful global advocacy and unflinching honesty about Parkinson's."

"It's so many things. But mostly it's just growing up in Canada, loving this country, loving what it stands for and how it's progressed and corrected course when it needed to, and stayed the course when it needed to," Fox told The Canadian Press following the ceremony.

"I picked all that up growing up. I love Canadian music, I love that Canadian content thing. At the end, you have a 65-year-old guy who's uniquely Canadian because of all those things."

Parkinson's is a progressive nervous system disorder that causes tremors, stiffness and slowness and is linked to depression and memory problems.

Fox, who went public with his Parkinson's diagnosis in 1998, has raised funds for research into the disease and has shared candid experiences about the challenges faced by those living with its symptoms.

"Canada was one of the early proving grounds for (deep brain stimulation)," Fox said, pointing to advances in Parkinson's research in Canada.

WATCH | Fox made companion of Order of Canada: Michael J. Fox promoted within Order of Canada | Duration 1:22 Famed actor Michael J. Fox has been promoted to companion of the Order of Canada, the highest level within the order. The Order of Canada is meant to recognize people who make 'extraordinary contributions to the nation,' according to the Governor General of Canada website. Fox is also a vocal advocate in raising awareness for people living with Parkinson's disease. The actor went public with news he had Parkinson's in 1998 and is a co-founder of the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research.

He was among 51 people inducted into, or promoted within, the Order of Canada on Friday.

Arbour said each inductee had demonstrated excellence and thanked them for their work.

"You could have used your talents solely to further your own success. Instead, you have chosen to use your skills, influence and energy to help others," she said in French.

"Because talent, as exceptional as it may be, is not sufficient on its own. It also takes the will to get involved and to take action to improve one's community and contribute to the common good."

Arbour said Fox is a "shining example of this."

"Your example reminds us of something that's very fundamental: sustainable progress requires that we move forward with courage, imagination and determination," she said.

"After all, back to the future has always been a much better idea than forward to the past."

The comment was in reference to Fox's iconic roles in the Back to the Future trilogy of movies.

Academics, artists among honourees

Yusuf Altintas, a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of British Columbia, was inducted as an officer of the Order of Canada, along with Nada Jabado, a professor at McGill University who is being honoured for her work in pediatric neuro-oncology.

Former Bank of Canada governor Stephen Poloz was inducted as an officer for helping facilitate Canada's international trade and promote its economic well-being.

Sculptor Ruth Elsie Abernethy was inducted as a member. Rideau Hall said she has created iconic life-size bronze pieces showcased around the world and that her work explores themes of gender, heritage and nation-building.

Pulitzer Prize-winning New York Times reporter Susanne Craig was invested as a member of the Order of Canada on Friday. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporter Susanne Craig was inducted as a member for her work with The New York Times, The Globe and Mail and The Wall Street Journal.

Rideau Hall described her as one of the most outstanding journalists of her generation, citing her coverage of contemporary issues in the United States.

Colin Roswell Clarke was inducted as a member for his work as founder and artistic director of the Toronto Youth Wind Orchestra program. Marcelle Dubois was inducted a member for her work revitalizing Quebec playwriting.

Patrick Joseph Lahey, co-founder of Triton Submarines, was inducted as a member for his work as one of the world's leading experts on submersibles and a leading voice for safe practices in the deep-diving industry, Rideau Hall said.

World.title: 12 Jewish teachers file human rights complaints against group of Ontario school boards, unions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Twelve Jewish teachers have filed human rights complaints against a group of Ontario school boards and teachers' unions, alleging they have experienced discrimination at their workplaces due to incidents of antisemitism.

The teachers, who have filed complaints with the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario, say institutions responsible for their workplaces not only failed to act, but in many cases penalized them when they did report discrimination.

Kathryn Marshall, an employment and human rights lawyer and founding partner of Marshall Law, a Toronto law firm, said Friday that the point of the complaints is to bring about change. She said the teachers face daily occurrences of hate.

"All of these teachers all went to their unions for support and the boards for support and help and they were ignored, which is why they're having to sue," Marshall said.

"We are asking the school boards and demanding that they protect the human rights of these teachers."

The complaints name the Toronto District School Board (TDSB), York Region District School Board (YRDSB), Simcoe County District School Board (SCDSB), Ottawa-Carleton District School Board (OCDSB), Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario (ETFO), the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation (OSSTF) and Ottawa-Carleton Elementary Teachers' Federation (OCETFO).

'There hasn't been action,' lawyer says

The teachers are seeking damages of $150,000 each for injury to their dignity and self-respect, as well as compensation for psychological counselling.

One teacher alleges the TDSB did not investigate or meaningfully address an incident in which a swastika was drawn on a desk in her classroom even though she made a complaint.

Another teacher said they witnessed students playing a game about Hitler in the schoolyard, while still another said a student played the Nazi anthem in class.

A third teacher said she was met with hostility and publicly reprimanded after she tried at a union meeting in Toronto to speak out about antisemitism at work.

A fourth teacher complained about the Star of David being removed repeatedly from the school's anti-hate bulletin board and said nothing was done.

"The common thing that a lot of these teachers have experienced is they've gone to their school boards to make complaints and there haven't been sanctions, there haven't been investigations, there hasn't been action," Marshall said.

"And in some cases, the teachers who made the complaints actually ended up being suspended, or they ended up being put on leave, or they even ended up being investigated and told: 'Actually, you're just being discriminatory.'"

Kathryn Marshall, an employment and human rights lawyer, says: 'All of these teachers all went to their unions for support and the boards for support and help and they were ignored, which is why they're having to sue.' (Olivia Bowden/CBC)

Teachers seeking financial compensation, policy changes

Along with monetary compensation, the teachers want the tribunal to order the boards and unions, within six months, to develop transparent, enforceable policies and processes to combat antisemitism in schools, with input from the Jewish community.

Although the teachers have filed applications to the tribunal individually, they will ask the tribunal to hear the complaints together.

Marshall said the teachers are not saying that having a view on the conflict in the Middle East, criticizing the Israeli government or supporting human rights in Gaza, is antisemitism.

"That is absolutely not what this case is about whatsoever. This case is about teachers who are scared to go to work because they are being subjected to hate because they're Jewish," she said.

Antisemitism has 'no place' in schools, TDSB says

CBC Toronto reached out to the school boards and unions for comment.

Ryan Bird, spokesperson for the TDSB, said the board doesn't comment on legal proceedings or matters involving individual employees but said it would respond to specific allegations during the tribunal process.

"All allegations of antisemitism and other forms of hate brought to the Board’s attention are thoroughly investigated and addressed," Bird said.

"Antisemitism has no place in our communities or schools. The Board has and will continue to work with community groups and agencies to combat antisemitism and to foster inclusive schools and workplaces where students and staff feel safe and welcome."

Christina Choo-Hum, spokesperson for the YRDSB, said the board is unable to comment on the complaints to "preserve the integrity" of the process.

She said the board is "committed to creating and sustaining safe, welcoming and inclusive learning and working spaces for all students and staff."

Boards to respond to allegations through tribunal

Sarah Kekewich, spokesperson for SCDSB, said the board also doesn't comment on legal proceedings or matters involving individual employees but it will respond to specific allegations through the tribunal process.

She said the board "remains committed to creating safe and inclusive working and learning environments for all staff and students."

Diane Pernari, spokesperson for the OCDSB, also declined to comment on the allegations, saying "all allegations of antisemitism and other forms of hate brought to the Board’s attention are thoroughly investigated and addressed."

Carla Pereira, spokesperson for the ETFO, said: "We do not comment on legal matters, including those that are before the Ontario Human Rights Tribunal."

The OSSTF and OCETFO did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.

World.content:
Article content

Whether this impression is fair or groundless, it exists (when I asked my 10,000 poll respondents to tap in the word or phrase they most associated with the Conservatives, they were as likely to write “Trump” as “Pierre”) and it could hardly be more damaging. Four years ago, my polling found that only a quarter of Canadians saw the U.S. as a threat. Today, only a quarter see their southern neighbour as an ally. Canadians are more likely to have an unfavourable view of Trump than of Vladimir Putin, and they think it’s more important to stand up to Washington than Beijing. Though Trump will be gone in fewer than 850 days, voters overwhelmingly think the U.S. relationship will matter at least as much in the next Canadian federal election as it does now. “Trump winning a second term proves we can’t trust them,” one Ontario voter told us. “Even if Pete Buttigieg or Kamala Harris is president in 2028, what’s going to stop President JD Vance doing the exact same thing in 2032?” In Canada, each party’s approach to the question will be a crucial test of its values, priorities and fitness for government.
