World.title: France: 400 schools closed as student protests continue
World.content:
Police have made around 2,000 arrests and dozens of people have been injured as student protests spread across France. Ministers have called for a "day of dialogue" but students have called for further strike action.

Over 400 schools and colleges across France remained closed on Friday as student protests over education-related grievances continued — with some turning violent.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray told reporters that 735 teaching establishments were "affected" in some way on Friday, "30% fewer than yesterday."

He said that three emergency services personnel had been injured responding, again an improvement on "31 yesterday," and condemned occasional "acts of extreme violence" among the wider protest movement.

Protests in Paris involved garbage containers and other detritus being set alight on the streets Image: Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo/picture alliance

The protests ​against teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and a lack of learning materials erupted at lycées (equivalent to US high schools) in the Paris region last month before spreading across the country this week.

Government ministers tried to strike a balance between empathetic messages to frustrated youth with presidential elections looming, and clear calls for calm in their public messaging.

"Calm must urgently return to high schools and universities," Europe and Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said online. "Yes, the right to demonstrate is inalienable. But the violence is inexcusable, and the cynical instrumentalization of youth for political ends is irresponsible."

Some of the roughly 400 schools or colleges that closed had sustained damage amid the demonstrations, with one of the worst hit being the Lycee Mandela in Nantes, which was expected to be out of action until mid-October after a fire in the entrance hall.

The facade of the Lycée Gaston Bachelard in Paris' 13th district also sustained severe fire damage on Friday Image: CLPRESS/ABACA/picture alliance

Student protests in France: damage, injuries, arrests

Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured, including 40 high school principals, according to Geffray.

Fires were started in at least two high schools on Thursday, while teachers were reportedly inadvertently ​splashed with petrol ⁠at a third in the southern city of Marseille, according to officials.

At ​least one car was torched in the eastern city of Strasbourg while riot police clashed with youths in Toulouse in the southwest.

In the southeastern region of Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes, authorities claimed that "at least €25 million" of damage has been done in their jurisdiction alone. The Ile de France region that includes Paris estimated damages around €7 million on Friday.

But students have also criticized what they see as a heavy-handed police response.

"You don't want to hear our words; you just fire tear gas," one student wrote on a placard outside the Lycée Voltaire in central Paris.



'Protest is a fundamental right,' reads one placard. 'You don't want to hear our words; you just fire tear gas,' reads another. Image: Sarah Meyssonnier/REUTERS

Minister Geffray told broadcasters on Friday morning that "violent individuals" were "infiltrating groups of students" and "taking the movement hostage" and called on parents to prevent their children from joining the protests.

"What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger," he said.

Geffray met with student representatives and trade unions later on Friday. After this meeting, student group leaders renewed their call for "concrete" responses to their demands, said the protests should continue, but also appealed to demonstrators to refrain from any violence or vandalism.

"If I could address a clear message to high schoolers: be smart. We are giving, once again, cause to those who wish to instrumentalize and discredit our cause. Be non-violent," Nahanael Combary of the Renouveau Lycéen group said.

France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Government blames far-left LFI

According to Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, French domestic intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Thursday that the movement has been instrumentalized by politicians from the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) – who have denied the allegations.

Veteran LFI leader and 2027 presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has indeed supported the protests but called on students to use non-violent methods.

"Students, teachers and educational staff are facing the same state of neglect and their positions and claims should be respected," he wrote in a statement earlier this week, calling for "disciplined struggle, no panic, no irritation."

Meanwhile, student union bodies have called for a day of mass protest next Tuesday, October 6, under the slogan: "Police out of schools! No to the repression of student mobilization!"

"The police have no place in front of educational establishments," read a statement. "We support the ongoing mobilization and call for it to be reinforced."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: FlyDubai 'hero' pilot speaks for first time
World.content:
India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Captain Smit Machchhar via video call. Meanwhile, authorities in the UAE and Israel said an investigation is making progress.

The Indian Flydubai pilot who was stabbed by his copilot in an apparent attempt to crash the plane has spoken about his ordeal for the first time.

After being seriously wounded, Captain Smit Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door. This enabled other passengers to enter the cockpit and restrain the copilot, while a deadheading pilot took control of the aircraft.

"I had so many wounds. I had fallen down," Machchhar told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi via video call from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi. "I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realized that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives."

Captain Smit Machchhar is currently hospitalized in Abu Dhabi Image: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP

Some 180 passengers were on board the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, which was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, due to the situation. Most passengers were Israeli nationals.

Anwar Gargash, an adviser to the UAE president, took to social media on Friday to say Machchhar deserved "the highest recognition for embodying courage and responsibility in the face of a terrorist act and an imminent catastrophe," all while calling him a "true hero."

The suspected attacker, an Omani national, was arrested upon landing in Saudi Arabia, with the motive still being unclear, with Israel saying it believes it was an attempted Islamist attack.

Official labels incident 'terrorist act'

A senior official from the United Arab Emirates on Friday labeled the incident as a terrorist attack. Israel used similar terms to describe the incident.

Flydubai CEO Ghaith Al Ghaith said the company will carry out a full investigation of the incident.

"It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts," he said in a statement.

The company said it will suspend its flights to Tel Aviv until at least October 15.

Flydubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attempt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Israeli officials to investigate suspect: report

A source also told Reuters that Israeli officials are expected to investigate the flight's co-pilot, currently held in the UAE. The source emphasized it was the UAE who's responsible for the investigation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the country was looking into whether the co-pilot had been instructed by anyone.

"Whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price, Netanyahu said.

Netanyahu said the suspect had gone through "Islamist radical indoctrination," adding it was clear the man was "suicidal."

Many Israelis were stranded in the UAE as a result of the flight suspension between the two countries following the incident, with Israeli airlines receiving the necessary approvals to start repatriating Israeli nationals back to Israel.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue
World.content:
Spain's minority government suffered defeat in parliament as it tried to push through a pair of emergency measures aimed at making housing more affordable. A pensioner's eviction and protests led to the bid.

Spain's parliament has narrowly voted down a pair of emergency government decrees aiming to quell widespread protests against rising rental costs for housing.

Hundreds of protesters were gathered outside the parliament in Madrid amid the marathon debate culminating in a pair of votes on Friday. They yelled "shame" and "your profits, our misery," as news of the measures being quashed filtered through.

Spain has been gripped by protests for around a week, including a tent city set up in central Madrid, ignited by the eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment that threw the more longstanding issue of unaffordable housing costs into sharp focus.

Why and how did the emergency decrees fail?

Left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority government in Spain and so relies on opposition support to legislate.

Sanchez spoke at the close of a marathon 5-hour debate in the Chamber of Deputies ahead of the vote, urging members: "Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think."

Sanchez tried to rally majority support for the measures at the last in parliament, but could not succeed Image: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

One Catalan party that sometimes supports Sanchez's government, the economically right-leaning Junts group, joined the opposition in voting down the measures.

The first emergency decree, which the government said would stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder and provide tax incentives to encourage renting, failed by a narrow margin of 178-172.

The second decree, which sought to make residential leases automatically renewable by tenants, fell further short of a majority at 184-166.

Opponents to the measures argued, among other things, that they risked compounding the situation by reducing housing supply.

Some also argued that Sanchez should respond to the deadlock by calling early elections, possibly initiating a wholesale change of government.

Rising rents were a sensitive issue in Spain for years, but one particularly emotive eviction brought it to the boil Image: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

What did protesters say after the vote?

The Tenants' Union which had led protests across Spain said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Saturday, aiming to continue heaping pressure on the coalition and opposition alike.

"The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighborhoods," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said. "We're aiming for a general strike."

The current wave of protests, albeit concerning an issue that's been bubbling away near the surface for years, was triggered by the high-profile eviction of 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had occupied for almost all of her life.

Maricarmen Abascal has since been granted a reprieve, but the more widespread attempts to improve the situation remain stalled for now Image: Francesco Militello Mirto/IPA/ZUMA/picture alliance

How tough is Spain's housing market?

The investment company owning Abascal's building reversed the measure in her case this week but only after the issue had become a symbol of growing frustration of housing costs.

Rents have roughly doubled in Spain in the last decade and young people, facing one of Europe's toughest labor markets for school-leavers and graduates, frequently live with their parents past the age of 30.

"People have said 'enough is enough;' this ⁠cannot ​go on. The housing problem must be resolved; structural measures must be taken, and this cannot ​continue," Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday.

The next step after Friday's failed vote in parliament is difficult to identify. Sanchez has so far ruled out calling early elections. He could try to formulate another emergency decree or decrees in response to the protests, but any such move would need to overcome the same hurdles in parliament.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: "NAZA": Israeli military issues statement on film
World.content:
The award-winning documentary "NAZA" continues to spark controversy in Israel. The Israeli military has now published a multi-page statement calling the film's portrayal "distorted."

When it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival in mid-September, "NAZA" received a 25-minute-long standing ovation and the Special Jury Prize. But in Israel, the documentary has fueled heated debate.

Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar described the work of filmmakers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham "treason against the state" and urged that their citizenship be revoked. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also sharply criticized the documentary.

Now the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has also rejected the film's allegations about its conduct during the war in Gaza. In a multi-page document , the military accuses the filmmakers of presenting a "distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture." The film, it says, is based on "substantial factual errors" resulting from "manipulative misrepresentations of reality."

An insider's look at the war

The 80-minute documentary examines the Israel Defense Forces' operations during the war in Gaza. It is based on interviews conducted with 24 anonymous military and intelligence personnel, who describe internal procedures and decision-making processes involved in selecting targets in the Gaza Strip. According to the interviewees, high civilian casualty estimates were, in some cases, deliberately factored into these decisions.

The IDF rejects those claims. It says it has never planned or carried out attacks while anticipating hundreds of civilian deaths. It also disputes the film's claim that artificial intelligence selected targets without human oversight, saying people have always made decisions about targets and attacks.

The military also accuses the filmmakers of omitting important facts. According to the IDF, the film fails to show the role of military legal advisors and commanders in reviewing and authorizing attacks or the measures it says it takes to protect civilians. It also argues that the film does not adequately address the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, in which over 1,200 people were killed and 250 people were taken hostage.

Several human rights organizations and a UN commission have accused Israel of committing acts of genocide in Gaza. According to health authorities in Gaza and other sources, at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began.

'NAZA' opens in theaters worldwide

Speaking at the awards ceremony in Venice in mid-September, co-director Yuval Abraham said: "We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist. That is why it's really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film."

Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham also worked on the film "No Other Land," which won an Oscar for Best Documentary Feature in 2025.

Israeli leaders condemn acclaimed Gaza documentary 'NAZA' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"NAZA" comes from the Hebrew term "Nezek Agavi," meaning collateral damage. According to a soldier interviewed in the film, the acronym is used within the military to refer to the estimated number of civilians who could be killed in an attack.

Numerous human rights organizations, including the Israeli group B'Tselem, have expressed their support for the filmmakers. After its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, "NAZA" is now showing in theaters worldwide.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: El Congreso tumba los decretos de vivienda y abona el terreno para un adelanto electoral
World.content:
Sánchez, a PP, Vox y Junts: “La historia les juzgará antes de lo que creen y con más contundencia de la que imaginan”

El debate de los dos decretos sobre vivienda, dominado por la presión en la calle, con centenares de personas llegadas de la acampada de la vecina Puerta del Sol gritando a las puertas, se ha convertido en una especie de juicio sumarísimo contra Junts, pero también contra el PP y Vox, por tumbar las esperanzas que miles de personas habían puesto en la aprobación de estos textos para impedir desahucios como el de Maricarmen Abascal. El Congreso los ha tumbado, lo que ha abonado el terreno a un posible adelanto electoral.

La Cámara ha rechazado los decretos que aprobó el Gobierno el pasado martes. La primera norma ha caído con 172 síes y 178 noes y la segunda, con 166 a favor y 184 en contra (en este caso, han votado no PNV y Coalición Canaria, que sí han apoyado el primer decreto).

La consigna era generalizada en toda la izquierda. Todos acusaron a Junts, y de paso al PP y Vox, de “entregarse a los fondos buitre”. Àgueda Micó, de Compromís, fue clara: “El PP, Vox y Junts venderían hasta a su madre por una caricia de los poderosos. Su patria es la cartera. Vienen tiempos oscuros. PP, Vox y Junts están trabajando para los fondos buitre. Que continúe la lucha, que esto acaba de empezar”, clamó. Muchos discursos parecían un arranque de campaña electoral, con el fantasma del adelanto sobrevolando el hemiciclo.

El Gobierno, algo más comedido, hizo un último intento de convencer a Junts de que cambie de opinión. La ministra de Vivienda, Isabel Rodríguez, ha recordado una por una todas las medidas de Junts que se han incorporado al decreto. Ha llegado a decir que están ahí el 90% de ellas. Y ha recordado que, mientras el PNV y Coalición Canaria, con ideas parecidas en estos asuntos a Junts, sí van a votar a favor, ellos ni siquiera asumen abstenerse.

El propio presidente del Gobierno, por sorpresa, subió al final del debate, algo muy poco usual, para exigir al PP y a Vox que reconsideren su posición y permitan pasar el decreto al menos con su abstención. “Si no, la historia les juzgará antes de lo que creen y con más contundencia de la que imaginan”, dijo, abriendo la puerta así a un adelanto electoral inminente con ese “antes de lo que creen”.

04:12 Cinco intervenciones del debate en el Congreso Pablo Monge Foto: El presidente Sánchez aplaude a la ministra de Vivienda tras su intervención en el pleno este viernes.

Después de una intensa negociación en la que el Gobierno se siente engañado por Junts, que le hizo creer que aprobaría el decreto después de negociarlo, Rodríguez mostró su enorme frustración, pero a la vez ofreció a los independentistas la tramitación vía decreto ley para poder incorporar modificaciones si dejaban pasar el decreto con su abstención.

Pero todo fue inútil. La decisión estaba tomada y, a pesar de este durísimo debate y de la presión en la calle, y en contra de la opinión mayoritaria de sus propios votantes —según explicó el portavoz de ERC—, Gabriel Rufián, la de Junts, Miriam Nogueras, se mantuvo inflexible y defendió que, aunque se queden solos, lo hacen para evitar que salga adelante un decreto “que es un engaño y no resuelve los problemas”.

El ambiente de fin de legislatura es muy evidente en el Congreso y por eso muchos diputados de la izquierda se molestaron cuando Nogueras dijo que ellos son los únicos que no están pensando en elecciones, cuando parece evidente que su decisión de tumbar los decretos puede precipitarlas. Varios portavoces dijeron que a Junts, PP y Vox “les mueve más la cartera que las ideas”, porque creen que están defendiendo los intereses de los fondos buitre.

La portavoz de JxCat, Míriam Nogueras. Pablo Monge

El ministro de Derechos Sociales, Pablo Bustinduy, que defendió el segundo decreto con vehemencia y aplauso de varios grupos, no solo el suyo, centró buena parte del tiro en poner a “las derechas” del PP, Vox y Junts ante una responsabilidad histórica. Les acusó de estar “vendiendo el país a la oligarquía extranjera” y les retó a las próximas elecciones: “El pueblo tiene memoria y se va a acordar de quienes le han traicionado”.

El portavoz de ERC, Gabriel Rufián, muestra un billete de 50 euros a los diputados de Junts. Pablo Monge

Rufián, de ERC, incluso mostró un billete de 50 euros para expresar su crítica a Junts y lanzó un mensaje muy duro: “Esta pasada de frenada es legendaria. No están calibrando lo que está pasando aquí. No son conscientes de lo que hay ahí fuera. Ustedes van con escolta policial. Pido contención a la gente. Pero usted, señora Nogueras, es una mala política; se está cargando a un partido que es necesario para mi país. Vuelvan al pujolismo, dejen de imitar a Orriols o Ayuso”, le espetó. El portavoz del PSOE, Patxi López, cargó también muy duro contra Junts, ya en un ambiente electoral. “Dejen de engañar, estos decretos funcionan, ya están parando desahucios. Señores de Junts, no vamos a retirar los decretos, no podemos perder más tiempo. Y además protegen a los pequeños propietarios, no hagan más trampas. Ustedes han negociado estos decretos. Cada voto en contra es una condena para todas las Maricármenes de este país”, insistió.

Muchos portavoces apuntaron a las urnas. Tesh Sidi, de Sumar, en un discurso muy aplaudido por su grupo, abrió esa puerta, como si ya fuera inminente. “La derecha siempre va a estar con los fondos, con Blackstone, pero nuestra patria son los barrios. La victoria está a la vuelta de la esquina. Frente a sus áticos, nuestras plazas. Frente a su miedo, nuestra esperanza. ¡Lo pagarán en las urnas!“, clamó.

La ministra Rodríguez hizo también un intento por no centrar toda la presión en Junts, sino enfocar también en el PP y Vox, imprescindibles también para tumbar el decreto. Si finalmente hay convocatoria electoral, esa parece ser ya la estrategia del Ejecutivo: movilizar a la izquierda con la vivienda y culpar a PP, Vox y Junts de todos los desahucios que puedan llegar ahora. “Hoy ustedes pueden ser relevantes para España”, le dijo Rodríguez al PP. “No lo hagan por nosotros. Háganlo por sus votantes. Cuando un fondo buitre echa a todos los vecinos de sus casas, no les pregunta a quién votan. Si se ponen del lado de los fondos buitre, están inhabilitados para gobernar este país”, les lanzó. Y después, tras recordar que Isabel Díaz Ayuso llegó incluso a burlarse de Maricarmen, aún en el hospital, fue más lejos: “¿Qué les ofrecen los fondos? ¿Qué clase de patriota elige a un especulador frente a una señora de 87 años que sale en camilla de su casa? Los próximos desahucios serán su responsabilidad”, les espetó.

El PNV y Coalición Canaria, frente al no de Junts, reivindicaron que a ellos tampoco les gusta todo el decreto, pero han entendido que había que ceder en algunas cosas para aprobar algo en esta situación de emergencia. Maribel Vaquero fue clara: “Hemos negociado, dejándonos pelos en la gatera como la ley del suelo [que el PNV aceptó retirar porque la vetaba Podemos], pero hemos apostado por un sí crítico, con muchas dudas, por responsabilidad”.

Mientras, Carlos Hernández Quero, de Vox, se burló de toda la política de vivienda del Gobierno y defendió el voto en contra de este decreto, pero sin entrar a los desahucios que eso puede provocar, concentrándose, como también dijo Nogueras, en que estos decretos sacarían viviendas del mercado y tendrían consecuencias aún peores para los que buscan una casa en alquiler.

El líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, saluda a Juan Bravo, tras su intervención durante el pleno este viernes. J.J. Guillén (EFE)

Juan Bravo, del PP, defendió también el no de su grupo y reivindicó que la principal solución al problema es construir más vivienda, y detalló las propuestas del PP, como una “ley antiokupas”. “Este decreto no habría evitado el decreto de Maricarmen; no le da una sola vivienda más a un joven. Votamos que no a que utilicen el drama de una mujer de 87 años para tapar su fracaso. Nosotros elegimos construir vivienda”, clamó. Las posiciones estaban muy claras, los dos bloques se han consolidado, pero la gran novedad es que Junts ya está definitivamente en el de la derecha, con PP y Vox, y con esa decisión puede precipitar el adelanto electoral.

World.title: La intervención para bajar el alquiler arrasa en la izquierda y se impone también entre los votantes del PP y Vox
World.content:
Más de dos tercios de la sociedad abogan por medidas para frenar los precios aunque sea a costa del casero, incluyendo más del 55% de los votantes del PP y Vox, según una encuesta de 40dB. en pleno debate tras el desahucio de Maricarmen

Ante la disyuntiva entre un mercado de la vivienda que se regula a sí mismo en base a la oferta y la demanda o una intervención del Estado para fijar reglas a costa del lucro privado, en la sociedad española se impone con claridad la segunda opción. Es decir, se imponen las visiones dominantes en los principales partidos de izquierdas. Pero no solo ganan entre los votantes progresistas, también entre quienes respaldan al PP y Vox, aunque por menos distancia. Así lo pone de relieve la encuesta sobre vivienda de 40dB. para EL PAÍS y la Cadena SER elaborada con 2.000 entrevistas online entre el 25 de septiembre, dos días después del desahucio de Maricarmen Abascal, y el 28 de septiembre, un día antes de que el Ejecutivo aprobara los dos decretos con los que ha intentado dar una respuesta urgente a la conmoción social suscitada por el caso.

Más información EDITORIAL | Hagan su trabajo

Un 67,5% de los encuestados —incluyendo la mayoría de los votantes no solo del PSOE (82,6%), Sumar (95,8%) y Podemos (85,4%), sino también del PP (56,5%) y Vox (55,2%)— están a favor de las políticas de limitación de los precios de la vivienda aunque su aplicación implique una pérdida de rentabilidad del casero. Quienes así lo ven son mayoría incluso entre los caseros (56,5%), según las respuestas recabadas. En cambio, los que piensan que solo el mercado debe establecer los precios sin que el Estado desempeñe ningún papel, aunque esto limite el acceso a la vivienda, se quedan en un 21,7%.

Así que el laissez-faire está en minoría cuando se habla de derecho a techo y menos de una cuarta parte de la sociedad defiende que el mercado imponga las reglas de la vivienda, de acuerdo con los datos de la encuesta, cuyos resultados muestran que importantes medidas en línea con las aprobadas por el Gobierno el martes —y cuya convalidación se votará este viernes en el Congreso con el anunciado rechazo de Junts— cuentan con un aval social mayoritario.

Aprobación mayoritaria

El trabajo demoscópico fue diseñado antes de la aprobación de los dos decretos del Gobierno, por lo que no se pregunta en concreto por puntos incluidos en los mismos, ni en el de función social —el que a priori parecía tener más opciones de salir adelante hasta que Junts anunció su rechazo este jueves por la noche— ni en el de estabilización de los contratos de alquiler. No obstante, sí lo hace por algunas medidas que encajan con lo recogido en el primero de ellos. Y obtienen aprobación mayoritaria.

Entre el 70% y 75% está “de acuerdo” o “muy de acuerdo” con aplazar los desahucios a personas vulnerables, regular el precio de los alquileres y ponerles topes anuales. Son medidas que además cuentan con más respaldo que rechazo en los electorados no solo de izquierdas y entre los inquilinos, sino también —aunque más tibiamente— en los de derechas y entre los caseros.

Las medidas que generan más consenso —y que también encajan con lo que recoge el decreto— son ampliar la oferta de vivienda social (82,4%), algo en lo que coinciden todos los partidos y en lo que también están ampliamente de acuerdo sus electorados; y dar ventajas fiscales a los pequeños propietarios (79,7%) para que alquilen a precio asequible, una opción que suele ser recibida con escepticismo o rechazo por Sumar y Podemos pero entre cuyos votantes genera, como en todos los demás, más adhesión que censura.

De menos apoyo, aunque superior al 50%, dispone la idea de subir impuestos a los propietarios de viviendas vacías, posibilidad que también figura en el decreto de función social. En contraste con el respaldo de los encuestados de izquierdas y los inquilinos, a este incremento fiscal se opone la mayoría tanto de los caseros como de los que prevén votar a Alberto Núñez Feijóo (PP) y a Santiago Abascal (Vox) en las generales.

La medida que menos apoyo cosecha, la única por debajo del 50% de apoyo, es limitar el número de viviendas que una persona puede tener en propiedad, a pesar de que entre quienes prevén votar al PSOE, Sumar y Podemos son más quienes la defienden que quienes se oponen. Esta medida no está recogida en ninguno de los dos decretos que se votarán este viernes. Tampoco la normativa que llega al Congreso se centra en los pisos turísticos, un asunto sobre el que la encuesta deja un dato: no permitirlos en edificios residenciales cuenta con el respaldo de un 67,9%, más de dos terceras partes de los encuestados. Aunque los de izquierdas defienden la posibilidad de este veto con más ahínco, también son más los que se alinean con esta posibilidad en la derecha.

De la encuesta también se desprende que hay un extendido apoyo a una de las principales medidas de la Ley de Vivienda impulsada por el Gobierno del PSOE y Unidas Podemos y aprobada en 2023. Casi dos tercios de la ciudadanía considera “necesario” limitar los precios del alquiler en zonas tensionadas, una bandera de la izquierda pero que también apoya más de la mitad de los votantes de derechas. Y ello a pesar de que las direcciones de los partidos conservadores se oponen, algo especialmente relevante en el caso del PP, que tiene la presidencia de 11 comunidades autónomas y sería clave para el pleno de desarrollo de esta previsión legal.

Un dato que permite aproximarse al pulso social antes de las votaciones de este viernes: casi el 70% valora negativamente el rechazo del Congreso al anterior intento del Gobierno de aprobar medidas para aplazar desahucios, tumbado por el PP, Vox y Junts. Aunque esta valoración negativa es más intensa entre los votantes de izquierdas y los inquilinos, también entre los electores del PP y de Vox y entre los caseros son más quienes la comparten que quienes no.

El ‘caso Maricarmen’

La encuesta muestra que el caso Maricarmen ha tenido un formidable impacto. Más de un 93% de los encuestados han oído hablar del tema. Pero no hay un consenso transversal sobre algunos de los debates que ha abierto. Son mayoría (61,8%) quienes consideran que “no se puede desalojar de su vivienda a una persona mayor sin alternativa habitacional”. Esta opinión es muy mayoritaria entre los votantes de izquierdas, mientras que los del PP y Vox priorizan el derecho del propietario a decidir sobre su vivienda.

También hay brecha ideológica sobre la respuesta en la calle a casos como el de Maricarmen. Casi dos tercios de la sociedad están de acuerdo con el ejercicio de la resistencia pacífica para impedir desahucios. Se trata de una opinión de consenso entre los votantes progresistas. Sin embargo, el asunto divide por la mitad a los electorados del PP y Vox.

La responsabilidad del Gobierno

La dificultad para acceder a una vivienda es el segundo problema que más preocupa en España, por detrás de la inflación, en realidad es un asunto relacionado. En 2023, era el cuarto tema que más inquietaba. Ha avanzado dos puestos. Se trata de una preocupación transversal, compartida —con matices— por todas las generaciones y votantes de todos los partidos.

Ahora bien, que preocupe a izquierda y derecha no significa que se le dé la misma prioridad. Mientras que los votantes del PSOE, Sumar y Podemos creen que es el asunto más urgente que debe atender la política, los del PP y Vox lo colocan por detrás de la inmigración. También hay diferencias ideológicas al preguntar por los factores que provocan el problema. Invitados a citar dos causantes principales, quienes prevén apoyar a partidos de izquierdas identifican en mayor medida a los “fondos buitre” y a los pisos turísticos que quien piensan a hacerlo al PP y a Vox.

Aunque el Gobierno del PSOE y Sumar se esmera en trasladar la idea de que no solo al Ejecutivo compete el problema de la vivienda, y que las comunidades autónomas —la mayoría en manos del PP— son las que tienen las mayores atribuciones, la ciudadanía identifica al al poder estatal como el principal responsable. A la hora de exigir soluciones, un 43,3% señalan al Gobierno central, muy por delante de los que apuntan a las comunidades (19,3%) y los ayuntamientos (5,3%).

La patata caliente de la vivienda pone así la mayor presión en el Ejecutivo de Pedro Sánchez, que cuenta para afrontar la situación con un dato a favor. El PSOE es el partido que un mayor porcentaje de la población ve como el más capacitado para afrontar el problema. Un 18,5% le otorgan este estatus, por delante del PP y Vox (empatados a 14,4%). Hasta un 22,6% cree que ninguno está capacitado para encarar el desafío.

World.title: La estafa del falso empleado de banca
World.content:
Recibir un SMS que alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en nuestra cuenta bancaria puede evitar que seamos víctima de un robo, excepto si no ha sido el banco quien realmente lo ha emitido

En la estafa del falso empleado de banca el delincuente primero envía un mensaje con una alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en la cuenta y facilita un enlace o un número de teléfono al que llamar. Ya en la conversación, intenta convencer a la víctima de que su dinero está en peligro para que autorice operaciones que resultarán fraudulentas

En 2025, Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) registró 25.133 casos de phishing. Durante los dos últimos años, tanto la Policía Nacional como la Guardia Civil y el Banco de España han emitido alertas sobre el aumento de las llamadas de falsos empleados bancarios.

TÉCNICAS DE MANIPULACIÓN

Autoridad Suplantan a profesionales pertenecientes a bancos a los que la víctima concede poder y confianza Urgencia Crean la sensación de que hay poco tiempo para actuar, lo que evita que la víctima reflexione o consulte con alguien Sobrecarga de información técnica Emplean jerga bancaria para intimidar y hacer creer que dominan una situación compleja Aumento gradual de las peticiones Incluye a la víctima en grupos de aplicaciones de mensajería para hacerle creer que mucha gente ya está ganando dinero

CIBEREXPERTO NOMBRE Jordi Sánchez CARGO Experto en fraude de CaixaBank “Durante la llamada, el estafador te hace creer que te está guiando para solucionar tu problema, pero en realidad, está intentando que tu hagas exactamente lo que necesita, emitir operaciones bancarias, descargar aplicaciones o facilitar información, como códigos o datos de tarjetas” Play / Pause CÓMO EVITAR LA ESTAFA DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA 1 Sospechar de mensajes inesperados. No clicar en ningún enlace que aparezca en el mensaje ni llamar al número que ofrecen. Ante la duda, siempre se debe llamar a los números oficiales del banco 2 Desconfiar de la urgencia y de las amenazas.Mensajes como “Su cuenta será bloqueada” buscan que se actúe sin pensar 3 No compartir claves ni códigos de verificación. El banco nunca solicitará contraseñas u otros códigos de seguridad 4 No descargar archivos ni instalar aplicaciones. Los estafadores pueden pedir que se descarguen programas que en realidad les están dando acceso al teléfono de la víctima

Una estafa que ha evolucionado. Este fraude comenzó como un SMS y una llamada, pero hoy se dan variantes como la que busca robar información de las tarjetas bancarias mediante el uso de la tecnología NFC del teléfono móvil. Este sistema de comunicación inalámbrica permite compartir información entre otros, tarjetas y móviles, y realizar pagos sin contacto. Los estafadores solicitan a la víctima que se descargue una aplicación maliciosa y que acerque la tarjeta al smartphone. Así, sus datos son enviados a otro teléfono de los atacantes, donde crearán una tarjeta de forma virtual con la que intentar sacar dinero o comprar en comercios.

El teléfono puede parecer auténtico. Los estafadores pueden hacer que en la pantalla del móvil de la víctima figure el mismo número que utiliza el banco para atender a sus clientes o que el SMS aparezca en el mismo hilo que las comunicaciones legítimas mediante una técnica que se conoce como spoofing (que significa suplantación).

Conocen datos personales de su víctima. En muchos casos, disponen de información de su objetivo, como el banco del que es cliente, parte del DNI o la dirección de correo electrónico.

Si ya se ha caído en la estafa. Se debe poner en conocimiento del banco de inmediato para que se puedan adoptar las medidas operativas oportunas. También es muy importante guardar las evidencias, como capturas de pantalla, SMS, correos y registro de llamadas. Presentar una denuncia ante la Policía Nacional o la Guardia Civil.

OTROS CASOS DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA

Cada semana aparecen noticias con nuevas maneras de embaucar a ciudadanos con una estafa de este tipo:

World.title: Soy presidente de mi comunidad y el administrador se niega a entregarme el acta de la última junta. ¿Qué puedo hacer?
World.content:
Pregunta. Somos una comunidad de cuatro portales y cuatro presidentes. Yo soy uno de ellos. El 12 de mayo tuvimos reunión general donde se acordó el cambio de presidentes y otras cuestiones, como los arreglos de los tejados. Pedí a la administradora cuatro veces el acta de la reunión general, tanto por WhatsApp como por email y no hay manera de que lo mande. ¿Qué puedo hacer? R. Calzada Gútiez

Respuesta. La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal (LPH) establece en su artículo 19 que el acta debe quedar cerrada con las firmas del presidente y del secretario al finalizar la reunión o dentro de los diez días naturales siguientes. Asimismo, dispone que el acta debe remitirse a los propietarios conforme al procedimiento previsto en la ley. Además, el secretario está obligado a custodiar los libros de actas y a conservar durante cinco años las convocatorias, comunicaciones, apoderamientos y demás documentación relevante de las reuniones.

Estas disposiciones implican que, una vez celebrada la junta, los acuerdos deben formalizarse mediante la correspondiente acta, firmada por el presidente y el secretario dentro del plazo legal, y comunicarse a los propietarios en el domicilio designado a efectos de notificaciones. Por tanto, el secretario-administrador tiene la obligación de remitir a todos los propietarios, incluidos los miembros de la junta, copia del acta con los acuerdos adoptados.

Además, el artículo 20 de la LPH establece entre las funciones del administrador actuar como secretario de la junta y custodiar, a disposición de los propietarios, la documentación de la comunidad. Entre esta documentación se encuentran las actas de las reuniones de los últimos cinco años, que el administrador debe conservar y poner a disposición de los propietarios, junto con cualquier otra documentación comunitaria que pueda solicitarse.

Por ello, si el administrador no ha remitido el acta con los acuerdos aprobados o no facilita el acceso a documentación de interés comunitario, puede exigírsele su entrega mediante un requerimiento fehaciente, como un burofax con certificación de texto y acuse de recibo, fijando un plazo para su cumplimiento.

Si, pese a ello, no atiende el requerimiento, su conducta podría considerarse contraria a sus obligaciones legales y profesionales. En ese caso, podría presentarse una queja ante el Colegio de Administradores al que pertenezca, reclamar los daños y perjuicios que, en su caso, se hayan ocasionado o acordar en junta de propietarios la resolución del contrato de prestación de servicios y el nombramiento de un nuevo administrador.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Fries with that? Homes near Amsterdam TikTok queue sell for less
World.content:
Homes near Fabel Friet, an Amsterdam chip shop whose TikTok-fuelled queues have become one of the city’s more unlikely tourist attractions, sell for less than comparable homes just streets away, according to a TU Delft study.

The research, reported by local broadcaster AT5, came out this week at the same time as the city council and the shop’s owners faced off in court over the queue and how to deal with public nuisance caused by it.

PhD researcher Rosa van der Drift compared the sale prices of 6,233 Amsterdam homes between 2015 and 2023, taking account of factors such as size and condition. Homes within 500 metres of the shop sold for 4.88% less on average, or about €41,000.

Within 70 metres, the gap widened to 11.4%. The study does not establish any correlation with causation.

Old licence

The court case was made by a group of residents against the city council, not the business. They argue the council did not properly weigh their interests when it granted Fabel Friet an operating licence, and want the licence withdrawn or its conditions tightened.

In 2024, a judge suspended a council rule limiting the queue to 10 people after Fabel Friet called it unworkable.

On Tuesday, one resident told the court there were people eating chips outside “every day, from 11 in the morning until 9 in the evening”, AT5 reported. The residents’ lawyer said a serious accident on the crowded bridge was only a matter of time.

The owners told the court their crowd managers keep the queue safe, the street is cleaned 4 times a day and crowds are down 23% since they opened other branches. For a while they hired a falcon 3 times a week to scare off the gulls, but stopped when residents began using it as evidence against them.

A representative of mayor Femke Halsema acknowledged that the old licence had not been effective enough, and said stricter conditions had been added to the current one about 6 months ago. “It is complicated,” the representative said, according to AT5. “You are so successful, is that not allowed?”

The judge urged both sides to find common ground, reminding the residents of the Dutch saying that a good neighbour is better than a distant friend. She will rule within 6 weeks, but only on the old licence, because objections to the current licence have yet to be decided.

World.title: Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings
World.content:
The cabinet has promised to rewrite part of its new tax plan for savings and investments, just two days after announcing it, so that fewer people with modest savings are impacted.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen, of the right-wing liberal VVD, made the commitment in parliament on Thursday after MPs from both opposition and coalition parties attacked the plan.

“I have discussed this with the prime minister and with the coalition,” the Financieel Dagblad reported him as saying. “We are prepared to make changes. There will be a proposal to spare small savers.”

Under the plan presented on Tuesday, people would pay 36% tax on returns above €1,000 a year from 2028, down from €1,800 in the earlier version of the reform. Heinen also said he still believed the plan would exempt couples with up to €100,000 in savings.

No funding yet

The minister said he did not yet know how the cabinet would make up the shortfall. Small savers were the main source of funding for the box 3 overhaul, which reports say could cost up to €20 billion.

“We don’t have many levers to pull,” Heinen said. “And every choice you make is enormously complicated.”

The cabinet will send the bill to the Council of State, the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, without an alternative source of funding. Heinen said he would come up with proposals by October 12, when MPs debate the cabinet’s annual package of tax changes.

He also said he would look again at a temporary measure for next year, which would cut the tax-free allowance from €59,357 to €30,846 per person and raise the tax rate. You can find out more about how the changes would affect you in our box 3 explainer.

World.title: Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch royal family, the House of Orange-Nassau, earned an estimated €576 million from slavery, mostly in the former Dutch East Indies, according to a new investigation into the monarchy.

The research was commissioned by king Willem-Alexander, who granted access to the royal archives and funded the inquiry.

“All stadtholders, kings, and queens, at least up to and including Wilhelmina, were convinced of the legitimacy of colonialism and its importance for the Netherlands,” lead researcher Gert Oostindie said during a ceremony on Friday to present the findings.

The 2,000 page report has been published into five books and was presented to the king. Willem-Alexander described the conclusions as “heartbreaking and confronting” during the gathering at the Academy Building in Leiden.

“I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future to the best of my ability,” he said.

According to the research, the royals earned very little from the transatlantic slave trade, not because they were opposed but because they were unsuccessful.

Oostindie’s work found that while monarchs voiced support for the institution, few had a direct impact on policy.

Only King William I, who was in power from 1813 to 1840, had a direct hand in colonial slavery. Prior to that, leaders left it to the States General, the country’s early administrative assembly, or to the powerful Dutch East India Company (VOC).

After the reign of William I, monarchs were forced to share power with an increasingly important parliament, which made most of the policy decisions.

Willem-Alexander asked Oostindie, a former professor of colonial history, to conduct the investigation in 2022. Sixty researchers were involved in the nearly four year project.

In 2023, the king formally apologised for the Netherlands’ slave trading history during an annual commemoration for the abolition of the practice.

The monarch also stopped using a ceremonial golden coach which has repeatedly come under fire for a painted panel that depicts scenes of colonialism.

Research by the home affairs ministry in 2023 came to a similar conclusion. That study, carried out following a 2021 parliamentary motion, involved some 30 academics and historians and was published as the book Staat en slavernij (State and slavery).

World.title: Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding
World.content:
Rivers in the east of the Netherlands have fallen so low that the authorities can no longer measure whether ships can pass safely, leaving skippers to decide for themselves whether or not to sail and risk getting stranded.

Rijkswaterstaat, the transport ministry department that manages the waterways, told broadcaster NOS its survey boats can no longer reach the shallowest stretches of the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and much of the Waal.

In certain places the channel is less than 125cm deep, leaving only three agency boats that are shallow enough, but they are also needed in other regions.

Without them, Rijkswaterstaat cannot publish its daily shipping readings of the depths, which barge operators use to avoid getting stranded. Commercial firms collect and sell similar data, but not every skipper has or can pay for a subscription.

Transport under pressure

“This is very worrying,” Fiona Oomen, of inland shipping association Koninklijke Binnenvaart Nederland, told NOS. “All transport is under pressure, on the roads and on the waterways. What if the water drops even further? Where is everything supposed to go?”

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, is now around 545 cubic metres per second. That is well below the record low of 614 set in August.

Last weekend a Dutch cruise ship carrying 140 passengers became stuck at Cologne as the Rhine dropped to new lows in Germany.

On the IJssel, a one-way system imposed last week has forced some vessels to take a detour of up to 300km.

Freight carried on Dutch waterways fell by 19% in August, according to CBS figures, with cross-border traffic with Germany worst hit.

The infrastructure ministry lifted the national water shortage in early September, but warned that river levels could stay low until the end of the year. The cabinet has ruled out compensation for businesses hit by the drought.

Rain needed

Rijkswaterstaat could not say how long the situation would last. “We need rain in the catchment area,” a spokesman told NOS, adding that it would have to fall mainly outside the Netherlands. Current forecasts suggest the flow will not get worse, but will not improve much either.

He warned that a different problem would follow. “When it’s over, we get the next problem,” he said. “Then we’ll have high water again.” The North Sea is currently exceptionally warm, which could mean a very wet autumn.

New numbers from the Dutch statistics agency CBS show the inflation rate rose slightly in August.

The preliminary estimate from the Central Agency for Statistics shows a 0.1% rise from August, putting September’s inflation rate at 3.4%.

World.title: The Netherlands had its first TV broadcast 75 years ago
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Seventy-five years ago today, the Dutch had their first opportunity to watch a television broadcast: a performance of the play De Toverspiegel, live from a studio in Bussum.

The Royal Family watched the 90-minute production from the Soestdijk Palace.

Concerns about television’s corrupting influence on society and a focus on post-war reconstruction meant that the Netherlands entered the television era only in 1951, later than the United Kingdom or the United States.

The BBC had begun broadcasting in 1936.

The country had around 500 television sets at the time. Radio was the much more widely consumed medium, with around 250,000 devices in homes across the Netherlands.

A television set cost 785 guilders, about a third of the average annual salary, putting the luxury good far out of reach for most of the country.

Media historian Huub Wijfjes told the NOS that initial television broadcasts simply copied whatever was on the radio. “TV took a dominant position and reached its peak in the 60s, 70s, and 80s. The medium displaced radio,” he said.

By 1956, there were 75,000 television sets in the country.

On the website for the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, you can watch the early broadcasts.

World.title: Israeli group disrupts Delft screening of Gaza documentary Naza
World.content:
A premiere screening of the documentary Naza, which investigates the killing of civilians by the Israeli military in Gaza, was interrupted in a Delft cinema on Thursday afternoon by a woman taking a microphone and addressing the audience about the October 7 massacres.

She stood in front of the screen midway through the film and began describing how her family members were murdered during the Hamas attacks that sparked the Gaza war in 2023.

The crowd booed her off stage, the microphone was disabled, some shouted “shame on you”, though some applauded her. The woman’s name is Sabine Taasa, a French-Israeli citizen from a town near the Gaza strip and who lost her husband and a son during the attacks.

An Israeli activist group Ad Kan accompanied Taasa to the screening. The group describes itself as former army and intelligence officers who infiltrate and obstruct what they say are anti-Israeli and anti-Semitic activities in foreign countries.

Another member tried to project footage from the October 7 attacks in the cinema while Taasa spoke, according to broadcaster NOS.

Naza, which has been lauded by critics, consists of anonymous interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military services. They describe how they attacked Gaza, how AI systems were used to select targets, and the policies toward collateral damage and loss of innocent life.

Some describe killing hundreds of civilians at a time to target single military figures; others describe using surveillance techniques to wait for militants to be at home with their families before striking – a tactic known as “where’s daddy”.

Israeli officials have condemned the film, with prime minister Netanyahu pledging to strip the film makers of their citizenship. Other military figures have disputed the claims made in the film and branded it propaganda.

Dutch-Israeli relations have been strained recently over the decision to ban imports of goods from illegal settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. Dutch diplomats have had their status stripped in response.

World.title: Remains of 115 Polish WWII soldiers exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Exhumations have taken place of the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two. The work, which was carried out jointly by Polish and Ukrainian researchers, continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries. ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie ⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026 During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht. They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September. On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year. Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives. Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains. “For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute for National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council. “Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”. Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”. The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced. The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 Last year, Ukraine also granted permission for the exhumation of Polish soldiers in Lviv. Researchers subsequently found the remains of 31 people, as well as possible remains of dozens more that were difficult to identify due to them having been reburied and the manner of their death in artillery fire. They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine. Previously, from 2017 to 2024, Ukraine had banned searches for Polish victims of World War Two on its territory in response to the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist partisan formation that fought against the Soviets but also led the massacre of ethnic Poles. However, in a major diplomatic breakthrough last year, Ukraine allowed exhumations to resume, including both the Polish soldiers in Lviv as well as victims of the UPA-led massacres, tens of thousands of whom are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Researchers have subsequently uncovered the remains of dozens of victims of the massacres, who have also been reburied in ceremonies attended by both Polish and Ukrainian officials. However, such steps towards reconciliation have been hindered this year by a dispute sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to name a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour. Since then, both sides have moved to calm tensions, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan to resolve the dispute, including issuing “a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year. The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal. Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3 — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026 On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March. “We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs. News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners. The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output. When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production. In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN. The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne. The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier. For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024. Polish state-owned mining giant JSW, the EU's largest producer of coking coal, has reported a record annual loss of 7.3bn zloty. It attributed the results to falling coal prices, lower production volumes, and the impact of a one-off write-off https://t.co/vrSgRu630b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 11, 2025 JSW’s announcement comes just as some officials and industry representatives are warning that the energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East could increase demand in Poland for coal, which is still used to generate around half of electricity and to heat almost a fifth of homes. Polish coal is among the most expensive in the world to extract, and the industry survives largely due to heavy public subsidies. In 2026, the state is expected to spend 5.5 billion zloty propping up the sector, after an outlay of 9 billion zloty last year. Successive governments have been seeking to move away from coal, which went from producing 87% of Poland’s electricity in 2015 to 52.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, between 2015 and 2024, the proportion of households using hard coal for heating fell from 40% to 17%, while those using natural gas doubled from 10% to 21%. However, the energy crisis prompted by US and Israeli attacks on Iran this year has resulted in natural gas prices soaring. As a result, Poland’s state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, said last month that the geopolitical situation meant coal’s role this year would be “larger than we anticipated”. “We are currently increasing output at coal companies and are aware of the energy sector’s demand for coal as a stabilising factor,” he said, quoted by news service Money.pl. World.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices. In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels. Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0 — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026 The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June. However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill. The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March. Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax. Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality. Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen. By signing the bill, the president said he was “ending the process of holding Poles hostage”. He now expected the government to “immediately” reintroduce measures to bring down prices at petrol stations, as well as the cost of fuel for farmers. To nie ja wygrałem. Wygrali Polacy, którzy już w weekend zapłacą mniej za paliwa. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 1, 2026 In response, government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVN that they were ready to make the necessary decisions to reduced prices on Friday and that the measures could be in force already by the weekend. “It’s good that the president has stopped blocking this,” he said. On Friday morning, the government announced that it would reduce VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and cut excise duty – both measures it also used earlier this year. The new policies will be in place until 31 December. Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told Polskie Radio that maximum daily prices would also be reintroduced. Earlier, on Thursday evening, finance minister Andrzej Domański announced on social media that he estimated fuel costs would be reduced by 1.2-1.3 zloty per litre once the subsidies were reintroduced. According to price monitoring service ePetrol, diesel prices are currently averaging around 9.14 zloty per litre while PB95 petrol is at 8.19 zloty. Those are both record highs. Ustawa o podatku od nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych właśnie wpłynęła do RCL. Jeszcze dziś będzie ogłoszona. Oznacza to, że już w weekend ceny na stacjach paliwowych będą niższe. Szacunkowo o około 1,2-1,3 zł na litrze. I po co były te gierki, Panie Prezydencie? — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 1, 2026 The dispute over financing fuel price cuts comes at a time of growing concern over Poland’s public finances, something Nawrocki referred to in his address on Thursday. Poland has been running one of the EU’s highest deficits, despite the government committing to bringing it down after being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time this year. Last month, Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The last time the country was at A3 level was in 2002. World.title: Leading Polish business owners invest in small nuclear reactor venture
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople have announced that they are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by the country’s richest man, Michał Sołowow. Among them are Rafał Brzoska, founder of delivery giant InPost, and Mati Staniszewski, CEO of ElevenLabs, a leading artificial intelligence firm. The group is investing 500 million zloty (€114 million) in Sołowow’s Synthos Green Energy (SGE), which, together with 1.35 billion zloty from foreign investors, will secure the company’s financing for the next two years as it seeks to roll out BWRX-300 reactors in Poland, Central and Eastern Europe and the UK. As a European SMR development platform headquartered in Warsaw, Poland’s energy security is of special importance to us. We are proud to announce that today our founder, Michał Sołowow, unveiled a PLN 500 million investment by a group of leading Polish entrepreneurs in SGE’s… pic.twitter.com/J2SerVjIlG — SGE (@SGE_Nuclear) September 30, 2026 The investment, which was formally announced at a business conference in Warsaw on Wednesday, comes as Sołowow seeks to expand his nuclear project beyond SGE’s troubled partnership with Polish state energy giant Orlen, where disagreements have delayed plans to build SMRs in Poland. Alongside Brzoska and Staniszewski, the other new investors are Dariusz Gałęzewski, co-founder of drinks maker Oshee; Krzysztof Pawiński, CEO of food company Maspex; Michał Brański of media group Wirtualna Polska; and Michał Wypychewicz of ZPUE, the largest manufacturer of transformer stations in Europe. “They invested their own private funds because they understood the problem and then believed in the concept and the solution,” Sołowow told Business Insider Polska. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed on site, are seen by their proponents as a fast and cost-effective way of installing nuclear capacity. In July, SGE announced plans to build 14 BWRX-300 reactors with a combined capacity of 4.2 gigawatts (GW) across three sites in the UK, which it said would generate enough electricity to meet 11% of the country’s demand. The company also hopes to deploy up to 26 reactors across six locations in Poland. The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt water-cooled small modular reactor. Construction of the first ever unit began in Canada in 2025, with completion planned for 2029 and commercial operation expected in 2030. Synthos Green Energy, a firm owned by Polish billionaire Michał Sołowow, has announced plans to build 14 small modular nuclear reactors in the UK. It says that the £35 billion project could deliver enough power to meet 11% of the UK’s demand https://t.co/YTMIzYERuJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Brzoska said that developing SMR technology “is an investment in Poland’s future”, because without “reliable, predictable and competitively priced energy…it is difficult to talk seriously about further growth in industry, data centres, artificial intelligence, automation or modern logistics”. Staniszewski, whose company recently received an $11 million investment from Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) to establish an AI development centre in Poland, said lower electricity prices were important for the sector. SGE notes that demand for electricity is set to rise 40% in Poland over the next 14 years, according to grid operator PSE. Electricity prices have risen rapidly in recent years and are now the second most expensive in the European Union in relation to the cost of living. Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Poland remains the EU’s most coal-dependent country, with more than half of its electricity generated from coal. Over the past decade, however, the country has diversified its energy mix, with the share of renewable energy sources tripling to nearly 30% in 2025. Poland plans to reduce its reliance on coal further, including through the construction of its first nuclear power plant (of the traditional type, not an SMR). The 3.75-gigawatt project is scheduled to be commissioned in 2036. Sołowow has also been pursuing the deployment of SMRs in Poland through Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), a joint venture between SGE and state energy giant Orlen, Poland’s largest company, to develop BWRX-300 reactors in Poland. OSGE is seeking a so-called contract for difference (CfD) framework, an agreement with a state that guarantees a fixed price for electricity and helps shield developers from market swings, covering 14 reactors at three sites. Polish state energy firm Orlen has announced an agreement to build the country’s first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR). It says Poland will be the first country in Europe to deploy an SMR developed by US-based firm GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy https://t.co/MPWXS3qZ1d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2025 The project, however, has been delayed by disagreements between the two shareholders. Sołowow told Business Insider Polska that they reached an agreement last month that would allow construction of two reactors to move forward, but said he regretted entering into the partnership with Orlen. “I find it deeply regrettable, because it is precisely due to Orlen’s unnecessary involvement that we are discussing this project in political terms, even though it is not a political project,” he said. Sołowow has argued that a private-sector model can shorten construction times and improve cost control compared with traditional state-led nuclear projects. At the same time, he has highlighted the importance of the state’s role in implementing the project, saying its success depends on coordination between private investors and state policy. This includes contracts for difference, administrative procedures and the preparedness of the nuclear regulator.
