World.title: Activists launch world’s first abortion pill delivery locker in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted. They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world. The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group. They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills. Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located. The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws. Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year. However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills. But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered. Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal. However, the case will now return to the lower court, where it will be heard again https://t.co/U3J5FmXdMw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 14, 2025 “The abortomat transforms a closely guarded, criminalised procedure into something as simple as picking up a package,” wrote ADT. “A door that opens when all others have slammed shut.” They say that the machine is intended for women who have an urgent medical need that means they cannot wait for the several days it takes to deliver pills by post, or who are in abusive, controlling relationships that make postal delivery unsafe. Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable. “The abortomat is not a human being, and the person collecting the pills, in accordance with the regulations, is not breaking the law,” said Wydrzyńska, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. WHW and ADT do not collect any personal information from women using the service. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Poland violated the rights of a pregnant woman who had to travel abroad to obtain an abortion after her foetus was diagnosed with a birth defect https://t.co/TgckusMxmJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 13, 2025 Under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, the abortion law was tightened and was strictly enforced. In December 2023, a new, more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power, promising to liberalise the abortion law. However, it has so far failed to pass any such legislation. In 2024, a move to decriminalise abortion assistance up to the 12th week of pregnancy was rejected by parliament, after the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Tusk subsequently admitted that it would be impossible during the current parliament to soften abortion laws. Instead, his government issued guidelines on when and how abortions can be carried out, with the aim of ensuring that doctors and prosecutors “take the women’s side” when making decisions on the issue. World.title: Fugitive opposition politician granted safe passage to return to Poland against prosecutors’ wishes
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Warsaw court has approved a request from Marcin Romanowski, a fugitive former government minister who has been on the run for almost two years, to receive safe passage back to Poland. Romanowski is believed to currently be in the pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region of Transnistria. Although Polish prosecutors have long been seeking Romanowski’s return, they opposed his request for safe conduct, arguing that he cannot be trusted to comply with its terms given that he has repeatedly sought to evade the law. Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, has already announced that prosecutors will appeal the court’s decision, which he claims was issued by an illegitimately appointed judge and in violation of regulations. Nie ma i nie będzie bezkarności dla ludzi Zbigniewa Ziobry. Prokuratura złoży ZAŻALENIE na decyzję o wydaniu listu żelaznego dla Marcina Romanowskiego. Spójrzmy prawdzie w oczy: kto jednoosobowo próbuje zapewnić nietykalność człowiekowi podejrzanemu o gigantyczne nadużycia w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served as deputy justice minister in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2019 and 2023. After PiS lost power, prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served in government, including participating in an organised criminal group. However, Romanowski fled Poland in December 2024 and was granted asylum by Hungary, which was then ruled by Viktor Orbán, a conservative ally of PiS. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, Romanowski went on the run, and for months his location was unknown. In August, it emerged that Romanowski had sent a letter to Poland requesting safe passage to return. The document indicated that he was in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, a region that sought to break away from Moldova in the 1990s and is now effectively under Russian control. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that, based on intelligence sources, Poland is now “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia https://t.co/mdvmJpkFf7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 18, 2026 At the time, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, said that there were “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. However, on Wednesday, Warsaw’s district court approved Romanowski’s request. A spokeswoman for the court said that the decision had been made as “previous methods used [to secure Romanowski’s return] were ineffective” and safe passage would “allow the case to be clarified”. The politician’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, said that safe passage meant his client could not be detained in Poland and that a European Arrest Warrant against him, which applies in other EU countries, would no longer be valid. ❗️Sąd Okręgowy Warszawie wydał @RomanowskiPL list żelazny, uchylając środek zapobiegawczy w postaci tymczasowego aresztowania od momentu uprawomocnienia się orzeczenia❗️ Mój Klient na terytorium Polski nie będzie mógł być zatrzymany i tymczasowo aresztowany, a ENA „upada”, jeśli… — Bartosz Lewandowski (@BartoszLewand20) September 30, 2026 In a subsequent justification for the ruling, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily, judge Konrad Mielcarek wrote that Romanowski had pledged to “voluntarily return to the country”. Conditions for his safe passage include Romanowski reporting to the court and prosecutors at designated times and places, not leaving his declared place of residence, and not seeking to obstruct the criminal proceedings against him. The judge said that prosecutors had failed to provide adequate arguments as to why Romanowski’s request should be denied. He also found that Romanowski had not obstructed proceedings against him, but had merely exercised available legal remedies. The fact that Romanowski had fled Poland does not count against him, argued the judge. In fact, “the very nature of safe passage is to provide a person residing abroad with a legal guarantee…in exchange for voluntarily submitting to the jurisdiction of Polish authorities”. The judge also clarified that safe passage is neither a “reward” nor a “privilege” and that, given that evidence in the case is already secured and Romanowski no longer has influence over justice ministry officials, the risk of tampering is low. The National Prosecutor’s Office immediately issued a statement declaring its opposition to the ruling and its intention to appeal. It noted that there had been no confirmation that Romanowski really is in Tiraspol and that the suspect had repeatedly sought to evade the law. “These circumstances do not provide assurance that the suspect will comply with the conditions of the letter of safe conduct,” wrote the prosecutors, who also pointed to the fact that Romanowski had admitted to using travel documents issued under a false identity. Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis. In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case. Sąd może wydać list żelazny, jeżeli podejrzany przebywający za granicą złoży oświadczenie, że stawi… — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served in the justice ministry when it was led by Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, who is also wanted by the Polish authorities on suspicion of 26 crimes relating to his time in office. Poland has requested that Ziobro be extradited, though that process could take years. Both Ziobro and Romanowski deny committing the crimes they are accused of and claim that they are being pursued as an act of “political revenge” by the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. To mark the occasion, the speaker of the lower-house Sejm, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, personally informed Cobra of the decision. “An application for transfer to retirement?” said Czarzasty, sitting opposite the extremely well-behaved Cobra in a video published by the Sejm. “Impeccable reputation. No disciplinary punishments. You’ve never barked in the Sejm,” he read from her files. “OK, signed. As of tomorrow, you are free.” Cobra idzie na emeryturę! 🐕‍🦺 Decyzję o przejściu w stan spoczynku przypieczętował podpisem Marszałek Sejmu @wlodekczarzasty. 😉 Psy Straży Marszałkowskiej to ważny element systemu ochrony Sejmu. World.title: Inflation hits 4% in Poland as fuel prices surge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s inflation accelerated to an annual rate of 4.0% in September, up from 3.4% a month earlier, driven primarily by higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the end of Polish government subsidies that kept down prices at the pump. The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely. The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August. The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month. To shield consumers from the energy crisis triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Poland has twice introduced temporary measures to curb petrol station prices, including daily price caps and cuts in VAT and excise duty. The system was in place from March to June and again during the the last two weeks of August. The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields. According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank. The breach of the upper end of the central bank’s inflation target and the 4% threshold could influence the stance of the NBP’s Monetary Policy Council (RPP), prompting it to hike rates, added Erste Bank analysts. Zahamowanie spadków cen żywności m/m. Inflacja bazowa prawdopodobnie w dół do 3,0-3,1%r/r, co oznacza że wciąż… pic.twitter.com/AqdIXBthFl — ING Economics Poland (@ING_EconomicsPL) September 30, 2026 Economists at ING Bank Śląski, meanwhile, expect the first rate hike – after a series of nine cautious cuts between September 2023 and March 2026 – to come in early 2027. “The RPP may opt to wait, leaving interest rates unchanged in October, with discussions on potential monetary policy tightening beginning in November following the release of the NBP’s new projections,” they wrote on X. Poland’s benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75%, down from a peak of 6.75% reached during the country’s last tightening cycle in 2021-2022, when policymakers were grappling with persistent inflation fuelled by the post-pandemic recovery and the war in Ukraine. Inflation peaked at 18.4% during that period.

World.title: Prague Passengers Can Now Request Czech or English Speaking Bolt Drivers
World.content:
Bolt has introduced two new ride categories in Prague that allow passengers to request drivers who speak either Czech or English.

The new options are available at the same price as a standard Bolt ride.



They are open to drivers of any nationality who can communicate in the relevant language at a level suitable for everyday conversation.

Czech-speaking passengers who are less comfortable communicating in English can request a Czech-speaking driver, while foreign residents, tourists and business travellers can choose a driver who speaks English.

Bolt already provides automatic translation for communication between passengers and drivers within its app. Booking information, addresses and messages can therefore be translated automatically. The new categories are designed to cover situations in which communication takes place outside the app, particularly during the journey itself.

The company said the new options are already available in Prague, where it has enough partner drivers who meet the language requirements.

Drivers can choose whether to participate in the new categories. They may offer rides in Czech, English, both languages or continue driving exclusively in the standard category.

Participation is voluntary.

Passengers will see the two new options directly in the Bolt app. The Czech-speaking category is identified by an icon featuring the Czech flag, while the English-speaking option uses an English flag icon.

World.title: Pegasus Airlines Completes Acquisition of Czech Airlines and Smartwings
World.content:
Pegasus Airlines has completed its acquisition of Czech Airlines and the Smartwings Group, marking a major change in the ownership of one of the Czech Republic’s most established aviation businesses.

The Turkish low-cost carrier announced the completion of the transaction on Thursday, October 1, following the approval of the relevant regulatory authorities and the fulfilment of the required closing conditions.



The deal brings together Pegasus Airlines and the Czech-based Smartwings Group, creating an aviation group with a combined fleet of more than 175 aircraft.

The two airlines also have firm orders for a further 140 aircraft.

For passengers in Prague and across the Czech Republic, Smartwings will continue to operate under its existing brand. Its day-to-day operations, customer relationships and service are expected to remain in place, while the company will gain access to new opportunities for expansion and development through its new ownership.

Pegasus expands further into Central Europe

Founded in 1990, Pegasus Airlines has operated as a low-cost carrier since 2005. The airline currently serves 161 destinations in 57 countries from its main hub at Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport and other bases in Türkiye.

Its network covers Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Asia, making the acquisition an opportunity to strengthen Pegasus’ presence in Central and Eastern Europe.

Smartwings, meanwhile, operates a network of around 80 destinations across 20 countries. The group has a particularly strong position in the Czech leisure travel market, with scheduled and charter services as well as private flights and special flights for international companies and organisations.

The Czech airline has been operating under the Smartwings name since 1998, while the Czech Airlines (ČSA) brand is one of the oldest names in European aviation.

The combined business is expected to benefit from the complementary networks of the two airlines. Pegasus brings a large international network and experience with the low-cost model, while Smartwings has an established customer base and strong relationships with tour operators in the Czech Republic and wider Central European market.

Pegasus said that Smartwings will continue operating under its established brand following the completion of the acquisition.

Pegasus carried a record 43.3 million passengers in 2025 and operates one of Europe’s younger aircraft fleets.

World.title: Ibiza Is Coming to Prague: A Night of DJs, Lasers and Tropical Vibes
World.content:
On April 17, 2027, OX Club in Prague will transform for one night into an Ibiza-inspired party featuring DJs, immersive visuals and tropical-themed spaces.

The Sound of Ibiza event will bring British DJ and producer Daxson, Dutch DJ and producer Laura Van Dam, Czech DJ Lucca and DJ TiGi to one stage.



The night will combine electronic music with a full immersive laser show, acrobatic performances above the dancefloor and Ibiza-inspired décor throughout the club.

There will also be a dedicated Sunset Experience for photos and social media, as well as a Chillout Zone with its own DJ programme and mentoring by Pavel Bidlo.

Daxson has performed at major festivals and clubs including Creamfields, EDC, UNTOLD and Ministry of Sound, while also creating several anthems for Transmission Festival. Laura Van Dam has appeared at Tomorrowland, Ultra, EDC, Sziget and Ushuaïa Ibiza and has built a following with her melodic techno and trance sound.

DJ Lucca, one of the country’s best-known electronic music artists, has performed alongside international names including Carl Cox and Paul van Dyk.

The event will also feature competitions for an iPhone and other prizes. An Ibiza Beach Outfit is suggested, although the dress code is optional.

With a capacity of 1,000 people, Sound of Ibiza aims to recreate the atmosphere of the famous Mediterranean party island in the centre of Prague for one night.

Tickets went on sale on October 1. Party packs are also available.

The event has no age restriction. Tickets are available through GoOut.

World.title: The Prague Post’s First Issue Goes Online 35 Years Later
World.content:
The Prague Post has launched a digital archive marking 35 years since the publication of its first issue.

October 1, 2026, marks the 35th anniversary of the newspaper’s debut.

Founded in 1991, The Prague Post was Czechoslovakia’s longest-running English-language weekly newspaper.



The newly launched archive begins with that very first issue, which is available to read in full, browse online and search by text.

A new issue will be added each week, corresponding to the same week 35 years earlier.

The project will allow readers to follow the political, social and cultural changes of the early 1990s through the newspaper’s coverage, much as readers did at the time.

The Prague Post Archive is also active on Facebook and Instagram, where updates about newly digitized issues and the project will be shared.

The archive is administered by Modrá sova z.s., a nonprofit English-language library and learning center in Loužnice, where The Prague Post’s physical archives are housed.

Issues published between 1991 and 1994 have already been scanned and processed.

Around two decades of additional issues remain to be digitized, making the project a long-term and costly undertaking. Modrá sova has independently funded the digitization work since the project began and is now inviting organizations and individuals interested in supporting the project to contribute through the archive’s website.

The archive will also continue to handle requests from people looking for specific articles and welcomes visitors by appointment.

For more information, contact Mimi Fronczak-Rogers at [email protected] or +420 721 518 385.

World.title: Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity to Return to Prague on October 22
World.content:
A Halloween charity event will bring children and families to several Prague neighbourhoods on October 22, combining trick-or-treating with fundraising for SOS Children’s Villages.

The Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity will take place from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. across Vinohrady, Vršovice, Žižkov, Prague 15, Holešovice and Barrandov.



The concept is simple. Children dressed in Halloween costumes and accompanied by their parents will visit participating host locations, which can include cafés, restaurants, shops, confectioneries, schools, children’s centres and other businesses or organisations.

The participating locations will remain a secret until children register for the event and receive a special map showing where they can go trick-or-treating.

At each location, children will make a contribution of at least CZK 10 to a sealed collection box supporting SOS Children’s Villages. In return, they will receive a sweet treat before continuing to the next location.

Last year’s event attracted more than 1,100 registered participants and raised CZK 296,157 despite rainy weather.

The entire amount was donated to SOS Children’s Villages, which has supported children, families, young people and foster carers in the Czech Republic for more than 50 years.

How it started

Dinah Spritzer-Richter and several of her friends organized the first American Halloween in Prague for her two children in 2017. The event has supported charity from the very first year, with the proceeds going to help children in SOS Children’s Villages.

Dinah sees the charity side as just as important as creating a joyful and memorable experience for the kids.

How to take part

Families who want to participate can register in advance and then use the secret map to find the participating locations on October 22.

Children are encouraged to come in costume and bring enough coins to make contributions at the individual stops.

Businesses and organisations can also join the event as hosts. Each host is asked to prepare sweets, add some Halloween decorations and wear at least part of a costume or Halloween accessory.

Hosts must be available for at least two hours between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m.

The organisers will provide the collection boxes, while hosts provide the sweets for visiting children.

World.title: Prague Study Reveals How Much Waste Tourists Leave in the City Center
World.content:
Specialists from Prague City Hall and the Institute of Circular Economy (INCIEN) have analyzed the contents of public waste bins in central Prague, finding that about one ton of rubbish is discarded on Wenceslas Square every day.

The latest analysis was carried out to examine how the composition of waste changes with the seasons and fluctuations in tourist traffic.

A similar measurement was conducted during the winter, providing a basis for comparison.



Beverage packaging made up roughly one-third of the waste collected from bins on Wenceslas Square. Cans and plastic bottles were among the most common items.

Another third consisted of disposable food-service items, particularly cups. The remaining third was made up of general household waste.

Researchers also found waste originating from businesses in the surrounding area, including cafes and shops. Some household rubbish appeared to have been left by tourists staying in apartments rented through short-term accommodation platforms.

Food waste was another recurring part of the findings. Partially eaten food was frequently found in the bins, with trdelník pastries among the more common examples.

The summer analysis gives Prague authorities a clearer picture of the waste generated in one of the city’s busiest public spaces during the peak tourist season and allows them to compare the results with the winter survey.

World.title: Prague Hospitals Warn of Critical Blood Shortages
World.content:
Several hospitals in Prague are reporting critically low blood supplies, prompting the Czech Ministry of Health to urge people to donate blood in the coming days.

The shortage is affecting more than individual blood groups. Hospitals and transfusion centers in several parts of the Czech Republic are reporting a broader decline in available supplies, with some facilities nearing the minimum levels needed to maintain safe operations.



The situation differs from one region to another. Some transfusion centers still have adequate reserves, while others are short of particular blood groups or are approaching critical levels.

The shortage also extends to individual blood components. In Prague, the Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine (IKEM) is currently seeking more platelet donors regardless of blood type.

People planning to donate are advised to check the latest information on the website or social media channels of their chosen transfusion center before visiting.

Why hospitals need more donors

Hospitals depend on regular blood donations not only during emergencies but also for planned medical treatment.

Blood is routinely needed for surgery, childbirth and the treatment of patients who require repeated transfusions. This includes some cancer patients whose treatment can interfere with the body’s production of blood cells.

Blood donations are also essential in cases of severe complications during childbirth. Heavy blood loss can become life-threatening within a short period, and an adequate supply of donated blood can be critical to saving the lives of mothers and newborns.

The demand for blood can increase during the summer and holiday period, when hospitals continue to perform scheduled procedures while also dealing with more injuries and traffic accidents. At the same time, the number of people coming to donate tends to fall as residents leave the country or travel elsewhere.

Number of donors continues to decline

Official figures indicate that the Czech donor base has been shrinking. Around 348,000 people donated blood last year, down from 362,000 the previous year.

Transfusion centers are also losing older regular donors as they reach the age limit, while the number of younger people replacing them has not been sufficient.

In the Czech Republic, adults can generally donate blood until the age of 65, provided they weigh more than 50 kilograms. Additional eligibility restrictions may apply, including for people who have recently travelled to countries where certain infectious diseases are present.

Donating blood in the Czech Republic is voluntary and free of charge. Donors are entitled to time off work on the day of their donation, while some health insurance companies provide additional benefits or rewards for regular donors.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation : The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy : A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance : The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

World.title: PM Magyar signals possible end to Hungary’s food margin caps
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Friday that the government should consider phasing out the country’s food retail margin caps, arguing that the measure is increasingly damaging farmers and small shops.

Speaking during a stop in Kisvárda as part of his nationwide tour, Magyar said the measure had originally been introduced by the previous government to slow food price increases, but had produced serious side effects across the agricultural and retail sectors.

According to the prime minister, low procurement prices are putting pressure on Hungarian producers, while large retail chains are increasingly turning to cheaper imported products in order to offset losses created by the margin restrictions.

He claimed that in Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg County alone, dozens of small shops had gone out of business as a result of the measure, MTI reported.

Small shops and farmers under pressure

Magyar said the previous government had tried to protect smaller retailers by exempting them from the margin cap, but argued that the policy ultimately strengthened larger chains, which were better able to absorb the losses.

He also criticised the effect of the measure on Hungarian agriculture, saying that artificially low procurement prices had made it harder for domestic producers to remain competitive.

Magyar said the government should now assess the future of the measure together with chambers of commerce, food retailers and other market participants.

His remarks come at a time when inflation in Hungary has fallen sharply compared with the levels seen during the previous government.

If you missed it: Danube water levels could fall way below 200-year low

Inflation has fallen sharply in 2026

Annual inflation stood at 1.7 percent in June, according to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office, while food prices were only 0.2 percent higher than a year earlier. Excluding catering services, food prices actually fell by 2.4 percent year on year.

Inflation eased further during the summer. The National Bank of Hungary reported that annual inflation fell to 1.2 percent in July and 1.3 percent in August, while food inflation also declined.

This has also strengthened the debate over whether extraordinary price-control measures are still necessary.

Central bank says removing the cap would not threaten price stability

The Hungarian National Bank has already signalled that the margin caps could be withdrawn without causing a major inflation shock.

In its June assessment, the Monetary Council said that even an immediate removal of the price margin caps would not push inflation above the central bank’s 3 percent target.

The central bank’s June Inflation Report also noted that the large international food retailers it examined were collectively loss-making in 2025, although the scale of losses had decreased compared with the previous year.

At the same time, the MNB has repeatedly stressed that the stronger forint, softer food price dynamics and weaker inflation expectations have all contributed to a more favourable inflation environment this year.

Magyar therefore argued that, with inflation now significantly lower than in previous years and several food prices already falling, the government should seriously consider gradually ending the margin cap regime.

World.title: Forint gets a boost from falling oil and a softer dollar
World.content:
The Hungarian forint strengthened against both the euro and the US dollar on Friday, supported by falling oil prices and weaker-than-expected US labour market data.

The Hungarian forint has enjoyed a stronger period since Hungary’s parliamentary election earlier this year, helped by improving investor sentiment, expectations surrounding EU funds and the government’s plans for eventual euro adoption. Friday brought another notable move, although the currency was far from stable throughout the session.

Friday brought another volatile session. The forint briefly strengthened below HUF 368 per euro and HUF 326 per dollar, before giving back part of those gains later in the day. The National Bank of Hungary’s official exchange rates for 2 October were HUF 367.87 per euro and HUF 326.94 per US dollar.

The National Bank of Hungary’s official exchange rates for 2 October were HUF 367.87 per euro and HUF 326.94 per US dollar.

Oil prices gave the forint a boost

Oil dropped by more than 3 percent during the day, with Brent crude falling back towards USD 100 per barrel after news that additional strategic fuel reserves could be released onto the market.

Lower oil prices are generally supportive for Hungary because the country is a major energy importer. A lower import bill can reduce pressure on the trade balance and ease some of the inflationary risks associated with expensive energy.

Portfolio noted that the combination of cheaper oil and changing expectations on US interest rates created a more favourable environment for the forint during Friday trading.

Weak US jobs report puts pressure on the dollar

The other major market-moving event came from the United States. The US economy added just 29,000 non-farm jobs in September, far below the roughly 90,000 expected by economists. August’s figure was also revised lower, while the unemployment rate rose to 4.2 percent.

The weaker-than-expected figures reduced expectations that the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again at its October meeting. The dollar weakened after the release, while stock markets moved higher.

A weaker dollar can provide support to emerging-market currencies such as the forint, particularly when global investors become more willing to take on risk.

If you missed it: Danube water levels could fall way below 200-year low

Global markets remain volatile

Friday’s move came after several difficult sessions for European currencies.

The US dollar has strengthened significantly in recent weeks, supported by high US Treasury yields and expectations that American monetary policy could remain tight for longer. The euro has also come under pressure amid fiscal and political concerns in several European countries.

At the same time, energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty continue to produce sharp movements across financial markets. For the forint, this means that favourable developments such as falling oil prices or a weaker dollar can provide short-term support, but international market sentiment remains an important source of volatility.

World.title: Budapest transport and parking could change dramatically from 2027 under new government-city deal
World.content:
A new agreement between Budapest and the Hungarian government could reshape how public transport and parking are organised in the capital from 2027.

The deal was reached at the first meeting of the re-established Budapest Development Council and includes changes to the capital’s finances, public transport system and parking management, as well as several major development projects.

One of the most significant elements is the planned transformation of the Budapest Transport Centre into a regional transport authority covering both Budapest and its wider metropolitan area. According to the capital, the state and Budapest would jointly finance public transport on a 50-50 basis.

One transport system for Budapest and its suburbs

Under the plans, the new organisation would operate as the Budapest Metropolitan Transport Centre and would be responsible for coordinating timetables, integrating fares and ordering transport services.

The aim is to reduce the long-standing separation between transport within Budapest and services connecting the capital with its suburbs. This could include closer coordination between BKK, MÁV and regional bus services.

According to 24.hu, Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said the state and Budapest could each contribute around HUF 170 billion to the system in 2027.

He also said the changes could eventually allow electronic ticketing and bank card-based travel to be expanded across the entire Budapest metropolitan region. For passengers, the goal would be a more integrated network in which journeys crossing Budapest’s administrative boundary are easier to plan and use.

If you missed it: Drivers beware: nationwide police checks begin in Hungary next week

Major changes could also be coming to parking

Under the current plans, responsibility for operating paid parking and collecting parking fees would move from the district municipalities to the Budapest municipality. Revenue would be reserved for running the parking system and maintaining and developing the capital’s road network.

Vitézy argued that the current fragmented model is highly inefficient. According to figures he cited, operating costs in some districts can consume between 60 and 97.5 percent of parking revenues, while some systems even operate at a loss.

Further technological changes are also being considered. Vitézy said traditional parking machines and the familiar paper penalties placed on windscreens could eventually be phased out, although the necessary legal changes would still have to be adopted.

The proposal has already sparked debate among district leaders, as transferring parking revenues to the capital would significantly change the way local authorities finance parts of their operations.

HUF 120 billion package for Budapest

The government will provide the capital with a one-off HUF 120 billion payment, while Budapest will withdraw lawsuits related to the solidarity contribution. The money can be used to settle outstanding taxes, contributions and other obligations.

According to Vitézy, around HUF 91 billion of the amount will be used to settle existing liabilities to the state, leaving roughly HUF 30 billion to support Budapest’s operations through the end of 2026.

The capital has also committed to at least HUF 20 billion in operating savings next year, while the solidarity contribution paid by Budapest is expected to be reduced from 2027.

Rákosrendező and other major projects also included

The government and Budapest also agreed to cooperate on the redevelopment of a large former railway area in northern Budapest, Rákosrendező, while further discussions will cover the Diákváros student district, the renovation of Budapest’s historic thermal baths and other major urban development projects.

Many details still need to be worked out, and several of the planned reforms will require further legal and organisational changes.

If implemented, however, the agreement could significantly alter how people travel, park and move between Budapest and its surrounding suburbs from 2027.

World.title: Drivers beware: nationwide police checks begin in Hungary next week
World.content:
Drivers in Hungary can expect stepped-up police checks next week, as authorities launch a nationwide operation targeting mobile phone use and other forms of distraction behind the wheel.

The Hungarian police will carry out enhanced road safety checks between 5 and 11 October, focusing particularly on the use of mobile phones while driving, the National Police Headquarters announced on Friday.

The operation is being organised as part of the ROADPOL “Focus on the Road” campaign, a Europe-wide initiative coordinated by the European Roads Policing Network. Hungary has joined similar campaigns in previous years as well.

What will Hungarian police be checking?

During the operation, officers will pay increased attention to drivers using mobile phones while their vehicle is in motion, as well as to other activities that could distract them from the road.

According to police, this includes the use of electronic devices and viewing visual or written content while driving, as such activities can significantly increase the risk of accidents.

Authorities stressed that driving already requires a high level of concentration, and that any activity diverting a driver’s attention can pose a serious danger.

Police say even greater risks arise when motorists write or read messages, browse social media or watch videos while driving. Photo: Depositphotos.com

If you missed it: Major step for the Hungarian minority in Ukraine as educational bill submitted to parliament

More than 1,500 drivers were caught last year

The upcoming operation follows a similar nationwide ROADPOL campaign held in October 2025. During that one-week operation, Hungarian police caught 1,564 drivers using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel. Officers were also looking for other forms of distraction that could affect road safety.

The figure suggests that mobile phone use while driving remains a significant issue on Hungarian roads. A year earlier, during the 2024 campaign, police reported catching more than 2,000 drivers using mobile phones while driving.

In Pest County alone, officers checked 4,745 motorists during the 2024 ROADPOL operation and found 134 drivers holding a phone while driving. Police also reported other distracting behaviour, including eating behind the wheel.

Police increasingly use technology to catch distracted drivers

Hungarian police have increasingly turned to technical tools to identify traffic offences that may be difficult to spot during conventional roadside checks. In recent operations, officers have used drones and other surveillance methods to detect drivers using handheld mobile phones behind the wheel, as well as other traffic violations.

This means motorists may not necessarily be stopped immediately after an offence is observed, as violations can also be documented from a distance and followed up by police afterwards.

World.title: Mineral water springs: 3 levels that set property value
World.content:
My previous article explained why Hungary’s geothermal and mineral water resources represent untapped natural capital and why property prices do not yet reflect their full potential. This article moves one step closer: it examines how a water-law permit and official recognition as natural mineral water can affect the value of a specific property, and why two neighbouring plots that appear identical may command very different prices simply because one is associated with an officially recognised, lawfully exploitable source and the other is not. The value of a property with mineral water springs is shaped not only by market demand, but also by the combination of permits, official recognition and restrictions on use.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Recognition as natural mineral water: a condition for market access

Natural mineral water is not merely a quality category; it is a legally regulated designation. In Hungary, the Government Office of the Capital City Budapest recognises water as natural mineral water, on application, under Joint Decree 65/2004 (IV. 27.) FVM–ESzCsM–GKM. Only water recognised through this procedure may be marketed under the designation “natural mineral water”. Recognition requires evidence of compliance with the prescribed chemical, microbiological, source-protection, extraction and bottling conditions.

It is not an exclusive market right or a legal monopoly. Rather, recognition is a condition for the lawful use of the designation and for placing the product on the market, while the geological characteristics of the source and the site-specific permits may create commercial scarcity.

According to the case files available to me, hydrodynamic modelling for one of the sources examined demonstrated an adequate degree of protection for the water base, while tritium analysis supported the conclusion that the water originated in deeper strata. The Government Office of the Capital City Budapest recognised the water as natural mineral water. That recognition, together with the relevant water-law permits and protection measures, may have substantial market value, but it does not create a statutory monopoly.

The Börzsöny case: mineral water springs, 150 metres and a decade-long process

I know the case of a mineral water source in the Börzsöny hills well. According to the documentation available to me, the well was drilled in 1979 to a depth of approximately 150 metres and produces high-quality aquifer water. Hydrodynamic modelling was prepared for the operating permit, using numerical simulation to examine the vulnerability of the water base and the origin of the water. Over the 50-year assessment horizon, the model indicated no recharge from surface sources; the calculation used a recharge zone with a radius of 448 metres, and the tritium content was negligible.

Official recognition of the water as natural mineral water, together with the completion of the related permitting process, materially strengthened the property’s market position. The point at which the recognition decision became final was the key legal milestone affecting value.

The protection system as both a value driver and a constraint

The protection of water bases is governed by Government Decree 123/1997 (VII. 18.). The system provides for inner and outer subsurface protection zones, hydrogeological zones A, B and C, and corresponding surface protection areas where a subsurface zone reaches the surface. The inner protection zone must be designated. Whether outer and hydrogeological A and B surface protection areas must also be designated depends in part on whether the corresponding subsurface zones reach the surface, while a hydrogeological C zone is not mandatory in every case.

Not every restriction appears on the land-registry title sheet. Inner and outer surface protection areas must be entered in the land register, while rights, obligations and prohibitions associated with hydrogeological protection zones are also recorded in the water-law register (vízikönyvi nyilvántartás). The protection system may restrict certain uses of surrounding land while reducing the risk of contamination of the water base.

A source with a properly established protection system may therefore embody two forms of value. The first is the verified water use authorised by a valid operating water-law permit. Ownership of the property and entitlement under the permit do not necessarily belong to the same person, however, and purchasing the property does not automatically transfer the permit. A change in the permit holder or the owner may require an authority review and an amendment to the permit. The second source of value is the protection of the water base, which may restrict certain uses of neighbouring properties and thereby help preserve water quality over the long term.

The Great Plain case: value held in suspension

A different situation arises where the resource exists, the well has been drilled and the water has been chemically tested, but exploitation has not begun. I am also closely familiar with a thermal well on the Great Hungarian Plain. It draws thermal water from a depth of nearly 950 metres at a temperature above 50 °C. According to the laboratory report available to me, its silicic-acid content, expressed as SiO2, is approximately 341 mg/l, nearly four times the silica content of Fiji Water, a frequently cited global premium benchmark.

The chemical profile alone, however, does not establish eligibility for recognition as natural mineral water or medicinal water, nor does it demonstrate suitability for beverage or therapeutic use. Separate testing and authority procedures are required. The well has not operated since it was drilled in 2007, not because of its geological characteristics, but because parallel permitting procedures became protracted.

This is a case in which the theoretical value of a property associated with mineral water springs or a thermal water resource may be high, while the market price does not yet reflect it. From an investment perspective, this may be the entry point, but only for a buyer who understands what is required to turn geological promise into a legally exploitable asset.

What is a spring actually worth in the property price?

The answer depends on the stage reached in the permitting and recognition process. The following three levels are not statutory categories, but a practical due-diligence model.

Level one: speculative. The presence of the water resource is suspected on geological grounds or has been documented, but no valid authority permit exists; any water-related premium is therefore largely speculative. Level two: permitted but not recognised. The well has been completed and has a valid operating water-law permit, but the recognition procedure required for the intended commercial or therapeutic use has not yet been completed. Level three: fully resolved. The relevant recognition decision has become final, the applicable subsurface protection zone or surface protection area has been designated, and all permits required for the intended bottling or other use are in place.

At that third stage, the property’s value can be assessed according to a different logic from that applied to ordinary land or buildings.

What comes next

Reaching the third level requires a complex process involving several authorities and overlapping fields of law. The next article examines this path in detail, including the roles of the regional water-management and water-protection authority, the mining authority where applicable, and the nature-conservation, agricultural-land-protection, building and land-registry bodies; it also considers Natura 2000 implications and the long-term sustainability of permits, drawing on direct experience of the two projects described here.

Legislation cited

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal, water-law or food-law advice. The project-specific data described above should be verified against the original laboratory reports, permits and authority decisions. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

World.title: Danube water levels could fall way below 200-year low
World.content:
The Danube has fallen to a historic low in Budapest, with water levels expected to decline further over the weekend as persistent dry weather continues across the river’s catchment area.

What do negative water levels mean?

On Wednesday, the Budapest water gauge recorded -1 centimetre, breaking a record that had stood for almost 200 years. The level had previously fallen to zero in early September, but continued drought has since pushed the river below that mark.

The gauge’s zero point corresponds to the lowest water level recorded during the 1834 low-water period. A negative reading does not mean that the riverbed is dry; rather, it indicates that the water level has fallen below the historic reference point.

Regular state measurements in Budapest began in 1823, and the river had never previously fallen below today’s zero mark. According to water-management authorities, the latest reading therefore represents an unprecedented low in the modern measurement record.

Danube water levels are expected to decline even further

Hungary’s General Directorate of Water Management predicts that the situation could deteriorate further, with the Danube potentially reaching -8 centimetres in Budapest by the weekend. The continuing lack of rainfall across the river’s catchment area is the main factor behind the decline. Little significant precipitation is expected in the Alps and along the upper reaches of the Danube, meaning there is currently no clear source of increased water flow, writes Időkép.

The effects are being felt elsewhere in Hungary as well. At Paks, the river could fall to around -113 centimetres, although an earlier record low of -140 centimetres is not currently expected to be challenged. A riverbed threshold constructed there in August has helped maintain water levels.

The exceptionally low conditions are also creating growing difficulties for river navigation, as sandbanks and obstacles on the riverbed come increasingly close to the surface. With little rainfall forecast, Budapest and other sections of the Danube may continue to experience unusually low water levels in the coming days.

World.title: Major step for the Hungarian minority in Ukraine as educational bill submitted to parliament
World.content:
Ukraine has taken a significant legislative step towards strengthening the educational rights of its Hungarian minority, submitting a bill to parliament that would expand protections for minority-language schooling. The move has been welcomed by Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, although the legislation still needs parliamentary approval.

The bill, registered in Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada on 1 October, is expected to be considered later this month. It follows a June agreement between Budapest and Kyiv concerning the linguistic, educational and cultural rights of Hungary’s ethnic Hungarian community in Ukraine.

What would change?

Under the proposed legislation, Ukrainian would remain the language of the education system. However, schools with classes or groups teaching in the language of an indigenous people or an EU-official minority language would be guaranteed the right to use that language. The bill would also create a formal status for secondary schools serving national minorities. Institutions where more than half of pupils receive education in a minority language could qualify for this status.

For Hungarian-speaking pupils, the proposed framework could allow schools to teach national history and preserve elements of their material and cultural heritage, including traditions, symbols and customs. Official educational documents could also be issued in the minority language at parents’ request. Parents would have the right to request an expansion of subjects taught in Ukrainian, provided that at least two-thirds of parents in the relevant class or group submit a written request.

A dispute stretching back years

Minority-language education has been one of the principal sources of tension between Budapest and Kyiv since Ukraine introduced changes to its language and education policies in the late 2010s. The June 2026 agreement was reached following several weeks of expert-level negotiations involving Hungarian and Ukrainian officials, as well as representatives of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia. The details of the agreement were not initially published, but its stated objective was to expand linguistic, educational and cultural rights.

The issue has also become linked to Ukraine’s European Union accession process. Hungary had previously opposed the opening of parts of the negotiations, while Magyar has said that progress on minority rights is a condition for Budapest’s support for further steps. Reuters reported that Ukraine’s latest bill is therefore closely connected to efforts to advance the accession process.

Budapest welcomes the move

Anita Orbán said the bill followed recent bilateral consultations and discussions with representatives of the Transcarpathian Hungarian community. Magyar likewise said it would strengthen the legal guarantees surrounding Hungarian-language education and the network of educational institutions.

The legislation nevertheless marks only the next stage of the process. Its final wording could still change during parliamentary debate, and its practical impact will depend on how the new provisions are implemented. For the Hungarian-speaking community in Ukraine, the parliamentary process will therefore be closely watched as a test of whether the commitments made in recent months become lasting legal protections.

Stay up-to-date: Orbán’s brother allegedly asked Austrian contact if he could stop another Ukrainian cash shipment

The new government also drew the line

Speaking to Bloomberg, deputy foreign minister and state secretary György Velkey shared the new government, just like the previous one, won’t send neither soldiers nor military equipment to Ukraine. Despite the Tisza government’s efforts to join the mainstream of the European Union, the EU and especially the Baltic states’ – due to the closeness of Russia – decided to fully support Ukraine against the Russian invasion. Velkey said they believe it is of utmost importance to guarantee peace within Hungary’s borders, hence their support consists of humanitarian aid and energy supply, not weapons and ammunition.

World.title: Revolut users in Hungary face new restriction from December: currency exchanges could be suspended!
World.content:
Revolut will introduce new terms in December, allowing it to temporarily suspend currency exchanges in exceptional market or technical circumstances, potentially affecting some transfers as well.

Revolut users will face a new provision from 3 December 2026 that could temporarily suspend currency exchanges in exceptional circumstances, according to information sent to customers and reported by Bankmonitor.

The new provision will be added to Revolut’s personal terms and conditions. It allows the service to suspend the exchange of certain currencies in situations including extreme exchange-rate movements, liquidity constraints, unavailable exchange rates, or technical or system failures outside Revolut’s control.

The change does not mean that every significant weakening of the Hungarian forint would automatically trigger a suspension. The provision specifically concerns exceptional market and technical circumstances. If a currency temporarily becomes unavailable, Revolut says customers will be informed through the app. However, the new terms do not specify how long such a suspension could last.

Some transfers could also be affected

The restriction could extend beyond straightforward currency exchanges. According to the detailed terms, transfers between Revolut customers that require a currency conversion could also be affected. For example, if someone wanted to send euros to another Revolut user after converting Hungarian forints, the transfer could fail while the relevant currency exchange was suspended.

The change does not, however, mean that Revolut accounts would be frozen or that all transfers would automatically be stopped.

The potential disruption could be particularly inconvenient for customers who need to make an urgent foreign-currency payment. This could include paying for accommodation abroad or settling an invoice issued in euros. If the required currency cannot be exchanged at the time, customers may have to use another payment method or wait until the exchange becomes available again.

A second bank account could provide a backup

Maintaining another bank account alongside Revolut could provide an alternative if a service becomes temporarily unavailable. However, simply having a second account is of limited use if there is no accessible money in it.

Customers who already know they will have expenses in euros could consider exchanging and setting aside the required amount in advance. This could reduce their reliance on currency exchange being available at the exact time a payment is due.

Other banks can also experience service outages or market-related restrictions, so a second account is not a guarantee against disruption. Having accessible funds with more than one provider can nevertheless provide an additional payment option if one service is temporarily unavailable.

Have you heard? Revolut Hungary set to enter ATM market – what will change for customers?

Check foreign-exchange fees before choosing a backup

Anyone considering opening another bank account should look beyond promotional offers and monthly fees. The costs of currency exchange and foreign-currency transfers can be particularly important for customers who regularly make payments in euros or other foreign currencies. A cheap or free Hungarian forint account does not necessarily offer favourable exchange rates or low fees for foreign-currency transactions.

Customers should therefore check how long promotional conditions remain valid, what fees apply afterwards, and what exchange rates and charges are used for foreign-currency transactions.

World.title: Biljana Plavsic, Bosnian Serb War Criminal Who Withdrew Her Remorse
World.content:
The Serb political elites do not recognise the legitimacy of the ICTY and believe, as Plavsic did, that the court was set up “to prosecute Serbs”. Lack of recognition of the court as a legitimate, bipartisan institution has led to many high-ranking war criminals returning to Serbia and being welcomed as heroes, and/or buried with the highest state honours.

Plavsic never changed her convictions. In her now infamous statement of guilt at the ICTY, she apologised for the persecution of “thousands of non-Serbs” during her sentencing hearing in 2002. “I have now come to the belief and accept the fact that many thousands of innocent people were the victims of an organised, systematic effort to remove Muslims and Croats from the territory claimed by Serbs,” she said.

“Although I was repeatedly informed of allegations of cruel and inhuman conduct against non-Serbs, I refused to accept them or even to investigate. The knowledge that I am responsible for such human suffering and for soiling the character of my people will always be with me,” she added.

But, two years later, in an interview from her prison cell in Sweden, Plavsic withdrew her expression of remorse, saying she had done “nothing wrong”. Her denial of any responsibility for the crimes she was convicted of was met with outrage on behalf of victims’ organisations and the international community.

Although Plavsic may be buried with honours in Republika Srpska, she remains a controversial figure among some Serbs because she was the only high-ranking Serb leader who expressed remorse. Some have not forgiven her for this move.

“She should have never apologised and admitted that Serbs committed crimes,” I was told by some of Plavsic’s close acquaintances during my research. I think the backlash Plavsic received from Serbs after her infamous statement of guilt made her adamant in denying it and ultimately withdrawing her remorse. My impression was that she had a strong urge to go down in history as unrepentant.

To regain the image she had lost because of her unpopular expression of remorse, she repeatedly insisted that she did not regret anything she was accused of. On the contrary, she told me on many occasions, “I would do the same again. I had to protect my people. If I contributed anything in establishing Republika Srpska, our Serb state, and I know I did, there is nothing to regret.”

But although she has been called one of the “founders of Republika Srpska”, Plavsic is no longer a household name for the post-war generations of Serbs like her compatriots Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic – who never apologised for their crimes.

Olivera Simic is a professor at Griffith Law School, Griffith University, Australia. She is the author of the book ‘Madam War Criminal: Biljana Plavsic, Serbia’s Iron Lady’, published by Hurst, 2025.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Week in Review: Elections and Struggles
World.content:
As Bosnia and Herzegovina heads to the polls, promises of political renewal are colliding with entrenched habits that cut across party lines. The governing Trojka [Trio] has struggled to deliver the clean break from clientelism and politicised institutions it promised, potentially opening a path back to power for the unreformed main Bosniak party, the Party of Democratic Action, SDA – less through renewed enthusiasm for the party than from voter disappointment and apathy.

Women’s participation in politics is another key issue. Although women account for more than 40 per cent of candidates as a result of legal obligations, they head just 15.5 per cent of the electoral lists, with parties often placing them low down, where their chances of winning are slim.

World.content:
More than a decade later, Dzeko was part of the team that secured Bosnia and Herzegovina’s second World Cup qualification, earning a place at the 2026 tournament. He reached his 150th international appearance during the group stage.

His 73 international goals include 26 in World Cup qualifying, 14 in European Championship qualifying, nine in the UEFA Nations League and two at World Cup finals.

Dzeko acknowledged that the occasion would be difficult for him personally but stressed that the match remained a competitive fixture rather than a farewell exhibition.

“It will be a difficult match for me personally but in the end everything is about the national team. We know it will be a difficult game. Sweden have been returning to their best in recent months, and you can see the progress under the new coach. They know what they are doing and that is why they have six points from two matches. It will be a difficult game for us, but for them as well,” Dzeko said.

World.title: Police From Three Continents Test Anti-Riot Tactics in Romania
World.content:
More than 500 riot police and gendarmerie personnel from 19 countries gathered at the Romanian Gendarmerie’s training centre in Ochiuri this week to act out security-crisis scenarios in which they tested tactics to quell angry rioters throwing projectiles, setting up barricades and attacking public buildings.

The Carpathian Blue Shield 2026 exercise was designed to test joint responses to complex security situations, including coordination, information-sharing and tactical intervention. Participants included forces from Ukraine, Moldova, Bulgaria and the US as well as Western European countries.

Romanian Interior Minister Catalin Predoiu said security risks “are becoming increasingly interconnected”, which requires public-order forces to adapt and train for real-world scenarios involving multiple threats.

World.title: Polish Activists Open the World’s First Parcel-Locker Machine for Abortion Pills
World.content:
Women Help Women, an international abortion-support network, this week unveiled the Abortomat, which it describes as the world’s first parcel-locker machine for abortion pills. It stands inside AboTak, an abortion-support clinic that opened opposite the Polish parliament in the spring of 2025.

The idea behind it is simple: make getting abortion pills closer to picking up an ordinary delivery. Poland has one of Europe’s densest networks of automated parcel lockers. More than 66,700 machines were operating across the country by the end of 2025 – roughly one for every 560 people – collecting clothes, books, groceries and whatever else people order online.

“Parcel lockers are everywhere in Poland – people joke about our ‘paczkoza’, our obsession with them,” Kinga Jelinska, director of Women Help Women, told BIRN. “So why not use that same technology for abortion pills, where getting them to someone faster can actually matter?”

The process involves a person contacting Women Help Women online and, after a consultation, receiving a six-digit code. That code opens one of 22 compartments containing the medication. The machine was designed by engineers and IT specialists commissioned by the organisation and, unlike commercial parcel lockers, does not store users’ personal data, Jelinska explained.

“Sometimes even waiting a few days can be too long,” she said. “For people whose health is at risk, or who are further along in pregnancy, every day really matters.”

In Poland, that wait exists partly because abortion care remains caught between a restrictive legal system and an extensive informal network built to work around it. Abortion is legal only when a pregnancy threatens a woman’s life or health, or results from a criminal act. Helping someone obtain an abortion outside those circumstances can be punishable by up to three years in prison under Article 152 of the criminal code. The pregnant person however is not criminally liable for ending their own pregnancy.

Donald Tusk’s governing coalition came to power in 2023 promising to change the law, but reform has repeatedly stalled. A bill partially decriminalising assistance in abortion has remained in a special parliamentary committee since 2024. In the meantime, activists have filled much of the gap. Abortion Without Borders, a network of Polish and international groups, says it supported 38,508 abortions in 2025, making it the largest de facto abortion care provider in Poland.

The Abortomat pushes that parallel system one step further – and tests the legal boundary surrounding it. “The person collecting the pills is not committing a crime, and the machine itself cannot be prosecuted,” Justyna Wydrzynska of Abortion Dream Team, the collective that runs the Warsaw clinic, said at the launch.

Wydrzynska has personal experience of that boundary. In 2023, she was convicted of assisting an abortion after sending pills to a woman who had sought help during the Covid pandemic. An appeals court later overturned the conviction and ordered a retrial.

Some lawyers are unconvinced that putting a machine between the activist and the person taking the pills changes much. “Assistance can cover a very broad range of actions,” criminal lawyer Pawel Matyja told Polish news outlet Zero.pl, arguing that sending the medication, arranging its collection and providing the access code could together still amount to assisting an abortion. “These are essentially a series of steps without which the woman would not be able to have the abortion.”

For the time being, the Abortomat will remain indoors for security reasons, Jelinska said. She would much rather put it outside, but since AboTak opened, anti-abortion protesters have regularly gathered outside its entrance. Some demonstrations have involved loudspeakers and vuvuzelas, while the premises have also been targeted with butyric acid.

“Our aim is to draw attention to an institution operating in the heart of the capital which, in our view, violates Polish law. We will continue protesting until it is closed,” Laura Lipinska of the Zycie i Rodzina Foundation, which participates in the protests, said in a statement after the centre opened in 2025.

Despite the protests and legal uncertainty, the activists are pressing ahead. “If we worried about what might happen, or how people might react,” Jelinska said, “we wouldn’t have done anything for the past 12 years.”

World.title: After Bosnia’s ‘Anaemic’ Election Campaign, Polling Day Sees New Challenge
World.content:
On Saturday, the day before Bosnians vote in general elections, election officials in some 5,700 polling stations are due to switch on scanners and fingerprint readers that most of the country has never used before. This is to run tests and so determine whether the technology works properly.
