Adgur Ardzinba: A real application would follow the results of such a debate. But what if the state apparatus, the executive branch, completely refuses to see public opinion?

Georgi Berzenia: We are talking about a new stage now. We are talking about a new stage. I am asking what you like and what you dislike, and you are delving into details that we, as laypeople in this matter…

Alkhas Gagulia: I would like to add something regarding agriculture. There is a program in the Ministry of Agriculture…

Adgur Ardzinba: There is a subsidy program within… It is a good, decent program. But that program is insufficient. There is no science in that program. If there is no science, there will be no result. That is what I am trying to convey. First, there is no consistent, systemic work. Second, simply distributing money—yes, that too is better than nothing when people’s costs are subsidized. That is also good. But my concern lies elsewhere. I want a maximum long-term effect to be achieved. Without making our countryside competitive, we will not make this sector profitable. Consequently, we will always have a negative balance sheet. Why do we speak so much about the countryside? Because it is a cornerstone. We all say that the countryside is the cradle of our traditions. It is not merely an economic category; it is also a social, political, and cultural one. That is why we dedicate so much attention to it here.

Georgi Berzenia: Yes. That is a very interesting topic. A topic about which, truly, a great deal can be said. I simply brought it up because I asked you to provide an overall assessment. It feels to me as though, judging by what you are saying, you concentrate heavily on certain critical moments and specific details, whereas you haven’t touched upon the positive aspects at all.

Adgur Ardzinba: No.

Georgi Berzenia: You simply stated that the president does not divide people, broadly speaking, and that was essentially all.

Adgur Ardzinba: I focused on certain details because I… I articulated the premise that work is being conducted in an un-systemic manner, and I provided a series of examples. I could cite a great many such examples.

Georgi Berzenia: Perhaps you could name some positive aspects after all? For instance, even with agriculture, my association—I understand a deep conversation is one thing, but as an example—they opened a dairy plant in the Ochamchira District. That is agriculture, and as I understand it, it is a high-tech facility.

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, that is the agro-industrial complex.

Georgi Berzenia: Which also engages local villagers, provides jobs, and allows us to consume local produce, even if the raw material isn’t local. Just to give such an example, broadly speaking. And if we look back at the past, Abkhazia previously had much less to take pride in and showcase. Today, there are also things that can be highlighted.

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, an economic forum was held. A rather interesting event. A great number of people came to Abkhazia—top officials, bureaucrats, ministers. I cannot recall anything like it since the time of recognition. We hosted an economic forum. That is wonderful. We introduced many people to the country and drew attention, including media coverage. Following that attention, when an ordinary Russian citizen watches the news on the Rossiya television channel and sees several federal ministers and the First Deputy Chief of the Presidential Administration in Abkhazia discussing the development of this country’s economy, a desire arises in some to go and do business there. Upon arriving here, he does not see the Deputy Chief of Staff or our president. He goes to the Technical Inventory Bureau, he goes to the district administration. And there, he gets caught in such a whirlpool that, God willing, he might escape from it only after several years. That is what needs to be addressed immediately.

Alkhas Gagulia: Back in 2024, you stated that relations between Russia and Abkhazia were at their lowest point. A couple of years—a year and a half—have passed since then. How do you assess these relations now?

Adgur Ardzinba: The most interesting part is that the very same thing was voiced on March 7 of this year during a concert here in our capital. A representative of the Presidential Administration, one of the department heads, spoke there. I cannot recall his surname at the moment, but he was a rather pleasant person. He mentioned that…

Georgi Berzenia: The Russian Administration?

Adgur Ardzinba: Yes, the Russian Administration. He mentioned that our relations had cooled somewhat over the recent period, but that we need to fix all of this. By the way, I was pleasantly surprised by such a sober assessment. However, a whole host of factors contributed to that state of affairs. Without speaking of oneself, one cannot speak of others. To a greater extent, it was the activity of the ex-president, who attempted to resolve his own economic matters and tried to smear everyone opposing him as pro-Western and so forth. Naturally, when an official of such stature writes briefing notes on his fellow citizens, that information is examined at a serious level, to say the least. And when the head of state visits a district and tells people that their pensions will stop being paid unless we vote for the Pitsunda state dacha, and so on—how can that not reflect in the minds and hearts of the people? Those errors were committed. Now, over this period of time, I see that in Russia, with the arrival of a new team of individuals responsible for our direction, they have drawn the correct conclusions from what occurred previously. Once again, as we discussed above, far from everything has been rectified yet.

Alkhas Gagulia: And what specifically needs to be rectified?

Adgur Ardzinba: The persecution of citizens. That is what causes harm. On the whole, however, the agenda has shifted. All those harmful initiatives have receded into the background. Incidentally, they themselves acknowledge that those were not beneficial. Right now, as I see it, very broad opportunities are open before us, before our small country. By the way, similar opportunities were open to us right after recognition, during that flourishing period. Later, to some extent, everything experienced a slight decline, but now there is such a surge. We cited the economic forum as an example. Several federal ministers, governors, heads of republics, and the First Deputy Chief of Staff came to Abkhazia, to the city of Sukhum, to discuss the development of our economy. Those are enormous opportunities. In other words, a tremendous amount of attention is being paid to our relatively small country in this regard. And that ought to be capitalized on in the best sense. I do not see that same level of initiative from our side—from the authorized bodies and structures—to make full use of all this. Because such chances may not present themselves again in the future. Russia is a vast country. It is navigating a very complex period right now. Further escalation could follow, and people will focus on solving their own problems. Why should they travel with entire government delegations to Abkhazia, sit with us here in Sukhum, and try to help us figure out how to make our lives better? That is primarily our own responsibility. There is transportation infrastructure—the train has started running, work is underway at the border, the airport has begun operations. Most importantly, what genuinely pleases me is that very positive information about Abkhazia is circulating across the Russian Federation’s media space. There is outright promotion of Abkhazia as a resort destination. That provides a huge impetus for the growth of our tourism sector and the overall economy.

Yet, returning to those matters: when such promotion is taking place and top officials are calling Abkhazia an ally, prioritizing it, we must work proactively right here on the ground. Do you understand? Rather than simply trailing behind, picking up scattered initiatives, and failing to carry even those through to completion. That is what I am concerned about. And I will tell you why I am so concerned, Georgi. Alkhas, 2008 brought recognition. Following that, starting in 2010, Abkhazia was provided with financial assistance. Substantial financial assistance—exceeding one billion dollars. However, those funds dissolved across various projects. Back then, too, there were no clear priorities or plans. As a result, where we had the opportunity to completely resolve the situation—at least within the energy sector, given the possibilities that opened up at the time—we would not be facing these problems today. We would not be talking about a deficit today had we utilized that opportunity wisely back then. Therefore, I simply do not want history to repeat itself this time, which is why I am so concerned. The fact that there is a warming of relations, a mutual understanding, and that people are frankly paying far more attention to Abkhazia than before—that is a reality. That is a fact. The other question is what we ourselves are capable of proposing and what we ourselves are capable of achieving; that is where the problem lies.

Georgi Berzenia: And what role do you see for Sergei Vladimirovich Kiriyenko?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, I already noted above that he is a person… First of all, let us be frank. Every official possesses a certain degree of capability. There are a number of leaders in the Russian Federation, and they all have differing levels of capability. As far as I can see, this individual possesses quite substantial capabilities. Within the scope of those capabilities, he is doing everything possible to assist Abkhazia and to involve as many federal leaders in this work as possible. Let us recall—we live here after all—past periods. Let us recall the period from 2020 to 2025. How many federal leaders visited Abkhazia over those five years? The Minister of Sports came. The Minister of Economic Development came a couple of times. To my memory, that was all. Yet now, in a span of a year and a half… Again, when these people visit, our officials and top leaders have the opportunity to sit down over a cup of coffee and discuss specific issues. I assure you, I know the situation in Russia: not every governor or regional leader has the opportunity to sit down with ministers and drink coffee whenever they wish. Yet we have that opportunity. And all of this is thanks to this new team.

At the same time, I cannot fail to mention our people here. Had our people not stood up in 2024—and throughout the period leading up to November 2024—to defend their core interests, none of this would exist. Absolutely no changes would have occurred. Had that entire proposed agenda passed quietly and silently, no one would have given us a second thought. The Abkhazian people courageously defended their interests, their core interests. And the Abkhazian people—who, by the way, are exceptionally friendly toward the Russian people—stood up, protected their interests, and drew attention to themselves. That commands respect, and I observe that respect coming from these leaders.

Georgi Berzenia: Speaking of the development of relations between Abkhazia and Russia, I have also recalled with several guests in this studio the 2014 treaty. It was signed more than 12 years ago now, back in 2014, so ten years have passed. Political events were taking place back then as well, yet no review was conducted, no outcomes were summarized, and it was extended automatically. How would you evaluate these 10 to 12 years of that treaty, and where do we go from here? Does it require refinement, or is a new treaty or a new phase in relations with Russia needed?

Adgur Ardzinba: The treaty is quite thoroughly developed. Moreover, when it was adopted, as you remember, there was a certain degree of opposition here as well. The very people who in the recent past accused us of being pro-Western and anti-Russian were themselves blocking the border to prevent that treaty from being signed, to speak specifically. But the treaty itself became a foundational document following the 2008–2009 post-recognition agreements. Coming after them in 2014, it served as a foundational document that touched upon economic forms of interaction, social matters, and other areas.

Of course, time moves forward. It keeps moving forward. And I am certain that we have not fully realized the potential of that agreement. There is still much to discuss within it. However, Georgi, we can also recall other agreements. We have a whole host of agreements that remain unfulfilled. If we return to defense and security, within the framework of signed agreements regarding joint efforts to strengthen the state border along the Ingur River, nothing has been done—neither from our side nor from the side of the Russian Federation. Furthermore, matters regarding the joint group of forces in that direction remain poorly developed.

If we speak about the economy, we have an agreement on the mutual protection of investments. In that direction, too, we need to look at what genuinely concerns investors from the Russian Federation—not those who sought to create a tailored, exclusive climate for themselves, but regular businesspeople. And they do not necessarily have to be billionaires; they can simply be people capable of investing 10 million rubles, or 20 million rubles, conditionally speaking. We need to communicate with them and examine the rules and standards that exist in the Russian Federation. They could be implemented here. For instance, the public service system in the Russian Federation—the MFC system, “My Documents”—which several years ago was announced to start operating here, has seen nothing done. That system is objectively considered one of the best and most efficient in the world. So, please, let us integrate it here.

Georgi Berzenia: In Russia, which…

Adgur Ardzinba: Yes, in Russia. We all use it, as we are Russian citizens. It is an incredibly convenient system. As for tax administration, one of the most effective systems has been established in Russia. That is a reality; you can see it in all surveys. Russia has specific criteria for evaluating the investment attractiveness of various regions. At the St. Petersburg forum every year, if memory serves, a specific rating and classification is assigned to one region or another. That, too, is a positive thing. Well, as I mentioned above, the entire local economy resides in the districts.

Georgi Berzenia: In September, elections to the State Duma will take place in the Russian Federation. These elections will also be held on the territory of Abkhazia, allowing citizens of Abkhazia who are simultaneously citizens of Russia to participate. What is your view on the significance of these elections for citizens of Abkhazia, and should citizens take part in them?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, look, posters reading “Abkhazia’s Voice Matters to Russia” are currently hanging all across Abkhazia, right? If Russia, which has provided us with such immense support all these years, sends a message that our voice matters to Russia, is it really that difficult to go and vote if it truly is so important? And it is important, first of all because we are almost all Russian citizens, for the most part, when provided with such an opportunity… I remember in past periods there were issues with the number of polling stations and so forth; as far as I can see, it is being approached more systematically now. Of course, people should go and vote. Why not? It isn’t that difficult to do. If people say it is important, and one can demonstrate civic engagement in that sense, I believe one should go and vote.

As for whom to vote for, that is a separate question. I do not have the right to engage in campaigning here right now, but one should also look at the retrospective. Various political forces have existed throughout Abkhazia’s history; you are younger, but Alkhas and I remember the blockade times and the post-blockade period when the new team came in. We must also understand for ourselves which political force is minded to help Abkhazia, and which political force recognized Abkhazia’s independence. These are different teams with different viewpoints, so here too, I believe our choice is straightforward; we simply need to understand it all.

Alkhas Gagulia: We have spoken at length about relations with Russia—it is our strategic partner—but an event took place in the Turkish parliament recently. People view it in different ways, and opinions vary. In my view, it is a very landmark event when 30% of the Turkish parliament raised the issue of ending the isolation of Abkhazia. Recognition was not on the table, and there were differing opinions regarding the motives behind that speech. It turned out to be primarily the opposition party. But anticipating your answer, I would say—as one Chinese sage or general secretary put it—it doesn’t matter what color the cat is, as long as it catches mice. What is your view on this initiative, and what, in your opinion, actually happened there?

Adgur Ardzinba: Alkhas, your late relative Gennady Leonidovich Gagulia once told me a story about cats and mice too. He said that when you try to play political cat-and-mouse, make sure that you are not the mouse. Yes, of course, it is a positive signal. Incidentally, our organization issued a statement on this matter. The signal itself is positive, even if, as some note, it represents an element of internal political struggle to attract our large diaspora and secure votes. Even if that is the case, it remains positive. It shows the role and significance of our diaspora, which we utilize very weakly—and not only in Turkey. But that is a vast, separate topic. Therefore, it is a positive signal, and that is how we assess it. However, actions and deeds matter most. Words are fine—we approve and welcome them—but deeds are what count. Russia went ahead in 2008 and established diplomatic relations with Abkhazia, recognizing our independence. Those are real actions.

Alkhas Gagulia: There was a caveat there, if I am not mistaken, that there was no question of any recognition.

Adgur Ardzinba: When politicians speak about it to attract votes, again, it is still a good thing that the topic of Abkhazia and ending its isolation is being discussed, forming a positive agenda to attract votes. But I very much hope it will not remain mere words.

Alkhas Gagulia: Adgur Ardzinba of 2024 and Adgur Ardzinba of 2026. What advice would you give today to the person you were back then?

Adgur Ardzinba: That is a good question; I hadn’t thought about it. That is actually too short a time frame. I wouldn’t have changed much.

Georgi Berzenia: Significant events have occurred. First of all, the elections. They surely brought about some…

Alkhas Gagulia: Takeaways from the elections. What mistakes were made?

Adgur Ardzinba: Look, yes, of course, we made a whole host of mistakes. But it is not a given that if I had told my former self to avoid those mistakes, other mistakes wouldn’t have been made instead. Mistakes are part of any process.

Alkhas Gagulia: Nor is it a given that he would have listened?

Adgur Ardzinba: I will tell you this: it has been a rather interesting period of time. I consider myself fortunate. I feel fortunate in that—and I say this sincerely—the Abkhazian people, a portion of the Abkhazian people, and a substantial portion at that, entrusted me with this responsible mission. That is a great, immense honor. There is nothing above that, Alkhas. Any obstacles or hurdles are minor by comparison. When serving your people is not mere rhetoric but a reality—if done sincerely and from the heart—there are no obstacles. That is the highest honor.

Therefore, what would I advise my former self? I would advise him not to doubt, because a person always experiences doubt when faced with immense difficulties. Alkhas, we speak about this so casually now. For instance, when people entered the building in November 2024, some said they shouldn’t have entered, while others asked what would have happened had they not entered. Someone had to take responsibility. Other politicians were there; we were all together. While we achieved a certain goal on the one hand, on the other hand, during all those days—and I slept inside that building for three nights to ensure people wouldn’t clash with one another—it was a difficult period, followed by the election process.

Naturally, any person experiences doubt. Our recent presidential elections were unique—they were engaging and event-filled. But those elections were particularly interesting because our team faced such a formidable, serious opponent equipped with vast resources. When you have a very serious opponent, it mobilizes you immensely. I assure you, had that not been the case, the elections might have turned out very dull. Instead, they unfolded the way they did.

Alkhas Gagulia: To be honest, I dream of dull elections for all branches of power.

Adgur Ardzinba: We are speaking about personality and perception right now. Yes, I too dream that our country, like Switzerland, could have dull elections. But if we talk about what existed then versus now, it has been a very fascinating period during which I came to respect my people even more. I feel immense pride in being part of this nation—small in numbers perhaps, but possessing a grand spirit and a vast heart—a people that cannot be intimidated, no matter how hard anyone tries. And with such a spirit in our hearts, we are bound for success.

I am absolutely certain that we will succeed in everything. All those misunderstandings and unpleasantries, including those in relations between Abkhazia and Russia, are entirely surmountable. I am confident that… Look, we are talking about certain incidents right now, and they are indeed unpleasant. Yet we had a period when the entire country was under a blockade for six to seven years. We were under a blockade—the whole country. Now we are talking about a few individuals being unable to travel, whereas back then it was the entire country.

Even then… Vladislav Grigorievich Ardzinba—for which I will always be grateful to him—was a great, exceptionally wise man. He always maintained that we must orient ourselves toward a union with the Russian Federation; that time would pass, people would change, and understanding would arrive. And he was right. Although you remember, Alkhas, how many different proposals there were, delegation after delegation, yet we did not deviate from our path. All these misunderstandings taking place are simply part of the process. Just as there are mistakes on our side, there are mistakes on theirs as well.

I am confident that everything will be fine. The main thing is to remain vigilant. Times are very dangerous. I will repeat it endlessly: defense and security.

Alkhas Gagulia: Well, I want to say thank you for today’s broadcast, for coming to join us so that a thorough conversation could take place on all the questions that interested us. The only thing I would like to add, of course, is that while we spoke about priority tasks—about defense and education—all of this stems from a single overarching priority: our sovereignty and our independence. If that serves as the main guidepost, everything else is meant to serve that exact priority. There are no other options. You mentioned my age twenty times today; in any case, my generation accepts nothing less. We lost far too many people for this land, and it is thanks to them that we stand on this land today. That is what I want to say to every single politician, without exception, on both sides. Thank you for the broadcast and for coming. I look forward to our next meetings.

Adgur Ardzinba: Thank you, friends. I believe that while our conversation was lengthy, it was candid, and we answered a number of questions. If we missed anything, I think we will have another opportunity to meet. As for sovereignty, Alkhas, that concerns not only your generation. The younger generation and the youth—the rising generation with whom I interact—see no other path across all generations than the building of an independent, sovereign Abkhazian state in Abkhazia. If anyone thinks otherwise, that would be their mistake. All of us have stood, are standing, and will continue to stand for this. Fundamentally, our entire conversation has been dedicated to strengthening that sovereignty, to making our state less vulnerable.

Today, our state is vulnerable. Let us be frank. To eliminate these weak points, we need systemic work, the establishment of priorities, societal consolidation, and defense to preserve our territory, as well as our language—which you raised, Georgi—and our culture. All of this is vital, because knowing a language alone does not make you Abkhaz. The upcoming parliamentary elections are also crucial; the quality and substantive content of that body are of great importance. All of this, as was rightly stated, Alkhas, exists in order to preserve, strengthen, and pass down. Thank you.

Georgi Berzenia: Thank you for an engaging conversation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘We will decide in the coming months’: Pashinyan on choosing model for Armenia’s new nuclear power plant
World.content:
Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has announced a change in the government’s position on the technology and design of a new nuclear power plant.

“I have said dozens of times before that we do not need anything more [powerful] than a modular nuclear power plant. That was our position. But now we have to understand that a modular plant will most likely not be enough to meet our needs,” Pashinyan said.

He explained that the government changed its position because of the construction of AI factories. Armenia now needs to import electricity to meet their power requirements.

Discussions continue over which technology would best suit the new nuclear power plant. The Armenian government expects to make a decision on the issue by the end of 2027.

A day earlier, the prime minister met a delegation led by Alexey Likhachev, director general of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. They discussed proposals from the Russian side.

Armenia is currently working to extend the operating life of the Metsamor nuclear power plant until 2036. Russia has taken part in efforts to extend the plant’s operating life and modernise it throughout this period. The plant originally entered service in 1977.

At the same time, Yerevan is discussing the construction of a new nuclear power plant with several countries, including the US. The prime minister has repeatedly said in recent months that the nuclear power issue is not a geopolitical choice for Armenia: “We will choose the proposal that serves us best.”

Pashinyan does not rule out accepting the Russian proposal

Speaking about the upcoming decision on the technology for the new nuclear power plant, the prime minister stressed that before Armenia signed memorandums of understanding with the US on 8 August 2025, Armenia had a surplus of electricity.

“We had to think about where to direct this surplus energy. A year later, Armenia had become a country with an electricity deficit,” he said.

According to Nikol Pashinyan, this resulted from the construction of two AI factories in Armenia during that period:

“The point is that, given the scale of the investment projects already approved, Armenia has faced an electricity deficit. In other words, these projects are fully absorbing the surplus we have. So we need to decide what to do next.”

The prime minister said the government would make a decision in the coming months. Pashinyan also said that Armenia could accept the proposal put forward by Russia:

“It is quite possible that building a 1,000 MW plant will prove to be the most logical solution. However, I cannot say for certain at this stage because experts are still assessing the issue.”

“The unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW” — Likhachev

Rosatom director general Alexey Likhachev told journalists some details of Russia’s proposal after talks in Yerevan. Likhachev said Armenia would continue to rely on nuclear energy for decades to come. Russia therefore plans to “formulate the most competitive proposal” for building a new reactor unit in the coming months.

“And in our view, this unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW,” Likhachev said.

According to him, the proposal involves a VVER-1000 reactor, a pressurised water reactor with a capacity of 1,000 MW.

The head of Rosatom stressed that this proposal is “the best currently available on the global market”. He added that Rosatom has built and continues to build VVER reactors of this type in India and Iran:

“They combine very high economic efficiency, namely a low cost of electricity, with all the necessary Generation III+ safety systems.”

Details of talks with Rosatom director general in Yerevan

The Armenian prime minister’s office said Pashinyan and Likhachev discussed:

work to extend the operating life of the existing second reactor unit at the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant;

Russia’s proposals for building a new reactor unit.

At the same time, the prime minister told Likhachev that the Armenian government was continuing to consider proposals from other international partners.

Pashinyan stressed that the final decision would depend solely on economic considerations. These would include price, quality, safety, construction timelines and guarantees.

The statement also said Alexey Likhachev described cooperation with Armenian partners as constructive. The Rosatom chief also provided detailed information about the construction of not only large VVER reactors, but also small and medium-sized reactors.

World.title: EU Council delegation visits Azerbaijan’s Aghdam district (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. A delegation of the Eastern Europe and Central Asia Working Party (COEST) of the Council of the European Union visited Azerbaijan’s Aghdam district on October 2.

As part of the visit, the delegation was briefed on mine clearance operations in the area of Saricali village.

Representatives of Azerbaijan’s Mine Action Agency (ANAMA) briefed the foreign delegation on the contamination of Azerbaijani territories with mines by Armenia and ongoing demining efforts. They noted that Aghdam district is considered one of the areas most heavily contaminated with mines and unexploded ordnance. The guests observed the mine clearance process.

The EU Council delegation later met with Emin Huseynov, the Special Representative of the President of Azerbaijan in the Aghdam, Fuzuli and Khojavend districts.

During the meeting, Huseynov spoke about the large-scale reconstruction and development work being carried out in the liberated territories.

A video highlighting the changes taking place in the liberated territories was then shown.

A representative of Azerbaijan’s State Commission on Prisoners of War, Hostages and Missing Persons briefed the delegation on the commission’s activities, including efforts to identify mass graves in the liberated territories and investigate the fate of Azerbaijani citizens who were taken prisoner or went missing.

The EU Council delegation had earlier visited the cities of Shusha and Khankendi as part of its visit.

World.title: WA's varied climate — rainfall to heat — captured in the first month of Spring
World.content:
Western Australia's first month of spring was anything but straightforward.

The state experienced a mixed bag of weather, from unusually heavy rain inland to sudden bursts of summer-like heat.

Photos from our viewers from the month of September perfectly illustrate just how different WA's climate can be from one end of the state to the other.

Grey clouds and a rainbow over a field in the Wheatbelt. (Supplied: Karen Siegert)

The month began against the backdrop of a notably dry winter for a large part of the state.

The first major downpour didn't deliver the rain to Perth or the South West, but hundreds of kilometres inland.

A slow-moving trough drew tropical moisture into the Goldfields and the Interior, producing widespread cloud, rain and thunderstorms across the area.

It brought well above average rainfall for many locations that often only see about 5 to 15 millimetres of rain in September.

Yellow blooms in a field in Toodyay. (Supplied: Greg Brown)

Leonora picked up 59mm in the 24 hours to 9am on September 7, its wettest September day on record and nearly double its old record of 32.6mm from 1984.

The heavy rainfall led to flooded roads around Leonora and the closure of the Goldfields Highway and the Leonora-Laverton Road.

Despite the rainy conditions in the interior, it was drier at Perth's City Beach. (Supplied: Robert Rouse)

By the end of the month, the town had accumulated more than 136mm, a significant increase from its monthly average of just 9mms and smashing the station's old record of 83.3mm for the month back in 1904.

Temperatures soar

Mid-way through the month, there was a large temperature contrast across the country.

While south-eastern states shivered through below average temperatures, western parts of WA were sweating through more summer-like conditions as day-time temperatures soared up to 12 degrees Celsius more than usual.

A dog walks on a beach in Mandurah beneath glowering grey skies. (Supplied: Regine Andersen)

That heat was also thanks to that same trough system that had been driving storm activity through the interior.

A strong high pressure system to the south helped push the trough back towards the south-west coast, where it dragged warm air down from the north, which had observed 40C temperatures during the month.

The northerly winds saw temperatures soar across the southern half, with many locations challenging September records.

Beachgoers enjoy the sunshine at Cottesloe in Perth. (Supplied: Clive Addison)

Perth rapidly climbed to 30.3C on September 16, its first "30" of the season and its warmest day since April.

It saw residents flood to Perth's beaches for a chance to soak up the summer-like conditions.

Locals at South Perth foreshore, young and old, are enjoying the warmer weather. (Supplied: Greg Brown)

The heat didn't ease after sunset, with the temperature only dropping to 18.2C early the next morning, just shy of its warmest September minimum ever.

It wasn't just Perth that sweated through some warm nights

A pair of black swans, and cygnets, swim on the Swan River in Perth. (Supplied: Stuart Davis)

Nearly a dozen spots observed their hottest minimums for September, including Wongan Hills which only got down to 21C.

Murchison smashed its record from 1990 after dropping to a warm 19.8C and Cunderdin, Beverley and Badgingarra all broke their 15-year records.

Blue skies and warm daytime temperatures were seen in many parts of the state. (Supplied: Rod Lawson Kerr)

And the records kept tumbling during the day.

Katanning reached a toasty 31.8C on September 17, just tipping over its previous record from 2006.

Albany was one of the locations which experienced temperatures higher than usual. (Supplied: John Rich)

Rocky Gully South, North Walpole and Albany Airport also set new September records after reaching well above average temperatures for the month.

More unseasonal rain

The unusual rainfall events continued in the state's interior.

By late September, another moisture-rich system was generating heavy rain and thunderstorms across parts of the Goldfields, Interior and south-eastern parts.

Rawlinna Station, located between Kalgoorlie and Eucla, experienced late-September thunderstorms. (Supplied: Stu Parker)

Kalgoorlie-Boulder recorded about six times its average September rainfall, picking up just over 80mm.

The storm activity was another unseasonal event for a part of the state that is often dry during Spring.

Some viewers took to the road to experience the springtime conditions. (Supplied: Peter Randell)

That trough system was pushed back towards the south-west coast where it developed into a low pressure system, delivering rain across the weekend to central and southern parts of the state.

After a run of warm sunny days, Perth decided to foreshadow the gloomy ending of the AFL Grand Final by recording its coolest day of the month at a top of 17C.

A visitor enjoys the view from a platform at Bibra Lake. (Supplied: Gloria Daniels)

While the city missed out on much of the rainfall over the month, it received one final good dumping on the last day, pushing its total to just over 38mm, less than half its monthly average for September.

The Bureau of Meteorology has forecast an increased chance of unusually high rainfall across much of southern and central WA over October, which could make up for that lack of rain.

World.title: Graziers step in to fix damaged roads after incomes 'decimated'
World.content:
Samantha and Richard Maiden of Mt Gipps Station estimate they have lost more than a quarter of their annual business due to ongoing road closures.

The couple's sheep station, which also offers farm-stay accommodation in remote Far West New South Wales, has had about 25 millimetres of rain this year, closing its mainly dirt roads on and off for more than five months.

Sam Maiden is concerned about the safety of road users. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

While they waited for repair crews, Ms Maiden estimated they lost about $60,000 in revenue after having to cancel reservations with guests unable to get in on flooded roads.

"It's decimated the tourist business," the grazier said, whose station is located about 40 kilometres north of Broken Hill.

"We would be running at about 80 per cent down compared to this time last year."

Outback businesses blame app for customer downturn Inaccuracies with Live Traffic NSW are causing confusion and a loss of vital customers, businesses say.

Mr Maiden said the road is also heavily utilised by livestock trucks, which could easily tip over on the unstable road and prevent them from moving their sheep.

Getting graziers on board

Transport for New South Wales (TfNSW) has launched an initiative to hire graziers and station owners like the Maidens as contractors to help fix roads in the Far West using equipment they already may own.

Craig Matthews, director of regional road network maintenance for the west region, said the decision was due to three natural disasters in the area over the past six months.

Craig Matthews says the project aims to speed up road repairs in the Far West. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

"The big challenge is we have 2,800km of unsealed road networks," he said.

"It's a very vast network of roads."

Mr Matthews said landholders wishing to become contractors would be paid hourly market rates through a tender process and would have to cover their own initial registration costs.

Red tape slowing repairs

However, graziers believe red tape is slowing road repairs because a trained spotter or safety supervisor must be present.

"We need to keep people safe, and we don't want people operating by themselves," Mr Mathews said.

Graziers say they have spent thousands of dollars for their own road-fixing machinery. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

However, Ms Maiden said it was "disrespectful" for TfNSW to think graziers did not already have the knowledge and safety requirements to work by themselves with their own workers.

Ms Maiden said the program was not fit for purpose as graziers did not want to take on "big contracts" and lengthy tender processes.

She suggested an "emergency response tender situation" where graziers who have the right equipment could be called upon to fix roads within 100km of them.

"We just want the road open. We don't want to make a billion dollars from it, [but] we need to be reimbursed for the costs and the time," she said.

Richard Maiden wants red tape to be cut to enable faster road repairs. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

Mr Maiden said he would like to see the red tape cut, but graziers would likely resort to doing the work to fix roads by themselves, and another worker spotting, if the wait was months.

"I know they've got to have all the rules and regulations, but it gets to a point that [if] they make it that hard, nothing gets done."

World.title: 'It breaks you': Friend of stabbed pilot speaks out
World.content:
When Smit Machcharr was training to become a pilot, his friends called him "Smit Mac".

Captain Dhaval Patel trained alongside him in New Zealand, and they have known each other for "close to two decades".

"I vividly remember him helping colleagues and peers, educating them on the concepts of aviation with so much clarity and knowledge," Mr Patel said.

"And I had the privilege of getting my fourth stripe on becoming a captain by his hand."

Smit Machchhar's LinkedIn profile shows he has been working for airlines for more than a decade. (X: India in Israel)

So when footage emerged this week of Mr Machchhar after he was attacked while flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, his friend could barely believe it.

"I saw the first glimpse, and I was just not ready to believe it was Captain Smit," Mr Patel told the ABC.

"It just was shattering to be listening and looking at the visuals.

"When it happens to the person you know, the person you love, it breaks you."

Mr Machchhar was allegedly attacked by his co-pilot, who "apparently tried to crash the plane", according to Israel's prime minister.

Now, as Mr Machchhar recovers in hospital, he is being hailed as a hero by his friends, his country, India, and people around the world.

Pilot takes a call from PM

Smit Machchhar spoke with Narendra Modi on video chat while continuing his recovery in hospital. (Reuters)

According to a statement published on X by the Saudi Arabia embassy to the US, preliminary investigations indicate "the first officer had assaulted the aircraft captain, resulting in both sustaining various injuries".

After the incident, Mr Machchhar was moved to Abu Dhabi for further treatment and was "recovering well," according to India's embassy in the United Arab Emirates.

His family flew from India to be by his side and is currently with him.

In a video call with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mr Machchhar said he had been "fighting for my life" on the plane.

"I have been flying for 17 years. I have been captain for 11 years. I know what is happening in flight even with my eyes closed," he said.

"When I was on the floor, I could sense that the aircraft was going down, and then I told myself, 'Smit, give a last push. Door is there.' I was getting stabbed at that point as well, but I opened the door, and others came inside.

"Everyone had [a] role in it. I was trying to save my life but [at the] same time I was also thinking I could not let [passengers] die.

"Afterwards, everyone supported me. I got the best medical attention here in Saudi."

Mr Modi told Mr Machchhar he had done "such a tremendous job that not just us Indians but people worldwide want to speak and meet you".

'Entire clan' full of pride

Captain Smit Machchhar spoke about his aviation career and mentoring young pilots in a vodcast in 2025. (YouTube: )

Mr Patel was glad to see his friend "recovering steadily, out of any danger and in good health".

"That was the first sight of relief, seeing he's actually recovering and responding well to all the medical treatments," he said.

He was also happy to see his friend honoured by Mr Modi and "leaders around the world".

"It's pride for our entire clan to see one of our colleagues being respected by our honorary prime minister," he said.

World.title: Labor's working holiday visa policy risks regional seats, experts say
World.content:
After six months working as a chef in a Far North Queensland kitchen, Rocco Raseri should from today be eligible for his third year working holiday visa.

However, under the federal government's changes to the system, the number of spots up for grabs has gone from 31,000 last year, to now just over 5,000.

"With this uncertainty, probably I wouldn't even have done these six months of work," the 27-year-old Italian backpacker said.

"That is a lot [of time working] to not even get the opportunity to stay here."

Mr Raseri is one of thousands of casual seasonal workers who power Australia's winter holiday destination, and the country's third-largest foodbowl, in Far North Queensland.

He said if he had known his spot was not guaranteed, he would have made different choices, such as seeking sponsorship in a capital city.

"Probably just travelling in Australia to see as much as I can see, instead of staying six months in Cairns," he said.

"It's beautiful, but the goal was to get these days to apply for a visa."

Mr Raseri has finished his six months regional work to apply for his third-year visa. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Mr Raseri's change of heart is what businesses in backpacker-reliant regions fear most, and political analysts say it could cost Labor at the next federal election.

Vulnerable seats

Australian National University political marketing expert Andrew Hughes said working holiday visa changes put regional MPs in a tight spot.

Dr Hughes said the visa policy protected Labor's core city voters at the expense of backpacker-dependant regions nationwide.

Backpackers fill the jobs during peak seasons in Australia's third largest food bowl, Far North Queensland. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

The NTs Lingiari, Bullwinkel in WA, and several regional Tasmanian and New South Wales seats could now be in question, he said.

"It creates that wedge and that perception that the government has forgotten about the regions," he said.

However, Dr Hughes said Queensland votes were more vulnerable than any other state, particularly with "the rise of One Nation", and the far north's seat of Leichhardt would be ground zero.

Labor's Matt Smith won the long-held Coalition seat, spanning from Cairns to the Torres Strait, on a 9.5 per cent swing at last year's federal election.

It was one of seven new Labor seats delivered by Queensland, lifting its contribution from five to 12 of the state's 30 seats.

However, the LNP narrowly won the statewide vote by just over 1 per cent.

Political expert Andrew Hughes says Matt Smith is facing a huge challenge amid the new immigration changes. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Since then, One Nation has surged in popularity, polling 36 per cent in Queensland, ahead of Labor's 25 per cent, according to this week's Newspoll.

Dr Hughes said the visa policy was a "significant" challenge to Mr Smith's hold on the crucial Labor seat.

"It shows whether he's connected and listening to the needs of all his electorate or just those in certain areas which are more Labor friendly," he said.

" He's going to have to try and defend a policy which he knows probably in his electorate does not work. "

He said Labor would be keen to retain Leichhardt, which was a Coalition stronghold for decades under Warren Entsch who regularly crossed the parliamentary floor.

Focus on solutions

James Cook University political scientist Maxine Newlands agreed Queensland was "certainly unique" when it came to "bucking the trend" at federal level elections, making it worth major party focus.

However, she said regional MPs like Matt Smith did not need to publicly oppose the policy to bring confidence back to voters if alternatives were offered.

"It's got to be solution-led and it's got to be community solution led," she said.

Dr Maxine Newlands says Labor MPs will need to focus on solutions. (Supplied: Maxine Newlands)

She said Working Holiday Visa holders were the second-largest contributors to Australia's net overseas migration, placing them at the centre of the debate.

"The concern with this is obviously we're going to see a repetition of the shortage of workers that we saw during COVID," Dr Newlands said.

"[Leading up to the election] people are going to look and say to their local members, 'Have you done enough for us in the last three years?'"

Smith's plan

Earlier this week, Mr Smith told ABC Far North he was already having conversations with peak tourism and agriculture bodies in Cairns to come up with solutions.

"Then I can take that back to [Immigration Minister Tony Burke] and say 'Hey this is some of the stuff that's being thought of up here'," Mr Smith said.

Federal MP Matt Smith says he is already speaking with stakeholders for a way forward. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The current scheme, he said, was not attracting enough workers to regional Australia.

He said more than a third of an estimated 211,000 working holiday-makers were British, who no longer needed to complete regional work for extra visas.

"They're all hanging out in Bondi … they're not helping us out here, and that's where the pressure is being felt," he said.

" The important thing throughout this process is to make sure regions like ours continue to get the workforce they need. "

Mr Smith said increasing the Pacific Area Labor Mobility scheme was a viable option for the regions, but he would continue to work with stakeholders in the meantime.

Mr Smith says most backpackers are relaxing at Bondi Beach instead of working in the regions. (AAP: John Fotiadis )

"The last thing that any of us want to do is put the brakes on the tourism industry, particularly up here which has gone through so much over the last five or six years," he said.

Dr Hughes agreed the altruistic element of assisting Pacific nations tied into Labor's policy of assisting island nations like Tuvalu in the face of climate change and rising sea levels.

"Labor believes the working holiday changes takes some of the heat out of the migration debate, whereas I don't think it's achieved that outcome," he said.

World.title: How do I know my child is ready to leave the house on their own?
World.content:
By the time children are around 12 years old, many will begin to ask if they can go out to the local park, playground or shops to spend time with their friends without adult supervision.

This may happen more often during the school holiday period. They might say:

All of my friends are going. Can I hang out with them?

When a child first asks this question, it can be difficult for parents to judge whether their child is ready. Parents might want experts to give them a specific age recommendation, but children develop at their own pace and readiness varies.

This means there is no single right age when children are ready to spend time with friends, out of the house, unsupervised.

As the parent of three children, I've faced this situation myself.

So how do you know when it's okay to let your child go out on their own?

The importance of independence

Children need opportunities for independent activities to build wellbeing.

The freedom to go out with friends without adult supervision gives children the chance to explore, make choices and navigate unexpected challenges. It allows them to develop their autonomy, confidence and resilience.

What is FAFO parenting and does it work? Is FAFO the 1980s parenting style today's generation of kids need, rebellion against gentle child-rearing, or exhausted parents just throwing their hands in the air?

It can also help kids get more active. Adventurous outdoor activities with friends, such as bike riding, allow children to learn how to cope with potentially risky situations and uncertainty, which may reduce their chances of developing anxiety.

Research on children whose parents allowed them to travel and play in their neighbourhoods also found it may help them cultivate friendships and create a sense of community.

What are the main concerns?

While many parents and carers acknowledge the benefits of letting their child have more independence, they may still feel nervous about the potential risks that come with it.

A 2019 New Zealand survey asked more than 2,000 parents about their attitudes towards risky play and children being out on their own, and the barriers that prevented them from allowing their children to be more independent.

The two biggest concerns were road safety (increased risks of traffic accidents) and "stranger danger" (children potentially having encounters with harmful adults).

So, with these concerns in mind, what are some things you can do to see if your child is ready?

Have a conversation

If your child asks to be out alone, you might start by asking them:

What makes you feel ready to be out on your own?

Your child's answer may give you a clearer idea of whether they're ready or not.

I've stayed at home alone before. I'm responsible. I think you should trust me enough to be able to do this on my own.

Evaluate their readiness

There are a number of things to consider when deciding if your child is capable.

Loading...

First, is your child aware of their surroundings? Do they notice potential hazards? For instance, would they notice if a storm was approaching and they needed to seek shelter?

Second, does your child have good judgement? Would they think clearly if they were faced with an unexpected problem, such as getting a flat bike tyre?

Third, is your child reliable? Do they follow instructions? Can they be trusted to return home at an agreed-upon time?

Agree on some rules

If you think your child is ready, it's important to set ground rules for when they're out. This might include your child agreeing to stay within a particular area, being home by a certain time, and communicating if they are going to be late. You might also ask them to stay with their friends the entire time they're out.

Start closer to home

For many families, it helps to begin with an activity closer to home, such as walking to the park and back. As trust and confidence build for both of you, your child can then be allowed out longer and further away.

It's also good to have a plan with your child about what to do if something goes wrong, they want your help or they need to contact you.

While it can feel daunting initially, independent time with friends without parent supervision helps your child to grow, develop and thrive.

This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

World.title: Fire at Glenorchy tip started in mattresses being set alight, police say
World.content:
An overnight fire at a tip in Hobart's north is being treated as suspicious, Tasmania Police say.

The blaze at the Jackson Street Landfill and Recycling Centre, in Glenorchy, began on Friday night, with fire crews attending overnight.

Police said mattresses were set alight, with the fire then spreading to other waste.

This photo shows the fire well alight. (Supplied: Rachel Smith)

Nearby residents posted photos of the fire on social media, with a smoke alert issued for people in the affected area.

As of 8.30am on Saturday, the fire had been brought under control.

The site is also home to Australia's first tip shop, which has operated since 1993.

The fire could be seen from some distance. (Supplied: Ben Holton)

Anyone with information about the fire can contact police on 131 444.

Information can also be supplied anonymously to Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online at crimestopperstas.com.au.

World.title: Complaint over senior NT public servant who ran private NDIS provider
World.content:
A senior Northern Territory public servant responsible for child and family services in Central Australia spent nearly three years as the sole director of a private National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider in Alice Springs, and for 15 months also owned a 50 per cent stake in the business's parent company.

The Department of Children and Families plays a significant role in the NDIS system in the NT, with the most recent figures from 2024 showing more than 300 children in its care had active NDIS plans.

An ABC investigation has confirmed public servant Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families, and held shares in the business's parent company, Japhin The Teacher Pty Ltd, from December 2024 to February 2026.

Life Aspects is registered to provide a range of disability services, including assistance with independent living and support coordination, an area that involves arranging other providers for people with disability.

Kudzai Mutsunge was the sole director of Life Aspects for almost three years. (Supplied)

The ABC has seen no evidence that any child in the care of the department was a Life Aspects client.

The department has referred a complaint about a potential conflict of interest to an internal integrity process.

Ms Mutsunge wound up her directorship and shareholding in Life Aspects earlier this year, one week before an anonymous complaint was sent to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission in March.

A separate complaint went to the Department of Children and Families in August, from the Alice Springs-based Disability Advocacy Service (DAS).

On August 21, the department told the service it had referred the information "through the appropriate internal integrity processes" and was coordinating with the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) "where relevant". The outcome of that process, if any, is unknown.

In response to questions from the ABC, the department declined to say whether Ms Mutsunge had declared a potential conflict of interest or sought approval for outside work, saying it could not comment on individual employment or conduct matters.

Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families. (ABC News: James Elton)

The ABC understands Ms Mutsunge quit the department on September 11.

Ms Mutsunge said she did not "endorse or agree to the allegations or characterisations" put to her by the ABC about whether her roles presented a potential conflict of interest, and said she could not respond to further questions within the timeframe provided.

Under the NT public service code of conduct, employees must declare any perceived, potential or actual conflicts of interest in writing to their chief executive.

The department's acting chief executive Karen Broadfoot said it had "zero tolerance" for a failure to declare a conflict.

Ms Broadfoot said that where integrity matters involved the NDIS, the department would also coordinate with the Australian Federal Police when relevant.

The NDIA said it could not comment on ongoing investigations.

DAS chief executive Scott Richardson said government officials needed to be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts, to ensure they "don't have access to participant information that they could then benefit from, or family could benefit from".

DAS chief executive Scott Richardson says government officials should be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In a meeting in March, Ms Mutsunge reportedly told DAS staff that she was "operationally removed" from placement decisions, and denied any role in referring children to NDIS providers.

Do you know more about this? If you know more about this story, please contact the reporter James Elton on elton.james@abc.net.au, or jameseltonabc@protonmail.com

Department toughens conflict of interest rules

As well as written declarations, the public service code of conduct in force since 2022 requires employees to get written approval from their chief executive before taking paid work outside the service.

The department went further and endorsed its own conflict of interest policy on May 29, 2025, while Ms Mutsunge was still sole director of Life Aspects.

The policy required staff to consider their own interests and those of their family, identify any conflicts and report them. It made clear conflicts were common and not necessarily a problem, so long as they were declared and managed.

The Department of Children and Families has recently changed its conflict of interest policy. (ABC News: Will Green)

Then on June 12, 2026, three months after Ms Mutsunge had offloaded Life Aspects, the department policy was updated.

The updated version created a tougher rule, which is being phased in, that all staff must complete an annual declaration covering any business or financial interests, including any jobs outside of the department, and submit paperwork saying "nil" if they have none.

The updated policy also includes extra measures for "higher risk" staff, specifically identifying staff who could influence referrals to NDIS providers.

Mr Richardson said it was a "real concern" that the policy was tightened soon after his organisation raised the case with the department, and questioned if the new policy was a "rushed reaction" while investigations were still underway.

Life Aspects provided services for NDIS clients. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Ms Mutsunge held senior roles in the department before she quit.

In June 2024, a document published by the NT government said she was Director of Remote Families for the Central Australia region.

By March this year, she was using an email signature that described her as Director, Youth and Family Support for the same region.

The NT's Public Guardian and Trustee, which acts for adults under guardianship orders, told the ABC two of the people it represents had been clients of Life Aspects in the past.

The restructure and the business with no identifiable owner

ASIC documents reveal that Life Aspects was restructured over four days in late February and early March this year.

They show Ms Mutsunge set up two new companies and then signed away her directorships on the day each was registered.

She also transferred her stake in the parent company back to Japhin Nyengera, the man who owned the other 50 per cent of its shares, and who recorded the same Alice Springs address as her in ASIC filings.

The Life Aspects companies then passed to Freejoy Murukayi, a New South Wales man whose LinkedIn profile describes him as an electrical technician working for mining giant BHP.

He now holds the sole share in Life Aspects Investments, which owns Life Aspects, but ASIC documents show his shareholding is "non-beneficial", meaning he holds the business for someone else.

ASIC filings previously listed the new parent company's registered address as occupied by "The Trustee" at the same address Ms Mutsunge had used for Life Aspects, but the beneficial owner can no longer be identified from public records.

In March, Life Aspects listed a new place of business at an address on Todd Street, in the centre of Alice Springs.

When the ABC attended in September, the premises carried signage for a different NDIS provider. A director of that company said they had never heard of Life Aspects.

Life Aspects and Mr Murukayi did not respond to questions.

Internet domain records show Ms Mutsunge remains the registrant and technical contact for the Life Aspects website, using a private, non-government email address, at the time of publication.

Life Aspects is still listed as an active provider.

'Did not think disclosure was required'

On March 12, two disability advocates from DAS held a meeting with Ms Mutsunge to discuss the matter.

In a complaint sent to the department in August, obtained by the ABC, they set out what they say she told them.

"Ms Mutsunge confirmed she has not lodged a formal conflict of interest declaration regarding her interest in Life Aspects through any Departmental system," DAS advocate Lachlan Imhof wrote.

This address in Todd Street in Alice Springs is the current registered place of business listed for Life Aspects Pty Ltd, although an unrelated company is presently operating there. (ABC News: Will Green)

"She stated that because she felt she 'did not do anything' with the business and did not believe she personally benefited, she did not think disclosure was required.

"She said a verbal disclosure was made at some point to a former supervisor who has since left the department, which cannot currently be verified."

According to Mr Imhof, Ms Mutsunge said her husband was "heavily involved" in the operation of the business and that it had been "sold via Facebook" in August last year.

But company records show Ms Mutsunge remained the sole director of Life Aspects until March 2026 and held her beneficial shares in the parent company until late February.

According to Mr Imhof, she told the advocates that selecting providers and signing agreements sat with case managers and foster parents, not with her.

NT Public Guardian and Trustee Beth Walker said her office had no capability to check whether the directors or owners of NDIS providers were employed by government agencies, and that privacy legislation prevented other departments from releasing that information.

The ABC is continuing to examine cases of Northern Territory public servants holding interests in NDIS providers.

World.title: Could exposure to sharks reduce fear and boost conservation efforts?
World.content:
There are quite a few objects on Juliana Gleaves's desk at Adelaide University that provide a clue into her PhD studies.

These include a figurine of Quint, the grizzled fisherman from the 1975 classic move Jaws, who sets out to catch the shark but ends up sliding into its gaping mouth.

Juliana Gleaves is studying fear, perceptions and attitudes towards sharks. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

While Ms Gleaves said the movie sparked her fascination with sharks, she conceded it was not great for their public relations.

This is despite shark numbers plummeting globally by more than 70 per cent since the movie was first released.

Conservation psychology

Her study is centred on conservation psychology and the first stage of research has found that those with better knowledge of sharks have less fear and were more likely to support efforts to save them.

Robert Shaw played the role of shark hunter Quint in Jaws. (Supplied: IMDb)

Her research is ongoing, and will include looking at how movies and media reporting shape people's view of sharks.

Then virtual reality will see if an immersive indirect experience, giving people a chance to "swim" with sharks as they behave neutrally could help encourage more positive views of sharks and a public with more concern for their conservation.

Following Australia's fifth fatal shark attack for 2026 in Perth last month, the Western Australian fisheries minister ruled out a widespread cull, saying it would not be appropriate. However, she did issue a "catch and kill" order for the shark responsible. In 2025, there were five fatal attacks, with 23 shark bite incidents in total.

Realistic risk

Surfers Duncan Chamberlain and Mal Biscoe were not surprised that people who regularly used the ocean tended to be more realistic about the risk of shark attack.

At 74, Mr Chamberlain has been surfing for 54 years, heading out into the Southern Ocean from his hometown beach at Middleton, south of Adelaide, three or four times a week

Duncan Chamberlain at Middleton Point, south of Adelaide. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Whenever he encounters sharks while out surfing, he enacts a 20-minute rule.

"You go in [to shore] for 20 minutes and you presume they're cruising along the coast, so they've moved on by then, so you go back out," Mr Chamberlain said.

" If you look at the statistics, you're in far more danger driving to the beach on the roads. "

Risk and reward

Ms Greaves's initial study found that surfers were more likely to be concerned about sunburn than sharks.

Mal Biscoe, who has been surfing for more than 30 years and runs his own surf school, agreed with that finding.

Mal Biscoe at Middleton Beach on the Fleurieu Peninsula. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

As a firefighter who had just returned from fighting Canadian forest fires, assessing risk was something he did naturally.

For him there was no comparison between the risk of a shark encounter and the reward of surfing, and the physical and mental health benefits.

He estimated he had had about eight encounters with sharks over the years, either swimming under or around him or appearing off in the distance.

In the closest encounter, he said a harmless wobbegong shark had climbed onto the back of his mate while they were surfing.

" We had a laugh about it and then we're like, 'I wonder what scared it out of the water?' But I've never had an incident where I feel threatened. "

Mr Biscoe said while some students did mention sharks when they came for lessons, he told them they were much more likely to step on a ray or that surfers were more likely to be injured by their own board than a shark.

While he was not sure that surfers might be more concerned with shark conservation over other species they encountered, he said he believed they were generally environmentally aware.

"I think surfers and people that live along the ocean are more concerned just about the natural environment itself, whether it be sharks or dolphins, whales or rays or just fish life," he said.
