World.title: Everyone loves to hate the Roosters. But we shouldn’t. Their fans have suffered too
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion Everyone loves to hate the Roosters. But we shouldn’t. Their fans have suffered too Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist October 3, 2026 — 9:30am

October 3, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

My favourite memory of the 2026 NRL season is the night I went to a Roosters home game in order to discover that their fans are human, too. It’s a difficult case to make this week, when approximately 110 per cent of the rugby league world is wishing for another Newcastle miracle. The Roosters are the appropriate villains, and will embrace being cast as the black princes of this fairytale. Loading The evidence against the Roosters’ humanity is old and basic: too much money and influence – the same reasons Manly and the Broncos have been rugby league’s most hated clubs. Of course you hate the rich and entitled – that’s the world, and that’s rugby league. Nick Politis’ billions have helped make the club what it is, but it’s not just the money.



There’s the shiny new home for the club supported by all those Scots College and Cranbrook boys, courtesy of the NSW taxpayer. There is the self-arrogating of the name “Sydney”. There is the cosy relationship with Fox Sports, whereby Roosters ease from the field to the commentary booth and studio, a promise of post-career employment that falls outside that mythical guardrail, the salary cap. Newcastle’s Francis Manuleleua and the Roosters’ Naufahu Whyte share a laugh during the week. Pleasantries will be set aside on Sunday night. Oscar Colman There is the barely sufferable coach Trent Robinson, a well-meaning would-be deep thinker who brings to mind the poet John Tranter’s priceless line about the scuba diver who keeps adding weights to his belt but can’t help floating back to the surface. The almost universal belief that the Roosters rort the salary cap is tempered by the possibility that they do not. Let’s just agree that they have made the cap work for them.



When the entitled get their own way by legal means, it feels even worse for those on the outside of the magic circle. It means the rules favour those clever and industrious enough to put their financial head-start to good use. There doesn’t need to be any corruption, and this masthead does not suggest there is. Loading None of this is new. But how to come to terms with it? How to still enjoy rugby league without boycotting Roosters matches? Is it worth placing money on the Roosters for the grand final, as an emotional hedge, so you can have sort of a win either way? V’landys might agree: there’s always another good reason to have a flutter.



The answer for me was to confront it. I have many close friends who support the Roosters, and I love them all. If you were a league-loving kid in the 1970s, and you picked your team based on their exposure, you chose Manly, Easts, St George or Souths, who won every title between 1970 and 1979 (today’s cartel is nothing new). Daly Cherry-Evans, James Tedesco and Sam Walker and Dominic Young (right) will all have a say on the decider. Oscar Colman I went with two of those friends to see the Roosters play Parramatta in round 19. I felt that this was going to be their year. They didn’t. Before the game, we discussed pertinent rugby league matters, and as usual were sucked into the past. What struck me was how nostalgic my friends were for the 1980s and 1990s, when Easts were often dismal. Many of their favourite players were from those years: Craig Salvatori, David Trewhella, Marty Gurr and, of course, the eternal Kevin Hastings.



My friends were still bruised by the mid-1990s, when they feared Easts would be lost to amalgamation. Success in rugby league is just an interruption to the permanence of suffering. During the Super League war, it was the big end of town, notably Politis and Kerry Packer, that stopped the club from jumping ship to the rebel league or merging, and set in train its rise to most-hated, or at least most-envied. The glue of rugby league is not only the memory of suffering but the weekly dose. We took our seats. There was a nice celebration for Daniel Tupou’s 300th game, but then Easts kept dropping the ball. Their attack was clunky. The groans of despair were very rugby league.



This will be forgotten if they win the grand final, but Roosters fans spent much of the season despairing over Daly Cherry-Evans and shouting in frustration at Siua Wong or Sam Walker or one of the Butcher brothers, gloomy about all those errors, another wasted year. Loading For much of that game, among the faithful, I felt like I was the only one thinking they didn’t need to worry. As Brisbane showed last year, you don’t have to be brilliant all season, just for three weeks in spring with a bit of luck going your way. Conversely, as Penrith discovered, you can be brilliant all year but lose it all in one catastrophic hour. The Roosters ground out a scrappy win, turning on enough power for 30 minutes to dispatch the injury-depleted Eels, gleaning another two points that kept them in the top four.



Throughout the match, I kept looking at this one man who was wearing a Roosters jersey. He must have been 85, maybe 90. He had pale, almost translucent hair and cheekbones that shone through his thin skin. He had come on his own, which was a pretty good effort in itself. James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga shape as game breakers on Sunday night. Oscar Colman No doubt Roosters regulars know the man. What kept drawing me to him was the complete bliss in his face. He was so glad to be alive, to be out on a Saturday night with his beloved team.



He had lived through those, at times, ordinary ’80s and ’90s, and other awful eras, too. I felt a great solidarity with him. His face expressed the truth of rugby league: fandom is all about suffering, punctuated by the briefest flashes of ecstasy. I’d have given him a hug – except for that damned jersey. I’m not sure if I’ve made the case, and if Sunday’s grand final goes the way the odds are predicting, most fans will have switched off before full-time. But for me, the experience was a reminder that success in rugby league is just an interruption to the permanence of suffering, and many Roosters fans, knowing they are expected to win, will just feel relief that their team hasn’t blown their bounty of good luck yet again. The Roosters’ suffering is a first-world problem, of course. If you want suffering, what about supporting the Dragons or the Tigers?



But those are just degrees of difference, not a fundamental break. Related Article NRL grand final Where does pressure really sit in this year’s grand final? Trent Robinson laughs and taps his temple Everyone suffers. Even followers of the Melbourne Storm, who have the least reasons for suffering, stew over their grievances. This exquisite pain, each year, lands finally on every club, except the one that is not eliminated. But even for that one (take Penrith), the joy is to be followed by future agonies. Why put yourself through it? I don’t know either. But every rugby league fan knows the feeling.

World.title: Man allegedly operated child abuse website from Redlands home
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Man allegedly operated child abuse website from Redlands home Julius Dennis October 3, 2026 — 9:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been charged with numerous child sex offences south-east of Brisbane, with police alleging he was the administrator of a website that hosted child exploitation material. Investigators from the Queensland police child exploitation taskforce, Argos, raided the 49-year-old Ormiston man’s home on Thursday and found several storage devices they allege had child abuse material on them. They will allege the man was active in several online networks dedicated to sharing the material. The Ormiston man was charged with 99 offences, including administering a child exploitation material website. Jessica Hromas He was charged with 99 offences, including possessing child abuse material, administering a child exploitation material website, and using a carriage service to distribute child abuse material.



He was remanded in custody by a Brisbane magistrate on Friday and will next appear in court on October 16. It comes as a Brisbane man who paid to watch children being sexually abused online in overseas live shows for years was jailed for almost two decades, police say. Kevin Raymond Doyle, 62, was also accused of travelling to the Philippines twice in a failed attempt to sexually abuse the children who featured in the livestreamed shows. He pleaded guilty to almost 100 offences related to child abuse after facilitating the sexual abuse of 25 children in the Philippines, including some with severe disabilities, police said. He spent $5000 over three years to livestream 28 child sexual abuse shows from the Philippines, according to the Australian Federal Police.



An investigation has to date led to the rescue of seven victims, aged five to 20. The AFP probe into Doyle, including his “prolific use” of live abuse, was launched after officers stopped him when he flew in to Brisbane from the Philippines in October 2019 and found child sexual abuse material on his phone. Kevin Raymond Doyle first came on the AFP’s radar in 2019 when he flew in to Brisbane. Glenn Hunt The probe related to offending involving live child abuse shows over video conferencing apps, the AFP said on Friday. “Consumers will typically direct the abuse, with victim children subjected to repeated, and increasingly degrading, sexual abuse over a prolonged period,” it said in a statement.



There was also evidence the man had been communicating directly with child victims and detailing the sexual offences he intended to commit on them, the AFP said. “He also travelled to the Philippines on two separate occasions with the intent to sexually abuse children he had observed being abused in the live shows. “However, he was unable to organise a meeting with those children after he arrived.” Information provided by the AFP led to the rescue of the seven victims and prosecution of three livestream facilitators by Filipino police. Police said inquiries to locate the remaining victims and facilitators was continuing.



Doyle was sentenced for 98 offences in Brisbane Supreme Court on Thursday. He received a 19-year jail term with a non-parole period of 12 years, the AFP said. - with AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Back once again, it’s the renegade (estate-grown fruit and vegetable) master
World.content:
Review Eating outPerth and Surrounds Back once again, it’s the renegade (estate-grown fruit and vegetable) master Max Veenhuyzen October 3, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 3 The Millbrook kitchen team from left to right, Bradley Beer, Ronald McCann, Figo Tsoi, Stephen Chen, Yui Okada, Byron Porter and Tamzin Bailey. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. 2 / 3 Estate Berkshire pork with charred cabbage. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. 3 / 3 Spanish mackerel with Lyonnaise fennel. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. Previous Slide Next Slide Good Food hat 15.5 / 20 How we score Millbrook Mediterranean$$$$ Millbrook is back, baby. Not Millbrook the West Australian wine label renowned for its estate-grown shiraz and viognier. And not Millbrook the tasting room that’s blessed with more stone, more timber and more photo ops of national forest and manmade lakes than your average Perth Hills cellar door.



But Millbrook the restaurant: an airy dining room perched atop said tasting room where guests can soak up all of the above. Not that Millbrook the restaurant had gone anywhere. It’s just that, the last time Good Food dropped by for a look-see, dishes such as buttery polenta and tomatoes accented with miso and sesame seeds felt (and tasted) very different to the restaurant’s established (farm)house style. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Or at least the Mediterranean, ingredient-first farmhouse style of cooking that chef Guy Jeffreys introduced to Millbrook when he came aboard in 2010. Head chef Stephen Chen. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. Crucially, his appointment also coincided with the establishment of a productive kitchen garden to supply Millbrook’s kitchen with the estate veg, fruits and herbs that helped define this cuisine.



That garden is still there, as is Jeffreys, although his title is now “Millbrook ambassador” rather than “chef”. Since July, the latter has belonged to Stephen Chow: a Southern Chinese-born cook that comes to Millbrook via Balthazar, Wildflower, Nieuw Ruin and other notable kitchens. Chow doesn’t just bring an impressive resume to his role: he also has the self-awareness to realise his job is to use technique to showcase ingredients and not the other way around. This is good news. Good news for tips of frilly broad bean leaves and gauzy white flowers that get cloaked in a sheer batter and fried tempura-style. Teamed with a garlicky aioli, these



crunchy fritters taste like God’s (gluten-free, vegetarian) gift to beer drinkers. Good news for what I’m calling “fennel regrowth”: tiny menorah-shaped spears that shoot out from older fennels that have started going to seed. You won’t find fennel regrowth at the shops or in cookbooks, but they seem to respond well to being slowly poached in an anise-licked stock made from fennel scraps. And, finally, Chow’s arrival is good news for eaters that get excited by tasting carefully handled fruit and vegetables as well as ingredients at life stages – young, old, in-between like that fennel regrowth – that were hitherto only accessible to gardeners. Assiette of garden vegetables with macadamia cream. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. But if Millbrook sounds a little too Close Encounters of the Third Veggie Kind for you, fret not.



Globe artichoke hearts are preserved the traditional way and feature in a poppy arrangement of spring vegetables. The taste of grilled red-veined chard could be aptly described as pure green. Those currently shredding for summer will be delighted to read that a summery salad Nicoise is part of the kitchen’s repertoire. If it’s been a while since you’ve climbed the stairs to Millbrook’s first-floor restaurant, the kitchen has discovered new ways to celebrate the property’s home-court advantage. This time last year was when team Millbrook, having jumped through the appropriate hoops, got the green light to cook with estate-laid chicken, duck and goose eggs. It was also around then when Millbrook started serving its own Berkshire pigs: a breed prized for its exceptional fattiness. If the kitchen has some estate pork at hand – it’s harder than ever, sadly, for small farmers to get their animals processed – you might find it showcased via slices of roasted loin that are milky of flesh and crunchy of crackling like the finest expressions of Hong Kong-style roast pork. Otherwise, piggy offcuts get slowly simmered with spice before being added to crème fraiche. The result is the warming, rillettes-style glory known as cretons in Montreal.



Served with slow-cooked lentils, these cretons – along with the salad nicoise, broad bean tips and sourdough bread – were part of the kitchen’s choice entree spread. The kitchen’s choice is act one of the $80 two-course menu (the minimum that adults need to put up to dine here) that concludes with a choice of five mains that might include the aforementioned pork loin or unexpectedly juicy Spanish mackerel whose dense meatiness has been tamed by careful roasting. While most eaters probably won’t need dessert, I am duty-bound to inform you that the $22 you’ll fork out for the crème caramel might be the best money you’ll spend all year on a dessert. Crème caramel with linseed tuile. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. Luscious and custardy and flecked with visible vanilla seeds, it’s a rousing reminder that strong foundations are important.



But now, the kicker. Following Millbrook’s return to form, it’s likely that most of the dishes – if not all of them – won’t be available when you dine there. Or at least exactly as described here. Maybe a different item from the larder of preserves, pickles and ferments will be called off the bench. Perhaps gardener Aaron Rampling will have finished picking the last bunch of one vegetable and moved onto another. According to Chen, dishes are in a constant state of flux and often change (and improve) as the working week progresses from day one on Thursday to the popular No-Waste Monday. For those that believe in the consistency of rigid, Michelin-esque dining, this fluidity may rankle. But for those that love the idea of a kitchen constantly sticking and moving and changing up its combinations, welcome (back) to your new happy place. The low-down Atmosphere: One of Australia’s great farm-to-table cellar door lunches is back! Go-to dishes: tempura broad bean leaves with aioli, estate Berkshire pork with charred cabbage, crème caramel with linseed tuile. Drinks: snappy, nicely priced estate wines from Millbrook supplemented by other

wines from the same family plus seasonal kombuchas and sodas Cost: Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: Rack and ruin: Australian fashion is going through its own spring cleaning
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Caitlin Stewart has been a personal stylist for more than 20 years. Most of her clientele are professional women looking to fill their wardrobe with versatile, polished pieces that work just as well in a boardroom meeting as they do on the weekend with a pair of slick jeans. Lately, she’s been hearing many of them say the same thing: “I used to know exactly where to shop, but now I don’t know where to go.” “There is a significant group of established professional women who feel caught between very youthful fashion, activewear, generic casual clothing and expensive designer labels,” says Stewart. “To me, this is a real gap.” Shoppers have never had better access to a diverse universe of options across which to spread their attention and their dollars. At any hour of the day, from bed, on the train, or at work, we are buying things from all around the world. Even as the nation buys $11.6 billion of fashion and apparel online, according to Australia Post’s latest e-commerce report, stiff competition has delivered a changing of the guard in our shopping strips as stalwarts pull up stumps, leaving many shoppers adrift. Cue and Veronika Maine’s descent into administration and receivership last month signalled that two titans of corporate womenswear had passed their heyday, joining a burgeoning list of well-known fashion retailers or brands that no longer exist in their original form. The Cue store at the Queen Victoria Building in Sydney. Oscar Colman





Is the middle market really dead? It’s a common refrain in the retail industry to hear “the middle market is dead”, but some industry experts don’t think this take is nuanced enough. Holding up mid-market fashion are major chains Zara, Cotton On, Kmart and Uniqlo, which has become a wardrobe staple for its high-quality but affordable minimalist everyday essentials. “The generic middle is in trouble,” says Stewart. “It has become a much harder place to be undifferentiated,” says fashion consultant and strategist Elizabeth Formosa. The evolution of Australia’s fashion industry isn’t about old versus new brands, she argues; it’s about brands that have and haven’t kept up. Formosa points to Zimmermann and Scanlan Theodore as examples of brands that have been around for decades and are still building a global reputation. Fashion businesses, inherently transient and linked to trends, can be remarkably adept at projecting an image of success while masking a very different reality. “Revenue, visibility and desirability don’t necessarily equal a healthy business. You still need the fundamentals underneath it – margin, inventory productivity, cash flow, channel profitability, disciplined buying, effective marketing investment and a clear strategy for profitable growth,” Formosa says.



Operating costs (fuel and transport, electricity, wages, manufacturing) have soared. Retailers, old and new, tied to expensive store leases – 134-year-old shoe brand Betts and luxury activewear brand Stax among them – can find those overheads to be a noose around their necks. Betts’ administrators announced in July it would close 20 of its remaining 35 stores. Janie Barrett “With leasing costs, you’re committed for a period of time. It’s not easy just to turn off that fixed-cost element of retail, particularly when you’ve opened a lot of stores,” says KPMG restructuring and insolvency leader Gayle Dickerson. And having a brilliant designer at the helm doesn’t necessarily translate to a commercially sound business. “You’ve got to be really, really tight on discipline and spend controls and have that capability. And I think that’s harder in some of those smaller fashion businesses,” Dickerson says. “I do generally think that it is really important that you have someone there to challenge the amazing creative-led founder who wants to do all these at once.” Owning the brand While mounting overheads create the financial pressure, says Stewart, it’s losing sight of your customer that can force a business to buckle. There is a line from a university lecturer from Stewart’s time studying styling in Milan that has stuck with her: fashion comes from the streets and from the people.



“The brands that connect with customers pay attention to how people actually want to dress, and listen to their customers while staying true to their own point of view,” she says. Related Article Exclusive

Retail Designers ditch David Jones: Is Myer winning the department store war? “The Australian woman hasn’t lost interest in fashion. She has become less loyal to brands that no longer understand her, and she now has far more places to go when they don’t.” Department stores around the globe are being forced to rethink their business models, while facing greater pressure to reinvest in the store and customer experience. David Jones and Myer, both unprofitable businesses, have each reduced store footprints over the years and are fighting over the best brands to bring customers through the door. The financial struggles of once-prevalent youth streetwear retailers General Pants and Glue Store have been existential. General Pants’ losses are in the tens of millions, and it is relying on cash injections to stay afloat, while Glue, which permanently closed its stores and online operation in June, is plotting a comeback under new ownership. “Multi-brand retailers in the middle are absolutely copping it from both sides,” says retail consultant Trent Rigby. “The only way to win is to own your brands.” Marcs, David Lawrence and Sass & Bide are among some labels Myer has collected but struggled to turn around, shutting dozens of underperforming stores at recently acquired mid-range labels Portmans and Jacqui E, where sales are rapidly declining.

World.title: How a friend’s encounter with a charming killer became Doctor Who guru Steven Moffat’s debut play
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows How a friend’s encounter with a charming killer became Doctor Who guru Steven Moffat’s debut play Michael Idato October 3, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Like all very clever ideas, the origin story of Steven Moffat’s new play, The Unfriend, is almost absurdly simple. It started on a holiday cruise. You know the type: a picture postcard journey, drifting through islands, sunsets and dinner buffets. Everyone is there to socialise, but do you really take a cruise to make friends? On just such a cruise, a couple – friends of Moffat and his wife, producer Sue Vertue – encountered a “charismatic and charming American lady, who seemed to be friends with everyone on board,” Moffat says. “They reluctantly exchanged email addresses, as we Brits always do, and she [subsequently] invited herself to stay.” Three of the stars of Sydney Theatre Company’s The Unfriend (from left to right) actors Alex Lee, Helen Thomson, and Huw Higginson. Oscar Colman At the very last minute, the couple Googled her unusual name and discovered she was a murderess, whose crimes had drawn headlines long before she’d embarked on her European holiday. To protect her anonymity, and the cruising couple’s safety, we will spare you the garish details of what actually transpired. “She was on the loose and making friends with people,” Moffat says. In real life, they emailed her, made their excuses, and the holidaymaker murderess was never heard from again. But when the story was related to Moffat, he said: “Oh please, can I have that, and can I just change one thing? Can she arrive before you managed to send the email?”



The Unfriend is Moffat’s first play and is now showing at Roslyn Packer Theatre for the Sydney Theatre Company. It seems almost strange Moffat had not written for the stage before, but writing for television kept him busy: Press Gang, Coupling, Sherlock, Dracula and Doctor Who are among his long list of credits. Steven Moffat at an event in London last month. Getty Images for National Youth Theatre To ice the cake, the play turned into a hit of its own. It has been mounted in London’s West End, in the United States – heaven help us all if the holidaymaker murderer ever sees it – and across Europe. There have also been more than 75 amateur productions in the UK, turning it into something of a vacationing parlour cousin to Agatha Christie’s The Spider’s Web, or Thornton Wilder’s Our Town. Elsa – the murderess of our story – is a formidable creature. In that sense, she’s akin to Beverly Moss, the status-obsessed dinner party hostess of Abigail’s Party. She’s not as detached as Mrs Danvers in Rebecca, nor as wretched as Madame Thénardier in Les Misérables, but the more you stare at her, you realise she’s cut from the same hideous (also: fabulous) cloth. “She’s a really awful person, she kills people, but, you can’t write someone that way,” Moffat says. “It’s that horrifying thing, the worst person you know is right sometimes, and Elsa is right sometimes. Her final monologue is relatively persuasive, you know ... edit humanity a little bit, who says you can’t kill the occasional person?



“You can’t write as a judgment,” Moffat adds. “You can’t decide this is an awful person; therefore they will only say awful things and be wrong all the time. That is what all liberals like me want to do; we always want to make the people who don’t agree with us evil all the time, [and] well, that’s just not true. Everybody’s right sometimes.” Helen Thomson (right) with Tim Walter rehearsing the play for STC. Daniel Boud In that sense, it’s easy to overlay a modern-day context to The Unfriend and go searching for hints of the modern political divide: meeting a new neighbour, workmate or, indeed, a woman on a cruise, and discovering she wears different political colours and the friendship is instantly poisoned. Where do we all go from there? The decade has changed, Moffat agrees, but the question is the same. “Go away, transplant yourself back in time and tell me what the lovely decade was,” he says. “What are you missing? Was it the Cold War, was that a breeze? How about World War II? Was everybody really placid about Ronald Reagan or Margaret Thatcher? No, they weren’t. They say it’s uniquely divisive now, I just don’t know when it wasn’t.” Alex Lee in full flight during rehearsals for the show. Daniel Boud



The difference, he thinks, is survival. “We’ve survived the past; therefore we think it’s all tame and nice. We haven’t survived the present yet.” Since its creation in 2020, the script has had to deal with tense changes – Donald Trump’s presidency, for example, went from present tense to past and then back again to present. And in the US production, which was staged in Florida, he was excised entirely. “Because, they said, whichever side of that divide you’re on, no one’s finding it funny,” Moffat recalls. Higginson, Thomson and Lee during a break in the rehearsals. Oscar Colman Having added playwright to an already long bow, it is also true that Moffat may never quite escape his own filmography. His iconic children’s series Press Gang is remembered – alongside Grange Hill, The Kids of Degrassi Street and Degrassi Junior High – for ambitious storytelling and sharp social commentary. So, where’s this generation’s Press Gang? The answer, he says, is complicated. There’s funding. And there’s also the fact that kids watch grown-up TV anyway. And then there’s the extent to which “young people, even my kids who are in their 20s, [are] actually that bothered about television. It’s not necessarily their first choice for entertainment.



Huw Higginson in rehearsals. Daniel Boud “We can’t expect the present day to be exactly the same as our childhood, any more than our childhood exactly resembled the childhood one generation before,” he says, adding: “If I’m to be traitorous to my own medium, I would say the best thing of all would be to read more. Where’s the new Harry Potter? To be very good at reading and to get joy out of reading is a massive skill.” And then there’s Doctor Who, a series beloved of him as a child and which, extraordinarily, he steered as showrunner between 2010 and 2017. The series was acquired by Disney in a $US220 million ($316 million) deal in 2022. But it has not been renewed and its future is uncertain. Ncuti Gatwa was the 15th and most recent Doctor - however the show is in a kind of hiatus after being sold to Disney. Moffat’s hot take on its future? “I assume there will be one,” he says. “I very much hope there is. It is, as I keep pointing out, a very, very old show. So it’s rather important that it’s always made out of new stuff, you know. You might say this thing is ancient, but it’s a new Doctor, it’s a new companion, it’s a new showrunner, it’s a new approach.



“That gives it a particular strength,” he adds. “It’s a great format. You have to be careful with it, and I’ve said that as well. You cannot bend it to your will. I am very fond of saying, the format of Doctor Who is cleverer than you are. So you do as you’re told.” The same goes for Sherlock Holmes and James Bond, Moffat adds. “Just do as you’re told. If you think you’re going to fix it, you are going to get your arse handed to you. You can’t. You can’t make it what it isn’t.” The Unfriend plays at Roslyn Packer Theatre for Sydney Theatre Company until October 31. World.title: Everyone loves to hate the Roosters. But we shouldn’t. Their fans have suffered too
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion Everyone loves to hate the Roosters. But we shouldn’t. Their fans have suffered too Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist October 3, 2026 — 9:30am

October 3, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

My favourite memory of the 2026 NRL season is the night I went to a Roosters home game in order to discover that their fans are human, too. It’s a difficult case to make this week, when approximately 110 per cent of the rugby league world is wishing for another Newcastle miracle. The Roosters are the appropriate villains, and will embrace being cast as the black princes of this fairytale. Loading The evidence against the Roosters’ humanity is old and basic: too much money and influence – the same reasons Manly and the Broncos have been rugby league’s most hated clubs. Of course you hate the rich and entitled – that’s the world, and that’s rugby league. Nick Politis’ billions have helped make the club what it is, but it’s not just the money.



There’s the shiny new home for the club supported by all those Scots College and Cranbrook boys, courtesy of the NSW taxpayer. There is the self-arrogating of the name “Sydney”. There is the cosy relationship with Fox Sports, whereby Roosters ease from the field to the commentary booth and studio, a promise of post-career employment that falls outside that mythical guardrail, the salary cap. Newcastle’s Francis Manuleleua and the Roosters’ Naufahu Whyte share a laugh during the week. Pleasantries will be set aside on Sunday night. Oscar Colman There is the barely sufferable coach Trent Robinson, a well-meaning would-be deep thinker who brings to mind the poet John Tranter’s priceless line about the scuba diver who keeps adding weights to his belt but can’t help floating back to the surface. The almost universal belief that the Roosters rort the salary cap is tempered by the possibility that they do not. Let’s just agree that they have made the cap work for them.



When the entitled get their own way by legal means, it feels even worse for those on the outside of the magic circle. It means the rules favour those clever and industrious enough to put their financial head-start to good use. There doesn’t need to be any corruption, and this masthead does not suggest there is. Loading None of this is new. But how to come to terms with it? How to still enjoy rugby league without boycotting Roosters matches? Is it worth placing money on the Roosters for the grand final, as an emotional hedge, so you can have sort of a win either way? V’landys might agree: there’s always another good reason to have a flutter.



The answer for me was to confront it. I have many close friends who support the Roosters, and I love them all. If you were a league-loving kid in the 1970s, and you picked your team based on their exposure, you chose Manly, Easts, St George or Souths, who won every title between 1970 and 1979 (today’s cartel is nothing new). Daly Cherry-Evans, James Tedesco and Sam Walker and Dominic Young (right) will all have a say on the decider. Oscar Colman I went with two of those friends to see the Roosters play Parramatta in round 19. I felt that this was going to be their year. They didn’t. Before the game, we discussed pertinent rugby league matters, and as usual were sucked into the past. What struck me was how nostalgic my friends were for the 1980s and 1990s, when Easts were often dismal. Many of their favourite players were from those years: Craig Salvatori, David Trewhella, Marty Gurr and, of course, the eternal Kevin Hastings.



My friends were still bruised by the mid-1990s, when they feared Easts would be lost to amalgamation. Success in rugby league is just an interruption to the permanence of suffering. During the Super League war, it was the big end of town, notably Politis and Kerry Packer, that stopped the club from jumping ship to the rebel league or merging, and set in train its rise to most-hated, or at least most-envied. The glue of rugby league is not only the memory of suffering but the weekly dose. We took our seats. There was a nice celebration for Daniel Tupou’s 300th game, but then Easts kept dropping the ball. Their attack was clunky. The groans of despair were very rugby league.



This will be forgotten if they win the grand final, but Roosters fans spent much of the season despairing over Daly Cherry-Evans and shouting in frustration at Siua Wong or Sam Walker or one of the Butcher brothers, gloomy about all those errors, another wasted year. Loading For much of that game, among the faithful, I felt like I was the only one thinking they didn’t need to worry. As Brisbane showed last year, you don’t have to be brilliant all season, just for three weeks in spring with a bit of luck going your way. Conversely, as Penrith discovered, you can be brilliant all year but lose it all in one catastrophic hour. The Roosters ground out a scrappy win, turning on enough power for 30 minutes to dispatch the injury-depleted Eels, gleaning another two points that kept them in the top four.



Throughout the match, I kept looking at this one man who was wearing a Roosters jersey. He must have been 85, maybe 90. He had pale, almost translucent hair and cheekbones that shone through his thin skin. He had come on his own, which was a pretty good effort in itself. James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga shape as game breakers on Sunday night. Oscar Colman No doubt Roosters regulars know the man. What kept drawing me to him was the complete bliss in his face. He was so glad to be alive, to be out on a Saturday night with his beloved team.



He had lived through those, at times, ordinary ’80s and ’90s, and other awful eras, too. I felt a great solidarity with him. His face expressed the truth of rugby league: fandom is all about suffering, punctuated by the briefest flashes of ecstasy. I’d have given him a hug – except for that damned jersey. I’m not sure if I’ve made the case, and if Sunday’s grand final goes the way the odds are predicting, most fans will have switched off before full-time. But for me, the experience was a reminder that success in rugby league is just an interruption to the permanence of suffering, and many Roosters fans, knowing they are expected to win, will just feel relief that their team hasn’t blown their bounty of good luck yet again. The Roosters’ suffering is a first-world problem, of course. If you want suffering, what about supporting the Dragons or the Tigers?



But those are just degrees of difference, not a fundamental break. Related Article NRL grand final Where does pressure really sit in this year’s grand final? Trent Robinson laughs and taps his temple Everyone suffers. Even followers of the Melbourne Storm, who have the least reasons for suffering, stew over their grievances. This exquisite pain, each year, lands finally on every club, except the one that is not eliminated. But even for that one (take Penrith), the joy is to be followed by future agonies. Why put yourself through it? I don’t know either. But every rugby league fan knows the feeling.

World.title: Man allegedly operated child abuse website from Redlands home
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Man allegedly operated child abuse website from Redlands home Julius Dennis October 3, 2026 — 9:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been charged with numerous child sex offences south-east of Brisbane, with police alleging he was the administrator of a website that hosted child exploitation material. Investigators from the Queensland police child exploitation taskforce, Argos, raided the 49-year-old Ormiston man’s home on Thursday and found several storage devices they allege had child abuse material on them. They will allege the man was active in several online networks dedicated to sharing the material. The Ormiston man was charged with 99 offences, including administering a child exploitation material website. Jessica Hromas He was charged with 99 offences, including possessing child abuse material, administering a child exploitation material website, and using a carriage service to distribute child abuse material.



He was remanded in custody by a Brisbane magistrate on Friday and will next appear in court on October 16. It comes as a Brisbane man who paid to watch children being sexually abused online in overseas live shows for years was jailed for almost two decades, police say. Kevin Raymond Doyle, 62, was also accused of travelling to the Philippines twice in a failed attempt to sexually abuse the children who featured in the livestreamed shows. He pleaded guilty to almost 100 offences related to child abuse after facilitating the sexual abuse of 25 children in the Philippines, including some with severe disabilities, police said. He spent $5000 over three years to livestream 28 child sexual abuse shows from the Philippines, according to the Australian Federal Police.



An investigation has to date led to the rescue of seven victims, aged five to 20. The AFP probe into Doyle, including his “prolific use” of live abuse, was launched after officers stopped him when he flew in to Brisbane from the Philippines in October 2019 and found child sexual abuse material on his phone. Kevin Raymond Doyle first came on the AFP’s radar in 2019 when he flew in to Brisbane. Glenn Hunt The probe related to offending involving live child abuse shows over video conferencing apps, the AFP said on Friday. “Consumers will typically direct the abuse, with victim children subjected to repeated, and increasingly degrading, sexual abuse over a prolonged period,” it said in a statement.



There was also evidence the man had been communicating directly with child victims and detailing the sexual offences he intended to commit on them, the AFP said. “He also travelled to the Philippines on two separate occasions with the intent to sexually abuse children he had observed being abused in the live shows. “However, he was unable to organise a meeting with those children after he arrived.” Information provided by the AFP led to the rescue of the seven victims and prosecution of three livestream facilitators by Filipino police. Police said inquiries to locate the remaining victims and facilitators was continuing.



Doyle was sentenced for 98 offences in Brisbane Supreme Court on Thursday. He received a 19-year jail term with a non-parole period of 12 years, the AFP said. - with AAP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Back once again, it’s the renegade (estate-grown fruit and vegetable) master
World.content:
Review Eating outPerth and Surrounds Back once again, it’s the renegade (estate-grown fruit and vegetable) master Max Veenhuyzen October 3, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 3 The Millbrook kitchen team from left to right, Bradley Beer, Ronald McCann, Figo Tsoi, Stephen Chen, Yui Okada, Byron Porter and Tamzin Bailey. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. 2 / 3 Estate Berkshire pork with charred cabbage. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. 3 / 3 Spanish mackerel with Lyonnaise fennel. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. Previous Slide Next Slide Good Food hat 15.5 / 20 How we score Millbrook Mediterranean$$$$ Millbrook is back, baby. Not Millbrook the West Australian wine label renowned for its estate-grown shiraz and viognier. And not Millbrook the tasting room that’s blessed with more stone, more timber and more photo ops of national forest and manmade lakes than your average Perth Hills cellar door.



But Millbrook the restaurant: an airy dining room perched atop said tasting room where guests can soak up all of the above. Not that Millbrook the restaurant had gone anywhere. It’s just that, the last time Good Food dropped by for a look-see, dishes such as buttery polenta and tomatoes accented with miso and sesame seeds felt (and tasted) very different to the restaurant’s established (farm)house style. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Or at least the Mediterranean, ingredient-first farmhouse style of cooking that chef Guy Jeffreys introduced to Millbrook when he came aboard in 2010. Head chef Stephen Chen. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. Crucially, his appointment also coincided with the establishment of a productive kitchen garden to supply Millbrook’s kitchen with the estate veg, fruits and herbs that helped define this cuisine.



That garden is still there, as is Jeffreys, although his title is now “Millbrook ambassador” rather than “chef”. Since July, the latter has belonged to Stephen Chow: a Southern Chinese-born cook that comes to Millbrook via Balthazar, Wildflower, Nieuw Ruin and other notable kitchens. Chow doesn’t just bring an impressive resume to his role: he also has the self-awareness to realise his job is to use technique to showcase ingredients and not the other way around. This is good news. Good news for tips of frilly broad bean leaves and gauzy white flowers that get cloaked in a sheer batter and fried tempura-style. Teamed with a garlicky aioli, these



crunchy fritters taste like God’s (gluten-free, vegetarian) gift to beer drinkers. Good news for what I’m calling “fennel regrowth”: tiny menorah-shaped spears that shoot out from older fennels that have started going to seed. You won’t find fennel regrowth at the shops or in cookbooks, but they seem to respond well to being slowly poached in an anise-licked stock made from fennel scraps. And, finally, Chow’s arrival is good news for eaters that get excited by tasting carefully handled fruit and vegetables as well as ingredients at life stages – young, old, in-between like that fennel regrowth – that were hitherto only accessible to gardeners. Assiette of garden vegetables with macadamia cream. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. But if Millbrook sounds a little too Close Encounters of the Third Veggie Kind for you, fret not.



Globe artichoke hearts are preserved the traditional way and feature in a poppy arrangement of spring vegetables. The taste of grilled red-veined chard could be aptly described as pure green. Those currently shredding for summer will be delighted to read that a summery salad Nicoise is part of the kitchen’s repertoire. If it’s been a while since you’ve climbed the stairs to Millbrook’s first-floor restaurant, the kitchen has discovered new ways to celebrate the property’s home-court advantage. This time last year was when team Millbrook, having jumped through the appropriate hoops, got the green light to cook with estate-laid chicken, duck and goose eggs. It was also around then when Millbrook started serving its own Berkshire pigs: a breed prized for its exceptional fattiness. If the kitchen has some estate pork at hand – it’s harder than ever, sadly, for small farmers to get their animals processed – you might find it showcased via slices of roasted loin that are milky of flesh and crunchy of crackling like the finest expressions of Hong Kong-style roast pork. Otherwise, piggy offcuts get slowly simmered with spice before being added to crème fraiche. The result is the warming, rillettes-style glory known as cretons in Montreal.



Served with slow-cooked lentils, these cretons – along with the salad nicoise, broad bean tips and sourdough bread – were part of the kitchen’s choice entree spread. The kitchen’s choice is act one of the $80 two-course menu (the minimum that adults need to put up to dine here) that concludes with a choice of five mains that might include the aforementioned pork loin or unexpectedly juicy Spanish mackerel whose dense meatiness has been tamed by careful roasting. While most eaters probably won’t need dessert, I am duty-bound to inform you that the $22 you’ll fork out for the crème caramel might be the best money you’ll spend all year on a dessert. Crème caramel with linseed tuile. Jessica Shaver for Good Food. Luscious and custardy and flecked with visible vanilla seeds, it’s a rousing reminder that strong foundations are important.



But now, the kicker. Following Millbrook’s return to form, it’s likely that most of the dishes – if not all of them – won’t be available when you dine there. Or at least exactly as described here. Maybe a different item from the larder of preserves, pickles and ferments will be called off the bench. Perhaps gardener Aaron Rampling will have finished picking the last bunch of one vegetable and moved onto another. According to Chen, dishes are in a constant state of flux and often change (and improve) as the working week progresses from day one on Thursday to the popular No-Waste Monday. For those that believe in the consistency of rigid, Michelin-esque dining, this fluidity may rankle. But for those that love the idea of a kitchen constantly sticking and moving and changing up its combinations, welcome (back) to your new happy place. The low-down Atmosphere: One of Australia’s great farm-to-table cellar door lunches is back! Go-to dishes: tempura broad bean leaves with aioli, estate Berkshire pork with charred cabbage, crème caramel with linseed tuile. Drinks: snappy, nicely priced estate wines from Millbrook supplemented by other

wines from the same family plus seasonal kombuchas and sodas Cost: Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: Rack and ruin: Australian fashion is going through its own spring cleaning
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Caitlin Stewart has been a personal stylist for more than 20 years. Most of her clientele are professional women looking to fill their wardrobe with versatile, polished pieces that work just as well in a boardroom meeting as they do on the weekend with a pair of slick jeans. Lately, she’s been hearing many of them say the same thing: “I used to know exactly where to shop, but now I don’t know where to go.” “There is a significant group of established professional women who feel caught between very youthful fashion, activewear, generic casual clothing and expensive designer labels,” says Stewart. “To me, this is a real gap.” Shoppers have never had better access to a diverse universe of options across which to spread their attention and their dollars. At any hour of the day, from bed, on the train, or at work, we are buying things from all around the world. Even as the nation buys $11.6 billion of fashion and apparel online, according to Australia Post’s latest e-commerce report, stiff competition has delivered a changing of the guard in our shopping strips as stalwarts pull up stumps, leaving many shoppers adrift. Cue and Veronika Maine’s descent into administration and receivership last month signalled that two titans of corporate womenswear had passed their heyday, joining a burgeoning list of well-known fashion retailers or brands that no longer exist in their original form. The Cue store at the Queen Victoria Building in Sydney. Oscar Colman





Is the middle market really dead? It’s a common refrain in the retail industry to hear “the middle market is dead”, but some industry experts don’t think this take is nuanced enough. Holding up mid-market fashion are major chains Zara, Cotton On, Kmart and Uniqlo, which has become a wardrobe staple for its high-quality but affordable minimalist everyday essentials. “The generic middle is in trouble,” says Stewart. “It has become a much harder place to be undifferentiated,” says fashion consultant and strategist Elizabeth Formosa. The evolution of Australia’s fashion industry isn’t about old versus new brands, she argues; it’s about brands that have and haven’t kept up. Formosa points to Zimmermann and Scanlan Theodore as examples of brands that have been around for decades and are still building a global reputation. Fashion businesses, inherently transient and linked to trends, can be remarkably adept at projecting an image of success while masking a very different reality. “Revenue, visibility and desirability don’t necessarily equal a healthy business. You still need the fundamentals underneath it – margin, inventory productivity, cash flow, channel profitability, disciplined buying, effective marketing investment and a clear strategy for profitable growth,” Formosa says.



Operating costs (fuel and transport, electricity, wages, manufacturing) have soared. Retailers, old and new, tied to expensive store leases – 134-year-old shoe brand Betts and luxury activewear brand Stax among them – can find those overheads to be a noose around their necks. Betts’ administrators announced in July it would close 20 of its remaining 35 stores. Janie Barrett “With leasing costs, you’re committed for a period of time. It’s not easy just to turn off that fixed-cost element of retail, particularly when you’ve opened a lot of stores,” says KPMG restructuring and insolvency leader Gayle Dickerson. And having a brilliant designer at the helm doesn’t necessarily translate to a commercially sound business. “You’ve got to be really, really tight on discipline and spend controls and have that capability. And I think that’s harder in some of those smaller fashion businesses,” Dickerson says. “I do generally think that it is really important that you have someone there to challenge the amazing creative-led founder who wants to do all these at once.” Owning the brand While mounting overheads create the financial pressure, says Stewart, it’s losing sight of your customer that can force a business to buckle. There is a line from a university lecturer from Stewart’s time studying styling in Milan that has stuck with her: fashion comes from the streets and from the people.



“The brands that connect with customers pay attention to how people actually want to dress, and listen to their customers while staying true to their own point of view,” she says. Related Article Exclusive

Retail Designers ditch David Jones: Is Myer winning the department store war? “The Australian woman hasn’t lost interest in fashion. She has become less loyal to brands that no longer understand her, and she now has far more places to go when they don’t.” Department stores around the globe are being forced to rethink their business models, while facing greater pressure to reinvest in the store and customer experience. David Jones and Myer, both unprofitable businesses, have each reduced store footprints over the years and are fighting over the best brands to bring customers through the door. The financial struggles of once-prevalent youth streetwear retailers General Pants and Glue Store have been existential. General Pants’ losses are in the tens of millions, and it is relying on cash injections to stay afloat, while Glue, which permanently closed its stores and online operation in June, is plotting a comeback under new ownership. “Multi-brand retailers in the middle are absolutely copping it from both sides,” says retail consultant Trent Rigby. “The only way to win is to own your brands.” Marcs, David Lawrence and Sass & Bide are among some labels Myer has collected but struggled to turn around, shutting dozens of underperforming stores at recently acquired mid-range labels Portmans and Jacqui E, where sales are rapidly declining.

World.title: How a friend’s encounter with a charming killer became Doctor Who guru Steven Moffat’s debut play
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows How a friend’s encounter with a charming killer became Doctor Who guru Steven Moffat’s debut play Michael Idato October 3, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Like all very clever ideas, the origin story of Steven Moffat’s new play, The Unfriend, is almost absurdly simple. It started on a holiday cruise. You know the type: a picture postcard journey, drifting through islands, sunsets and dinner buffets. Everyone is there to socialise, but do you really take a cruise to make friends? On just such a cruise, a couple – friends of Moffat and his wife, producer Sue Vertue – encountered a “charismatic and charming American lady, who seemed to be friends with everyone on board,” Moffat says. “They reluctantly exchanged email addresses, as we Brits always do, and she [subsequently] invited herself to stay.” Three of the stars of Sydney Theatre Company’s The Unfriend (from left to right) actors Alex Lee, Helen Thomson, and Huw Higginson. Oscar Colman At the very last minute, the couple Googled her unusual name and discovered she was a murderess, whose crimes had drawn headlines long before she’d embarked on her European holiday. To protect her anonymity, and the cruising couple’s safety, we will spare you the garish details of what actually transpired. “She was on the loose and making friends with people,” Moffat says. In real life, they emailed her, made their excuses, and the holidaymaker murderess was never heard from again. But when the story was related to Moffat, he said: “Oh please, can I have that, and can I just change one thing? Can she arrive before you managed to send the email?”



The Unfriend is Moffat’s first play and is now showing at Roslyn Packer Theatre for the Sydney Theatre Company. It seems almost strange Moffat had not written for the stage before, but writing for television kept him busy: Press Gang, Coupling, Sherlock, Dracula and Doctor Who are among his long list of credits. Steven Moffat at an event in London last month. Getty Images for National Youth Theatre To ice the cake, the play turned into a hit of its own. It has been mounted in London’s West End, in the United States – heaven help us all if the holidaymaker murderer ever sees it – and across Europe. There have also been more than 75 amateur productions in the UK, turning it into something of a vacationing parlour cousin to Agatha Christie’s The Spider’s Web, or Thornton Wilder’s Our Town. Elsa – the murderess of our story – is a formidable creature. In that sense, she’s akin to Beverly Moss, the status-obsessed dinner party hostess of Abigail’s Party. She’s not as detached as Mrs Danvers in Rebecca, nor as wretched as Madame Thénardier in Les Misérables, but the more you stare at her, you realise she’s cut from the same hideous (also: fabulous) cloth. “She’s a really awful person, she kills people, but, you can’t write someone that way,” Moffat says. “It’s that horrifying thing, the worst person you know is right sometimes, and Elsa is right sometimes. Her final monologue is relatively persuasive, you know ... edit humanity a little bit, who says you can’t kill the occasional person?



“You can’t write as a judgment,” Moffat adds. “You can’t decide this is an awful person; therefore they will only say awful things and be wrong all the time. That is what all liberals like me want to do; we always want to make the people who don’t agree with us evil all the time, [and] well, that’s just not true. Everybody’s right sometimes.” Helen Thomson (right) with Tim Walter rehearsing the play for STC. Daniel Boud In that sense, it’s easy to overlay a modern-day context to The Unfriend and go searching for hints of the modern political divide: meeting a new neighbour, workmate or, indeed, a woman on a cruise, and discovering she wears different political colours and the friendship is instantly poisoned. Where do we all go from there? The decade has changed, Moffat agrees, but the question is the same. “Go away, transplant yourself back in time and tell me what the lovely decade was,” he says. “What are you missing? Was it the Cold War, was that a breeze? How about World War II? Was everybody really placid about Ronald Reagan or Margaret Thatcher? No, they weren’t. They say it’s uniquely divisive now, I just don’t know when it wasn’t.” Alex Lee in full flight during rehearsals for the show. Daniel Boud



The difference, he thinks, is survival. “We’ve survived the past; therefore we think it’s all tame and nice. We haven’t survived the present yet.” Since its creation in 2020, the script has had to deal with tense changes – Donald Trump’s presidency, for example, went from present tense to past and then back again to present. And in the US production, which was staged in Florida, he was excised entirely. “Because, they said, whichever side of that divide you’re on, no one’s finding it funny,” Moffat recalls. Higginson, Thomson and Lee during a break in the rehearsals. Oscar Colman Having added playwright to an already long bow, it is also true that Moffat may never quite escape his own filmography. His iconic children’s series Press Gang is remembered – alongside Grange Hill, The Kids of Degrassi Street and Degrassi Junior High – for ambitious storytelling and sharp social commentary. So, where’s this generation’s Press Gang? The answer, he says, is complicated. There’s funding. And there’s also the fact that kids watch grown-up TV anyway. And then there’s the extent to which “young people, even my kids who are in their 20s, [are] actually that bothered about television. It’s not necessarily their first choice for entertainment.



Huw Higginson in rehearsals. Daniel Boud “We can’t expect the present day to be exactly the same as our childhood, any more than our childhood exactly resembled the childhood one generation before,” he says, adding: “If I’m to be traitorous to my own medium, I would say the best thing of all would be to read more. Where’s the new Harry Potter? To be very good at reading and to get joy out of reading is a massive skill.” And then there’s Doctor Who, a series beloved of him as a child and which, extraordinarily, he steered as showrunner between 2010 and 2017. The series was acquired by Disney in a $US220 million ($316 million) deal in 2022. But it has not been renewed and its future is uncertain. Ncuti Gatwa was the 15th and most recent Doctor - however the show is in a kind of hiatus after being sold to Disney. Moffat’s hot take on its future? “I assume there will be one,” he says. “I very much hope there is. It is, as I keep pointing out, a very, very old show. So it’s rather important that it’s always made out of new stuff, you know. You might say this thing is ancient, but it’s a new Doctor, it’s a new companion, it’s a new showrunner, it’s a new approach.



“That gives it a particular strength,” he adds. “It’s a great format. You have to be careful with it, and I’ve said that as well. You cannot bend it to your will. I am very fond of saying, the format of Doctor Who is cleverer than you are. So you do as you’re told.” The same goes for Sherlock Holmes and James Bond, Moffat adds. “Just do as you’re told. If you think you’re going to fix it, you are going to get your arse handed to you. You can’t. You can’t make it what it isn’t.” The Unfriend plays at Roslyn Packer Theatre for Sydney Theatre Company until October 31. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from books editor Jason Steger. Get it every Friday.

World.title: Flames and smoke billow from Masterton pub fire
World.content:
Fire broke out in Farriers Bar & Eatery, on SH2 in Masterton, on the morning of Saturday 3 October, 2026.

Firefighters have brought a large fire in a Masterton bar under control.

Former Masterton mayor, and current councillor, Gary Caffell posted about the fire at Farriers Bar & Eatery on social media just after 8am on Saturday, asking people to please stay clear of the area.

There were a number of fire trucks at the Trust House's Farriers complex, he said, "with flames and heavy black smoke billowing out of the roof area".

The complex is a distinctive landmark at the north end of the Wairarapa town.

FENZ received an automatic fire alarm triggered at the bar about 7:30am, a FENZ spokesperson said: "Further 111 calls reported a building fire. When firefighters arrived, the building was well involved and the response was subsequently increased to a third alarm," they said.

Flames coming out of the roof of Farriers Bar and Eatery on Saturday morning, while firefighters worked to put the fire out. Supplied/ Masterton Matters - Gary Caffell

Just before 9am, Fire and Emergency said at least ten crews were at or responding to the fire, including from nearby towns and two specialist appliances from Remutaka and Avalon fire stations, as well as resources from Wellington: "The fire is located on the first floor of the two-storey building, with aerial operations underway."

The blaze had been brought under control about 10am, they said in an update, and aerial firefighting had stopped: "Crews remain at the scene carrying out minor internal firefighting and salvage operations to protect unaffected areas of the building and its contents."

John Prendergast, chief executive of Trust House, which owns Farriers bar, told RNZ they had been lucky the response by firefighters was so quick.

"The fire service, luckily, were straight across the road. They're based straight across the road from us, so they got there quickly. But even with that, there's extensive damage to the building and we'll be out of it for quite some time, I expect," he said.

Damage to the roof of the building. Supplied/ Masterton Matters - Gary Caffell

Prendergast said they did not yet know what could have caused the fire, but FENZ investigators and police would be working at the site for the rest of the day.

"[The] fire started in the roof space at our Farriers Eatery and our head office.

World.title: Northern Marianas battered by Choi-wan as outages and flood threat grow
World.content:
Typhoon Choi-wan continued to disrupt life across the Northern Mariana Islands, bringing strong winds, intermittent power outages, dangerous seas, and the threat of flash flooding.

On Saipan, pedestrians were seen struggling to walk against powerful wind gusts, while some businesses remained closed because of the bad weather.

The island also experienced intermittent power outages, while neighbouring Tinian suffered an island-wide power outage on Friday.

The Northern Marianas College and Public School System remained closed Friday as hazardous weather continued.

Saipan Mayor's Office crews were, meanwhile, clearing sand and debris washed from beaches onto coastal roads by rough seas.

The Department of Public Works also reminded election candidates to remove campaign placards because they could become dangerous projectiles in the strong winds. Many of the signs are made from plywood.

One motorist said a wind-blown campaign placard nearly struck his vehicle.

The cone contains the probable path of Typhoon Choi-wan centre but not the size of the storm NOAA

The bad weather had already disrupted the Saipan Chamber of Commerce gubernatorial debate Thursday night, when electricity went out at the Gilbert C. Ada Gymnasium and forced organisers to postpone the second half of the event.

The outage came shortly after candidates had discussed the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation and the territory's continuing power problems.

Authorities have also placed Saipan, Tinian, and Rota under a flood watch through late Sunday night, warning that excessive rainfall could cause flash flooding in low-lying, poorly drained and urban areas.

Choi-wan's slow movement and strong monsoon flow to its south are expected to keep conditions wet into early next week.

Forecast rainfall during the watch period is five to eight inches for Saipan and Tinian and four to six inches for Rota and Guam.

Residents near streams and other flood-prone areas have been advised to remain alert and make sure nearby storm drains are clear.

Marine conditions also remain dangerous, with a small-craft advisory in place and large breaking waves expected along exposed reefs.

Saipan and Tinian are under a high surf advisory, coastal flood watch and high rip-current risk, with waves of 10 to 14 feet possible along north- and west-facing reefs.

Authorities warned that some coastal roads could be closed and low-lying homes, businesses, and infrastructure could be inundated.

Governor David Apatang has urged people to stay out of dangerous waters and advised residents of Saipan, Tinian and Rota to monitor forecasts and be prepared to act if flash flood warnings are issued.

Choi-wan was north of Saipan early Saturday with maximum sustained winds of about 80 miles per hour.
