World.title: Police cyber crime capabilities weak, official reports show
World.content:
Cyber crime is becoming the new front line for police, but official reports show they have weak capability to fight it.

This remains the case five years after the landmark cyber attack on Waikato Hospital, and as a new race is underway to prepare for cyber criminals getting their hands on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) within months.

RNZ can reveal a 2024 assessment by Australian Federal Police (AFP) of cyber crime capabilities here found many weaknesses and gaps.

"NZPol lacks the capability and capacity to undertake high-level cyber-dependant crime investigations," said the assessment, newly released under the Official Information Act (OIA).

This meant officers were quick to drop cyber investigations or to leave them to "technology enthusiasts amongst the ranks and those few with 'an interest' in technology", it said.

Two years on, the threats have worsened - yet an internal review in April 2026 said police still lacked the tools to tackle what many stakeholders called "the new front line" of crime.

Police told RNZ they have been developing initiatives and exploring what capabilities they need.

When RNZ asked for more details late last week, and an interview, police said this would be an OIA request that takes at least 20 working days to respond to. RNZ's original request in June took till late September to get a response.

'Police will not keep pace'

Police's cyber weaknesses extend way back to before the 2019 mosque terrorist attack, when they lacked proper IT systems for monitoring the internet for extremist talk or plots.

They called in the AFP in late 2023 to look particularly at investigations into cyber crime or that relied on cyber skills.

"Few crimes nowadays do not involve some prominent use of technology," the AFP inquiry said.

Official reports show police have weak capability to fight cyber crime. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Police did not make the report public, but RNZ came across reference to it in the April 2026 review: "The recent review of police's cybercrime capability by the Australian Federal Police highlighted gaps in structure, skills, and strategy.

"It found that police lacks a formal cybercrime strategy, clear performance indicators, and sufficient specialist capability to investigate high-level cyber-dependent crime."

The gaps persist today.

"Police will not keep pace with the volume of traditional crime and expanding digital and borderless crime with their current tools, systems, and data capabilities," the April report said.

Police as the primary agency for investigating and prosecuting cyber crime face a threat that has been ramping up very quickly and obviously.

"Historically you could avoid dangerous places, but online every user is exposed to risk," said April's performance review.

"New Zealanders are already more likely to suffer fraud or cybercrime than interpersonal violence - and this trend will continue to intensify."

A new threat has just emerged globally with experimental AI models breaking out of testbeds and hacking companies and governments on their own volition. This prompted computer legend Bill Gates to warn the threat of a bio-attack is very real now.

'Officers look for opportunities to terminate cybercrime matters'

The AFP inquiry report in 2024 said the public expected police to be skilled and knowledgeable in cyber crimes and "prepared to investigate such matters".

The reality it found was different.

They missed crimes: "The fractured nature of cybercrime reporting in NZ leaves the cybercrime team without knowledge of many incidents and potential referrals."

They dropped investigations: "Officers look for opportunities to terminate cybercrime matters when certain triggers are reached i.e. need for overseas enquiries, reduced chance of a result."

They got little training. "Cybercrime elements and general technology concepts are not incorporated into current internal training."

Australian Federal Police said the public expected police to be skilled and knowledgeable in cyber crimes. 123RF

'Very limited'

Overall, "recent exposure of NZPol to cyber-dependant crime investigations is very limited", the assessment concluded.

NZ police districts usually led cyber investigations but largely did not see it as a priority when they were focused on violent or other high-profile crimes. The 105 reporting system gave reports, even of cyber crime "against the national interest", a low priority.

The districts "falling behind" turned to rely on the high tech crime group (HTCG). Some of that group's support was effective but its expertise was "dispersed decentralised".

This was "not sustainable".

The AFP report referred to an existing cybercrime team, though one with no key performance measures or target for how it should be set up.

Yet it also stated, "NZPol should strongly consider the primary role of the cybercrime team to be the investigation of a range of cyber-dependant crimes.

"A local cybercrime team dedicated to cyber-dependant crime will need to be in place before any real gains can be made" on international capability.

Internationally, efforts were "ad hoc" and police contributions to investigations offshore were "limited".

Estimates were that over 70 percent of cybercrime targeting locals originated offshore and the cyber threat was not just personal but society-wide, the April 2026 report said.

"Police need to work closely with these networks to counter the growing threat of foreign interference, where unfriendly states use cybercrime and organised crime to pursue their goals.

"Other jurisdictions are adopting aggressive transnational prevention approaches, including disrupting cybercriminals 'on their own turf' through joint operations with foreign law enforcement. Police must follow this path."

2024 to today - 'An initial review... has been completed'

Five years ago, the ransomware attack on Waikato Hospital was widely seen as a lesson and a wakeup call.

Though that attack sparked a three-year, $75 million cyber security uplift programme in health, this did not extend to a cyber crime investigation uplift among police. And cyber is not an outlier. The April report found police investigation skills generally had been declining over time.

Five years ago, the ransomware attack on Waikato Hospital was widely seen as a lesson and a wakeup call. Supplied/ Waikato Hospital

But cyber crime threats are on their own fast track.

The National Cyber Security Centre recently warned cyber criminals would have access to advanced AI models with hacking superpowers by early next year.

The reports showed police repeatedly identifying the cyber gaps and suggesting fixes.

The AFP in 2024 made some obvious suggestions - plug the strategy, targets and training gaps - and some more novel ones, like put police bosses through a "specially designed masterclass" in cybercrime investigations, and put a cybercrime officer into Europol or the joint cybercrime centre in Sydney.

This year, a performance improvement plan that accompanied April's report said, "An initial review of police cybercrime and fraud capability has been completed to establish a baseline of current strengths and gaps."

Last month police told RNZ they had explored an integrated and phased approach to addressing demand for cyber investigations through development of a future-focused cybercrime operating framework. RNZ asked for the framework but has not received it.

"This work has focused on identifying the capabilities required to strengthen police's response to cyber-dependent and cyber-enabled offending."

Wellington police headquarters has now put the uplift work on a two-year track.

Initiatives mostly remain in the planning or start-up phase, or tied to a future capability plan or to a review of the investigations operating model. The overall police tech uplift programme has not been fully funded.

The current performance improvement plan included an increase in specialist training in cyber crime "supported by better technology tools and international partnerships". This was "under action", as was a new workforce strategy.

Police were poised in April to set up a 15-strong National Economic Crime Team to coordinate online fraud and digital harm investigations.

At the same time, they were still trying to make clear who was in charge when they worked with other justice, intelligence, defence, and regulatory agencies.

"Police recognises these challenges and has begun laying the foundations for change" said April's report.

World.title: Country Life: Lessons from the dry years as El Niño gathers force
World.content:
When the going gets tough during a drought, there's nothing like hopping in the side-by-side with some of your mates and getting their eye over the farm.

That's one of the tips offered by Wairarapa farmer Willie Falloon, who's had 30 years' experience farming sheep and beef on 1400 hectares at Gladstone during dry summers.

"I found that when it's been a prolonged drought, you actually get tired and probably make some fundamental mistakes," he told Country Life.

Audio player for " Lessons from the dry years as El Niño gathers force " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/country/1695067%2Fcountry-life-lessons-from-the-dry-years-as-el-nino-gathers-force

Lessons from the dry years as El Niño gathers force Country Life Download MP3 17m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Being in "the detail every day" during a stressful time can sometimes cloud decision-making, whereas if your neighbours come around the farm with you, they're likely to pick up on things you may have missed, he said.

Falloon was sharing his knowledge with other farmers, many of them the next generation on the land, at a Beef and Lamb NZ field day called Planning for Dry Success in late September.

With hailstones pelting down outside and a southerly blast sweeping up the country, drought couldn't be further from the minds of the beanie-and-wool clad farmers forced indoors for the event.

They were urged to make drought plans now, as forecasts point to an intense El Niño bringing dry and windy conditions to northern and eastern parts of New Zealand, including Wairarapa.

Heat spikes are also expected in eastern New Zealand, and the wind and lack of rain meant an increased risk of wildfires, according to forecasters.

Only the country's southwest is expecting increased rainfall because of El Niño.

Dry farm land in Wairarapa, east of Masterton. RNZ / Alexander Robertson

Falloon said over the decades he had learnt to build resilience and flexibility into his operation, and he was expecting El Niño to have the biggest impact through summer and into the autumn.

"We have an A to D lever system where we just keep pulling levers all the way through."

He said it was important to act early before drought makes decisions for you - don't just keep your plans in your head, write them down and even pin them to the wall.

"We also have 30 percent of our stock on our farms that are trading stock, so they are there as a flexibility to be able to get out of it any time we feel a grass pinch."

Another lever he pulls is around choice of feed crop for his stock. This year he's going with a kale-plantain mix rather than crops like chicory because of the larger seed, which he found was easier to germinate in low moisture.

Setting up sources of extra feed early is also advisable, Falloon said.

Bales donated from Wairarapa farmers to Hawkes Bay during 2020 drought RNZ/Sally Round

Good pricing and high lambing percentages at the moment were working in farmers' favour, Baker Ag farm consultant Hannah French told the audience.

She said pulling the trade stock lever is the earliest move for most farmers, ensuring feed is managed for capital stock, the base for future progeny.

"We've noticed a lot through our drought files that the people who deal with droughts the best are the ones that actually keep their capital stock numbers pretty consistent and the reason for that is because they can be profitable out the other end of a drought.

"[That] might be grazing off, it might be a bit of supplementary feeding.

"We're in really good pricing at the moment so we've had quite a few people thinking about exiting some R2 (rising 2-year-old) cattle early, whether that's a store trade or whether they're feeding a bit of supplement like pumpkin or baleage to bring the kill forward from say December, January into kind of that October, November sort of timing."

Wairarapa farmers gather to hear how to prepare for El Nino RNZ/Sally Round

Robert Hickman, who farms sheep and beef on the coast near Castlepoint, had already sold a quarter of his mature in-calf cows in preparation, as well as non-replacement ewes with lambs at foot.

"That's probably reduced our total carrying capacity by about 30 percent."

Normally he would be fattening lambs in the summer through to finishing by July.

"We've decided to forego quite a bit of that purely on the concern that we don't want to get stuck and be doing fire sales if it does go bad over summer."

Hickman said he was concerned he may have moved too early, but having farmed in drought in northern Australia, he had grown up understanding "the best drought decisions are early drought decisions".

That was echoed by Falloon.

"Don't put everything at risk and just make sure, if you're happy with [the price], don't be greedy. Just take the money and move on to the next thing."

Wildfire risk is expected to be high for northern and eastern parts of NZ RNZ/Sally Round

Having already weathered a series of damaging floods over the winter, Wairarapa farmers face another test.

They were urged to take care of themselves as well as their stock, making sure they had good nutrition, rest and social contact.

"Stock are resilient through droughts, but people often aren't," French said.

"If you've got someone who's usually pretty chirpy and they're starting to not get back to you or not be at as many things, just keeping in touch, that's really good."

And have that plan, farmers were told.
